s23d-s100101-s1.bodyHtml:
Overview

Infections of the gut and liver are tested on Step 1 through three lenses: the structure and replication strategy of the organism, the molecular action of its toxins, and the tissue response it provokes. Recognising the incubation period and the stool character (watery, bloody, fatty) narrows the differential before any test is ordered.

Hepatitis viruses

All five classic hepatitis viruses infect hepatocytes, but liver injury is largely immune mediated: cytotoxic T cells recognise viral peptides on MHC class I and kill infected cells, producing apoptotic (Councilman-type) bodies, lobular inflammation and portal lymphocytes. Chronic infection adds interface hepatitis and progressive fibrosis.

VirusFamily and genomeTransmissionChronic infectionExam hook
HAVPicornavirus; nonenveloped positive-sense ssRNAFecal-oral (food, water, shellfish, daycare)NeverIgM anti-HAV marks acute infection; vaccine-preventable
HBVHepadnavirus; enveloped, partially double-stranded circular DNA; replicates through reverse transcriptionBlood, sexual, perinatalMost infants infected at birth, few healthy adultscccDNA persists in the nucleus; integration can cause HCC without cirrhosis
HCVFlavivirus; enveloped positive-sense ssRNABlood (injection drug use, older transfusions)Most infected adultsHypervariable envelope regions explain the lack of a vaccine; mixed cryoglobulinemia, porphyria cutanea tarda
HDVDeltavirus; defective circular negative-sense ssRNABlood, sexualCommon after superinfection of an HBV carrierNeeds HBsAg as its envelope; cannot exist without HBV
HEVHepevirus; nonenveloped positive-sense ssRNAFecal-oral (contaminated water); undercooked pork or gameOnly in immunosuppressed hostsFulminant hepatitis in pregnancy

HBV enters hepatocytes through the bile acid transporter NTCP. Its relaxed circular DNA is repaired into covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which is transcribed by host RNA polymerase II. Pregenomic RNA is packaged with the viral polymerase and reverse-transcribed into DNA inside the capsid. Nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir) block that reverse transcription step, so they suppress viremia but rarely clear cccDNA; that is why therapy is usually long-term. Extrahepatic immune-complex disease includes polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy.

HCV encodes a polyprotein cleaved by the NS3/4A protease; NS5A organises the replication complex and NS5B is the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Each is a drug target (the -previr, -asvir and -buvir suffixes). Its extrahepatic effects include mixed cryoglobulinemia with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, lichen planus and porphyria cutanea tarda.

A negative HBsAg does not exclude acute hepatitis B. In the window period HBsAg has cleared and anti-HBs is not yet detectable; IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker. Anti-HBs alone (no anti-HBc) means vaccination, because the vaccine contains only surface antigen.

Helicobacter pylori

A curved, flagellated, gram-negative rod that is catalase-, oxidase- and urease-positive. Urease converts urea to ammonia, buffering the acid around the organism; flagella carry it into the mucus layer. CagA (injected by a type IV secretion system) and VacA increase virulence. Antral-predominant gastritis raises gastrin and acid output and drives duodenal ulcers; pangastritis with atrophy and intestinal metaplasia predisposes to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma. Chronic antigen stimulation of B cells can produce gastric MALT lymphoma, which often regresses after eradication.

Bacterial diarrhea and food poisoning

OrganismMechanismClinical clue
Staphylococcus aureusPreformed heat-stable enterotoxin (a superantigen)Vomiting within hours of mayonnaise salads or custards
Bacillus cereusEmetic toxin cereulide (preformed, heat-stable); diarrheal enterotoxin made in the gutReheated rice; rapid vomiting
Clostridium perfringensEnterotoxin released during sporulation in the gutWatery diarrhea after meat dishes kept warm
Vibrio choleraeToxin ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha; cAMP rises and CFTR secretes chlorideRice-water stools, massive volume loss
Enterotoxigenic E. coliHeat-labile toxin (raises cAMP) and heat-stable toxin (raises cGMP)Most common cause of travelers' diarrhea
Shigella and STEC (O157:H7)Shiga toxin removes an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit, halting protein synthesisBloody diarrhea; STEC is afebrile and causes hemolytic uremic syndrome
Campylobacter jejuniInvasive; comma- or S-shaped, grows at 42 °CUndercooked poultry; later Guillain-Barré syndrome or reactive arthritis
SalmonellaInvades via M cells, survives in macrophages; H2S-producing, flagellatedPoultry, eggs, reptiles; typhoid fever with rose spots for S. Typhi
Yersinia enterocoliticaInvades Peyer patches; mesenteric adenitisPseudoappendicitis; pork, chitterlings
Vibrio parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificusMarine organismsRaw oysters; V. vulnificus causes sepsis in liver disease

Viral causes are common: norovirus (nonenveloped ssRNA calicivirus) causes explosive outbreaks on ships and in care homes; rotavirus (segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus) causes infant diarrhea, partly through the NSP4 enterotoxin, and is prevented by a live oral vaccine with a small intussusception risk; enteric adenovirus serotypes 40 and 41 cause longer childhood diarrhea.

Clostridioides difficile

A spore-forming, gram-positive anaerobic rod. Antibiotics (classically clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins) disrupt the commensal flora; spores germinate and the organism releases toxin A and toxin B. Both glucosylate Rho-family GTPases, depolymerising the actin cytoskeleton, opening tight junctions and killing colonocytes. The result is watery diarrhea and, in severe cases, yellow-white pseudomembranes of fibrin, mucus and neutrophils that erupt from damaged crypts ("volcano" lesions). Spores resist alcohol, so soap-and-water hand washing is required. Gastric acid suppression is a recognised risk factor.

Parasites

  • Giardia: flagellated, binucleate, pear-shaped trophozoites attach by a ventral disk; no invasion. Cysts in untreated stream water or daycare. Causes bloating and greasy, foul stools (fat malabsorption). Humoral defects such as selective IgA deficiency or common variable immunodeficiency predispose to chronic infection.
  • Entamoeba histolytica: cysts with up to four nuclei are ingested; trophozoites that contain ingested red cells invade the colon, producing flask-shaped ulcers and bloody diarrhea. Spread through the portal vein causes an amebic liver abscess with "anchovy-paste" contents.
  • Cryptosporidium: acid-fast oocysts; self-limited watery diarrhea in healthy hosts (outbreaks from swimming pools because oocysts resist chlorine) and chronic severe diarrhea when CD4 counts are low.
  • Echinococcus granulosus: dogs are the definitive host; sheep the usual intermediate host. Humans ingest eggs, and larvae form slow-growing hydatid cysts, most often in the liver, with daughter cysts and calcified walls. Cyst rupture can cause anaphylaxis.

Whipple disease and liver abscess

Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinomycete. Defective macrophage killing lets the organism accumulate, and small-bowel biopsy shows the lamina propria packed with foamy macrophages containing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant material. The lacteals are compressed, so fat malabsorption follows. Typical patients are middle-aged men with arthralgia that precedes diarrhea and weight loss; cardiac, ocular and CNS involvement occur.

Pyogenic liver abscess usually arises from the biliary tree or from portal spread of intra-abdominal infection and is often polymicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci of the anginosus group, anaerobes). A hypervirulent capsular type of Klebsiella pneumoniae causes primary liver abscess in people with diabetes, sometimes with metastatic endophthalmitis. Amebic abscess is usually solitary in the right lobe of a young man with travel or residence in an endemic area.

Mycobacterium avium complex in advanced HIV also fills small-bowel macrophages with PAS-positive material. The tie-breaker is an acid-fast stain: positive in MAC, negative in Whipple disease.

s23d-s100102-s1.bodyHtml:
Inflammatory bowel disease: concept

Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (UC) arise when a genetically susceptible host mounts a sustained mucosal immune response against commensal gut flora. Defects in barrier function, microbial sensing and regulatory pathways all contribute. NOD2 variants (an intracellular sensor of bacterial muramyl dipeptide expressed in Paneth cells and monocytes) are the best-known Crohn susceptibility genes, along with autophagy genes such as ATG16L1. Variants in the IL-23 receptor pathway raise risk for both diseases. Crohn disease is driven mainly by Th1 and Th17 cytokines (IFN-gamma, IL-12, IL-17, IL-23); UC shows an atypical Th2-like pattern with IL-13 from natural killer T cells. Smoking raises the risk and severity of Crohn disease but is associated with a lower risk of UC.

FeatureCrohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
DistributionMouth to anus; terminal ileum most common; skip lesions; rectum often sparedAlways involves the rectum and extends proximally without skips
DepthTransmuralMucosa and submucosa
GrossCobblestone mucosa, linear (knife-like) ulcers, creeping fat, strictures ("string sign")Friable mucosa, continuous ulceration, inflammatory pseudopolyps; loss of haustra ("lead pipe") when chronic
MicroscopyNoncaseating granulomas (in a minority of biopsies), lymphoid aggregatesCrypt abscesses, crypt distortion, no granulomas
ComplicationsFistulas, abscesses, perianal disease, strictures, B12 and bile-acid malabsorption, gallstones, oxalate kidney stonesToxic megacolon, severe bleeding
CancerColorectal cancer risk with extensive colitis; small-bowel adenocarcinomaColorectal cancer risk rises with extent and duration
Serology (supportive only)ASCA more often positivep-ANCA more often positive

Enteric oxalate stones in Crohn disease follow ileal disease or resection: unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in the lumen, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed in the colon. Ileal loss also causes vitamin B12 deficiency and bile-acid diarrhea; bile-acid depletion promotes cholesterol gallstones.

Extraintestinal manifestations

Some extraintestinal manifestations track intestinal activity (peripheral large-joint arthritis, erythema nodosum, episcleritis, aphthous ulcers), while others run an independent course (axial spondyloarthritis and sacroiliitis, anterior uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis). Pyoderma gangrenosum often but not always parallels activity. Venous thromboembolism risk is increased, especially during flares and hospitalisation.

Drug mechanisms

  • 5-aminosalicylates (mesalamine, sulfasalazine): topical anti-inflammatory action on the colonic mucosa; sulfasalazine is split by colonic bacteria into 5-ASA and sulfapyridine, which causes most adverse effects (oligospermia, rash, folate malabsorption).
  • Glucocorticoids: broad suppression of cytokine transcription; budesonide has high first-pass hepatic metabolism, limiting systemic effects.
  • Thiopurines (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine): purine analogues that block lymphocyte proliferation. Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) or NUDT15 deficiency causes severe myelosuppression; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and raises toxic metabolites.
  • Methotrexate: dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor; used mainly in Crohn disease.
  • Anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab): neutralise TNF-alpha; reactivation of latent TB and HBV, drug-induced lupus, demyelination and worsening heart failure.
  • Anti-integrin: vedolizumab binds alpha4beta7 integrin and blocks lymphocyte binding to MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium, so it is gut-selective; natalizumab binds the alpha4 chain more broadly and carries a risk of JC virus progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
  • Interleukin blockers: ustekinumab binds the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23; risankizumab, mirikizumab and guselkumab bind the IL-23-specific p19 subunit.
  • Small molecules: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) block cytokine receptor signalling and carry warnings for serious infection, herpes zoster, thrombosis, cardiovascular events and malignancy; sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod) trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes and can cause bradycardia and macular edema.

Vedolizumab and natalizumab both target alpha4 integrin, but only natalizumab blocks alpha4beta1 binding to VCAM-1 in the brain, which explains its PML risk. Do not confuse the two on a question about gut-selective therapy.

Celiac disease

An immune reaction to gluten (gliadin and related prolamins in wheat, barley and rye) in people carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) deamidates gliadin peptides, converting glutamine to glutamate; the negatively charged peptides bind DQ2/DQ8 more tightly and activate CD4 T cells, which help B cells make anti-tTG antibodies. IL-15 drives intraepithelial cytotoxic lymphocytes. Histology shows intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia and villous atrophy, worst in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Consequences are iron deficiency (duodenal absorption), folate deficiency, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, osteoporosis, hyposplenism and a small risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma. Associations include type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, selective IgA deficiency, Down syndrome and Turner syndrome. Dermatitis herpetiformis is its skin form: itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces with granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae, targeting epidermal transglutaminase.

Absence of both HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 makes celiac disease very unlikely, so HLA typing is useful for ruling out the disease, not for confirming it.

Other immune disorders of the gut and liver

DisorderKey pathologyAssociations
Microscopic colitis, collagenous typeThickened subepithelial collagen band with intraepithelial lymphocytes; normal-looking mucosaOlder women; NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs; other autoimmune disease
Microscopic colitis, lymphocytic typeIncreased intraepithelial lymphocytes without a thick collagen bandSame as collagenous; celiac disease
Eosinophilic esophagitis15 or more eosinophils per high-power field; rings, furrows, white exudatesAtopy; Th2 response to food antigens (IL-5, IL-13, eotaxin-3)
Autoimmune gastritisT-cell destruction of parietal cells in body and fundus; antral sparingAnti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies; B12 deficiency; type 1 gastric NET
Autoimmune hepatitisInterface hepatitis with plasma cellsType 1: ANA, anti-smooth muscle; type 2 (children): anti-LKM1; raised IgG
Primary sclerosing cholangitisConcentric "onion-skin" periductal fibrosis; beaded intra- and extrahepatic ductsMost patients have UC; p-ANCA; cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, colorectal cancer

In autoimmune gastritis, loss of parietal cells causes achlorhydria; the antrum is spared, so G cells respond to the high pH with marked hypergastrinemia. Gastrin drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia, which can progress to type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours. Loss of intrinsic factor causes B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration. Iron deficiency often appears first because acid helps iron absorption.

Polyps: definitions

A polyp is any mass projecting into the bowel lumen. It may be pedunculated (on a stalk) or sessile (broad-based), and the key question is whether it is neoplastic. Non-neoplastic polyps (hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous) are usually harmless; neoplastic polyps (conventional adenomas and sessile serrated lesions) are precursors of colorectal cancer.

PolypHistologyTypical siteMalignant potential
HyperplasticSerrated (saw-tooth) lumens limited to the upper crypt; normal crypt basesRectosigmoid; usually smallNegligible when small and distal
Tubular adenomaDysplastic epithelium forming tubules (less than 25% villous)Anywhere in the colonLow when small; rises with size
Tubulovillous and villous adenomaFinger-like fronds of dysplastic epithelium (villous more than 75%)Rectum and sigmoid commonHighest among adenomas
Sessile serrated lesionSerration reaching the crypt base, with dilated, horizontally spreading (boot- or L-shaped) crypt basesProximal colon; flat, often with a mucus capPrecursor of MSI-high cancer via the serrated pathway
Inflammatory pseudopolypIslands of regenerating mucosa between ulcersColitis (IBD)None in itself
Hamartomatous (juvenile, Peutz-Jeghers)Disorganised normal tissue: cystic glands in juvenile polyps; branching smooth muscle cores in Peutz-Jeghers polypsJuvenile: rectum of children; Peutz-Jeghers: small bowelLow for a sporadic polyp; increased in the syndromes

The risk that an adenoma contains or becomes cancer rises with size (especially 10 mm or more), villous architecture and high-grade dysplasia; together these define an advanced adenoma. Large villous adenomas of the rectum can secrete abundant potassium-rich mucus, causing watery diarrhea and hypokalemia.

Two molecular routes to cancer

In the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence (chromosomal instability), loss of APC is the initiating event. APC is part of the destruction complex that degrades beta-catenin; when it is lost, beta-catenin accumulates and activates Wnt target genes that drive proliferation. Activating KRAS mutations promote growth of the adenoma, and loss of TP53 (with loss of chromosome 18q genes such as SMAD4) permits progression to carcinoma. COX-2 is overexpressed in many adenomas, which is the rationale for aspirin chemoprevention.

In the serrated pathway, a BRAF V600E mutation initiates a sessile serrated lesion. Widespread CpG island methylation (the CpG island methylator phenotype) then silences tumour suppressor genes, including MLH1. Loss of mismatch repair produces microsatellite instability. These lesions are flat, pale and proximal, so they are missed more often at colonoscopy and account for a share of interval cancers.

A small hyperplastic polyp in the rectosigmoid and a sessile serrated lesion in the cecum can both look serrated, but they behave differently. Serration extending to dilated, L-shaped crypt bases defines the sessile serrated lesion, which is neoplastic.

Polyposis syndromes

SyndromeGene and inheritancePolypsOther features
Familial adenomatous polyposisAPC (chromosome 5q), autosomal dominantHundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas from adolescence; duodenal and periampullary adenomas; fundic gland polypsColorectal cancer nearly certain without colectomy; desmoid tumours, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, papillary thyroid cancer, hepatoblastoma; medulloblastoma in some families
MUTYH-associated polyposisMUTYH, autosomal recessiveTens to hundreds of adenomasBase-excision repair defect; siblings at risk rather than parents
Peutz-Jeghers syndromeSTK11 (LKB1), autosomal dominantHamartomas mainly in the small bowelPigmented macules on lips, buccal mucosa and digits; intussusception; raised risk of colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, breast and gonadal tumours
Juvenile polyposis syndromeSMAD4 or BMPR1A, autosomal dominantMultiple juvenile polyps in colon and stomachRectal bleeding and anemia in children; SMAD4 carriers may also have hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (Cowden)PTEN, autosomal dominantHamartomatous and other polypsBreast, thyroid and endometrial cancer; trichilemmomas

A single juvenile (retention) polyp in a child is common, usually sporadic, and often autoamputates; it is not a polyposis syndrome.

Benign liver lesions

  • Hemangioma: the most common benign liver tumour; a cavernous collection of blood-filled vascular spaces lined by endothelium. Imaging shows peripheral, nodular, discontinuous enhancement with gradual centripetal fill-in. Biopsy is avoided because of bleeding risk.
  • Focal nodular hyperplasia: a polyclonal hyperplastic reaction of hepatocytes to an anomalous artery; a central stellate scar carries a thick-walled artery and contains bile ductules. It has no malignant potential and does not depend strongly on estrogen.
  • Hepatocellular adenoma: a monoclonal proliferation of hepatocytes without portal tracts or bile ducts, linked to estrogen-containing contraceptives, anabolic androgen use, obesity and glycogen storage disease type I. Subtypes include HNF1A-inactivated (steatotic), inflammatory and beta-catenin-activated; the beta-catenin type has the highest risk of transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma. Thin-walled vessels lacking supporting tissue explain the risk of hemorrhage and rupture, which increases with size and during pregnancy.
  • Simple hepatic cyst: a thin-walled, fluid-filled cyst lined by biliary-type epithelium with no communication with the biliary tree; multiple cysts occur in polycystic liver disease, often with ADPKD.

Mesenchymal tumours

Lipomas are submucosal, soft and yellow; on endoscopy they indent when pressed with closed forceps (the "cushion" sign) and can act as a lead point for intussusception. Leiomyomas are the most common benign esophageal tumour; they arise from the muscularis propria and express smooth muscle markers (desmin, smooth muscle actin) but not KIT (CD117) or DOG1, which separates them from gastrointestinal stromal tumours that arise from interstitial cells of Cajal.

Peutz-Jeghers polyps are the classic hamartomas with a tree-like core of branching smooth muscle; recurrent small-bowel intussusception in a young person with pigmented lips should suggest the syndrome.

Non-neoplastic polyps (hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous) are usually harmless; neoplastic polyps (conventional adenomas and sessile serrated lesions) are precursors of colorectal cancer.

The risk that an adenoma contains or becomes cancer rises with size (especially 10 mm or more), villous architecture and high-grade dysplasia; together these define an advanced adenoma. Large villous adenomas of the rectum can secrete abundant potassium-rich mucus, causing watery diarrhea and hypokalemia.

In the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence (chromosomal instability), loss of APC is the initiating event. APC is part of the destruction complex that degrades beta-catenin; when it is lost, beta-catenin accumulates and activates Wnt target genes that drive proliferation. Activating KRAS mutations promote growth of the adenoma, and loss of TP53 (with loss of chromosome 18q genes such as SMAD4) permits progression to carcinoma. COX-2 is overexpressed in many adenomas, which is the rationale for aspirin chemoprevention.

In the serrated pathway, a BRAF V600E mutation initiates a sessile serrated lesion. Widespread CpG island methylation (the CpG island methylator phenotype) then silences tumour suppressor genes, including MLH1. Loss of mismatch repair produces microsatellite instability. These lesions are flat, pale and proximal, so they are missed more often at colonoscopy and account for a share of interval cancers.

A small hyperplastic polyp in the rectosigmoid and a sessile serrated lesion in the cecum can both look serrated, but they behave differently. Serration extending to dilated, L-shaped crypt bases defines the sessile serrated lesion, which is neoplastic.

s23d-s100202-s1.bodyHtml:
Malignant tumours of the digestive tract share a theme: a chronic injury or an inherited defect drives a stepwise accumulation of mutations, often through a recognisable pre-malignant lesion. Knowing the precursor, the driver genes and the histology lets you predict the location, the spread and the tumour marker.

Esophagus: two cancers, two epithelia

Squamous cell carcinoma arises from the native stratified squamous lining, usually in the upper and middle thirds. Risks are irritants that injure squamous cells: tobacco, heavy alcohol, very hot beverages, caustic (lye) strictures, achalasia with food stasis, and nutritional deficiencies. Histology shows nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. It remains the dominant type worldwide.

Adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third and at the gastroesophageal junction from Barrett esophagus: chronic acid and bile reflux replaces squamous epithelium with columnar epithelium showing intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells). Barrett progresses through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to invasive cancer. Obesity, male sex, white race, long-standing GERD and smoking raise risk. In the United States adenocarcinoma is now the more common type.

FeatureSquamous cell carcinomaAdenocarcinoma
LocationUpper and middle thirdsDistal third, GE junction
PrecursorSquamous dysplasiaBarrett metaplasia, then dysplasia
Key risksSmoking, alcohol, hot drinks, lye, achalasiaGERD, obesity, smoking
HistologyKeratin pearls, intercellular bridgesGland-forming, mucin-producing

Stomach

Gastric adenocarcinoma has two Lauren types. The intestinal type forms glands, often in the antrum or lesser curvature, and follows a sequence of H. pylori chronic gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia; smoked and salted foods and nitrosamines add risk. The diffuse type is made of discohesive signet-ring cells (mucin pushes the nucleus aside) that infiltrate the wall and make it rigid (linitis plastica). Loss of the adhesion protein E-cadherin underlies the discohesion; a germline CDH1 mutation causes hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and also lobular breast cancer. Gastric cancer spreads to the left supraclavicular node, the periumbilical skin, the ovaries and the liver.

Gastric MALT lymphoma is an extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma driven by chronic H. pylori antigen stimulation of lymphoid tissue that the stomach normally lacks. Early lesions can regress when the infection is eradicated; the t(11;18) translocation predicts resistance to eradication alone.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) is the commonest mesenchymal tumour of the GI tract, most often in the stomach. It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal (the pacemaker cells) and carries an activating mutation of the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT (CD117) or, less often, PDGFRA. DOG1 and CD117 stain the tumour. Imatinib inhibits the constitutively active kinase.

Signet-ring cells are a pattern, not an address. They are typical of diffuse gastric cancer but also occur in some colorectal and appendiceal cancers, and an ovarian mass made of them (Krukenberg tumour) is almost always a metastasis.

Colon and rectum: three molecular routes

The chromosomal instability (adenoma-carcinoma) pathway accounts for most sporadic cancers. Loss of the APC tumour suppressor frees beta-catenin to drive proliferation and starts a tubular adenoma; activating KRAS mutations enlarge the adenoma; loss of TP53 (and of chromosome 18q genes such as SMAD4) permits invasion. A germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with hundreds of adenomas and near-certain cancer without colectomy.

The serrated pathway begins with sessile serrated lesions, often in the right colon, driven by BRAF V600E and widespread promoter hypermethylation (CpG island methylator phenotype). Methylation silences MLH1, producing sporadic microsatellite-unstable cancers.

Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is autosomal dominant, caused by a germline defect in a mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM deletions that silence MSH2). Failed repair of replication slippage leaves insertion-deletion errors in short repeats (microsatellite instability). Tumours tend to be right-sided, mucinous and rich in lymphocytes, and appear at a young age. Extracolonic cancers include endometrium (the most common), ovary, stomach, small bowel, hepatobiliary tract and urothelium.

Clinically, right-sided cancers bleed occultly and present with iron-deficiency anaemia; left-sided cancers narrow the lumen and change bowel habit or cause obstruction. Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) bacteraemia or endocarditis should prompt colonoscopy. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a glycoprotein useful for follow-up after resection, not for diagnosis.

Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours

Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours arise from enterochromaffin-like cells, most commonly in the small bowel (ileum) and appendix. They stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin and secrete serotonin. Serotonin from a gut primary drains to the liver and is inactivated by monoamine oxidase, so carcinoid syndrome (flushing, secretory diarrhoea, bronchospasm, wheeze) generally needs liver metastases or a primary outside portal drainage. Serotonin reaching the right heart causes fibrotic plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves; the lungs inactivate it, so the left heart is spared. Diversion of dietary tryptophan into serotonin can cause niacin deficiency (pellagra). The breakdown product 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) appears in urine. Somatostatin analogues (octreotide) bind tumour somatostatin receptors and reduce hormone release.

Liver and biliary tree

Hepatocellular carcinoma arises mostly in cirrhosis from any cause (alcohol, chronic hepatitis C, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, haemochromatosis). Hepatitis B is special: viral DNA integrates into the host genome and can cause cancer even without cirrhosis. Aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus-contaminated grain and nuts induces a characteristic G:C to T:A transversion at codon 249 of TP53. Tumours receive blood mainly from the hepatic artery, which explains arterial-phase enhancement with venous washout on imaging. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) may be elevated. Spread is hematogenous with a tendency to invade the portal and hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari physiology).

Cholangiocarcinoma is an adenocarcinoma of bile duct epithelium. Risks are primary sclerosing cholangitis (often with ulcerative colitis), choledochal cysts and the liver flukes Clonorchis sinensis and Opisthorchis species acquired from raw freshwater fish. A hilar tumour (Klatskin) causes painless obstructive jaundice. Gallbladder carcinoma is linked to gallstones and chronic inflammation, including a calcified (porcelain) wall; it is often found late or incidentally at cholecystectomy.

Pancreas and anus

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma follows pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia; activating KRAS mutations are found in the great majority, then loss of CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk; chronic pancreatitis, obesity, long-standing diabetes and germline BRCA2 also contribute. A head tumour obstructs the common bile duct and causes painless jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign); a body or tail tumour presents later with back pain and weight loss. Mucin-related hypercoagulability causes migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome). New-onset diabetes in an older thin adult can be an early clue. CA 19-9 is a follow-up marker.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma arises below the dentate line and is caused mainly by high-risk human papillomavirus (especially type 16), whose E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb. Risk is highest with HIV infection, receptive anal intercourse and immunosuppression. Above the dentate line, rectal adenocarcinoma predominates.

Map each cancer to its marker by follow-up use: CEA for colorectal, CA 19-9 for pancreatic and biliary, AFP for hepatocellular, urine 5-HIAA and chromogranin A for neuroendocrine tumours.

s23d-s100203-s1.bodyHtml:
Metastasis, not the primary tumour, causes most cancer deaths. The digestive tract is both a frequent source of metastases and a frequent destination. Exam questions test the route a tumour takes, the anatomic reason it lands where it does, the histologic clues that reveal a primary, and the pharmacology of therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer.

The metastatic cascade

To spread, carcinoma cells must detach, invade, travel, survive and grow at a new site. Loss of E-cadherin loosens cell-to-cell junctions, and an epithelial-mesenchymal transition gives cells a motile phenotype. Tumour and stromal cells secrete matrix metalloproteinases that degrade the basement membrane (type IV collagen) and stroma; cells then attach to laminin and fibronectin through integrins and migrate. Inside vessels they travel as emboli, often coated by platelets, and exit at sites whose capillary beds trap them or whose microenvironment supports them (the "seed and soil" idea). Most circulating tumour cells die; established metastases usually need angiogenesis driven by VEGF.

Three routes of spread

RouteTypical tumoursClassic destinations
LymphaticCarcinomas (gastric, esophageal, colorectal, pancreatic)Regional nodes, then the thoracic duct and left supraclavicular node
Hematogenous, portalStomach, small bowel, colon, upper rectum, pancreas, neuroendocrineLiver first
Hematogenous, systemicLower rectum, anal canal, esophagus; tumours beyond the liverLung, bone, brain
TranscoelomicGastric (diffuse), colorectal, appendiceal, pancreatic, ovarianPeritoneum, omentum, ovaries, pouch of Douglas

Lymphatic spread is typical of carcinomas. Abdominal lymph drains through the cisterna chyli into the thoracic duct, which empties into the left venous angle at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. A hard, enlarged left supraclavicular (Virchow) node is therefore a sign of intra-abdominal cancer, classically gastric. A firm periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) reflects spread along lymphatics, the falciform ligament or the peritoneum to the umbilicus and indicates advanced disease.

Hematogenous spread follows venous drainage. Blood from the stomach, small intestine, colon, upper rectum, pancreas and spleen returns through the superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric and splenic veins to the portal vein, so the liver's sinusoids are the first capillary bed that tumour emboli meet. This is why the liver is the commonest site of GI metastasis and why, in Western countries, metastases to the liver greatly outnumber primary liver cancers. The lower rectum and anal canal drain through the middle and inferior rectal veins into the internal iliac veins and inferior vena cava, so low rectal cancer can metastasise to the lung without passing through the liver. Esophageal venous drainage is mixed (azygos to the systemic circulation above, left gastric to the portal vein below).

Transcoelomic spread occurs when tumour cells shed from a serosal surface into the peritoneal cavity. Peritoneal fluid circulates toward the right paracolic gutter and subdiaphragmatic spaces and pools in the pelvis, so implants are common on the omentum ("omental cake"), the undersurface of the diaphragm, the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch (a palpable "shelf" on rectal examination) and the ovaries. A Krukenberg tumour is bilateral ovarian metastasis composed of mucin-filled signet-ring cells, most often from diffuse gastric carcinoma; colon, appendix and breast are other sources. Appendiceal mucinous neoplasms can fill the abdomen with gelatinous mucin (pseudomyxoma peritonei).

A left supraclavicular node points to the abdomen because of the thoracic duct, but a right supraclavicular node drains the right hemithorax and mediastinum and suggests a thoracic primary (lung, esophagus) instead.

Liver metastases: pathology and blood supply

Metastases are usually multiple, of varying size, and scattered through both lobes, unlike a solitary primary. Subcapsular deposits may outgrow their blood supply and undergo central necrosis, producing an umbilicated surface. Although normal hepatocytes receive most of their blood from the portal vein, established metastases (and HCC) are supplied mainly by the hepatic artery, the basis for intra-arterial therapies such as chemoembolisation and radioembolisation. Extensive replacement of liver tissue can raise alkaline phosphatase and GGT out of proportion to bilirubin, and late disease causes hepatomegaly, jaundice and liver failure.

Malignant ascites

Peritoneal carcinomatosis causes ascites through increased capillary permeability of tumour-lined peritoneum (partly VEGF-driven) and obstruction of subdiaphragmatic lymphatics. The fluid has a serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) below 1.1 g/dL and a high total protein, with malignant cells on cytology. In contrast, massive liver metastases without peritoneal spread can cause portal hypertension, giving a SAAG of 1.1 or more with negative cytology.

Mechanism of ascitesSAAGTotal proteinCytology
Peritoneal carcinomatosisBelow 1.1 g/dLHighUsually positive
Massive liver metastases (portal hypertension)1.1 g/dL or moreLowNegative
Cirrhosis1.1 g/dL or moreLowNegative

Metastases to the GI tract from elsewhere

The GI tract is also a destination. Melanoma is the commonest tumour to metastasise to the small bowel; deposits cause bleeding, anaemia or act as a lead point for intussusception, and they stain for S-100, SOX10, HMB-45 and Melan-A. Lobular breast carcinoma metastasises to the stomach and bowel more often than ductal carcinoma; because its cells lack E-cadherin they infiltrate singly and can mimic diffuse (linitis plastica-type) gastric cancer. Estrogen receptor and GATA3 positivity favour a breast origin. Lung cancer can seed the small bowel and cause perforation or obstruction. Ovarian cancer spreads transcoelomically over bowel serosa.

Immunohistochemistry often identifies the primary: CDX2 with CK20 (and CK7 negative) for colorectal, TTF-1 for lung, ER and GATA3 for breast, S-100 and SOX10 for melanoma, chromogranin and synaptophysin for neuroendocrine tumours.

Pharmacology of metastatic colorectal cancer

5-Fluorouracil is converted to FdUMP, which inhibits thymidylate synthase; leucovorin (folinic acid) stabilises the inhibitory complex and potentiates it. Capecitabine is an oral prodrug that causes hand-foot syndrome. Deficiency of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD), which breaks down fluoropyrimidines, causes severe toxicity. Oxaliplatin, a platinum agent that forms DNA crosslinks, causes acute cold-triggered dysesthesias and a cumulative sensory neuropathy. Irinotecan inhibits topoisomerase I and causes diarrhoea and neutropenia, worse in patients with reduced UGT1A1 activity (Gilbert genotype). Bevacizumab binds VEGF-A; it causes hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, impaired wound healing and GI perforation. Cetuximab and panitumumab block EGFR and cause an acneiform rash and hypomagnesaemia; they work only in tumours without activating RAS mutations, because mutant KRAS signals downstream of the receptor regardless of EGFR blockade. Tumours with BRAF V600E or mismatch repair deficiency have specific targeted and immunotherapy options.

s23d-s100301-s1.bodyHtml:
Many GI complaints are symptoms before they are diagnoses. Step 1 tests the physiology behind them: why visceral pain is vague, how the brainstem coordinates vomiting and which receptors antiemetics block, how diarrhoea is classified by mechanism, what vomiting does to acid-base balance, and how laxatives work.

Abdominal pain: visceral, parietal and referred

Visceral pain arises from stretch, distension, ischaemia or inflammation of hollow organs and capsules. Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic nerves, are few and enter the cord bilaterally over several segments, so the pain is dull, poorly localised, felt in the midline and accompanied by autonomic effects (nausea, sweating, pallor). The level reflects embryologic origin: foregut structures (stomach, duodenum to the ampulla, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) refer to the epigastrium; midgut structures (small bowel, appendix, proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) to the periumbilical region; hindgut structures (distal colon, rectum) to the hypogastrium.

Parietal (somatic) pain arises when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which is innervated by the same somatic nerves as the overlying abdominal wall. It is sharp, well localised, worsened by movement or coughing, and produces guarding, rigidity and rebound tenderness. Appendicitis shows the shift: early periumbilical visceral pain (afferents entering at T10) moves to the right lower quadrant once the inflamed appendix irritates adjacent parietal peritoneum.

Referred pain is felt at a distant site supplied by the same spinal segment. Irritation of the diaphragm (blood, abscess, a ruptured spleen) refers to the shoulder tip through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5); biliary pain often radiates to the right scapula; pancreatic pain bores through to the back; renal colic radiates from the flank to the groin.

TypeNervesCharacterExample
VisceralAutonomic afferents with sympathetic fibresDull, midline, poorly localised, with nauseaEarly appendicitis, periumbilical
ParietalSomatic segmental nervesSharp, localised, worse with movementPeritonitis at McBurney point
ReferredShared spinal segmentFelt at a distant dermatomeDiaphragmatic irritation to shoulder

Nausea and vomiting

Vomiting is coordinated by a network in the medulla (the "vomiting centre", centred on the nucleus tractus solitarius and nearby nuclei) that drives the sequence of salivation, retching, glottic closure, abdominal muscle contraction and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. It receives four main inputs:

  • The chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema, on the floor of the fourth ventricle outside the blood-brain barrier, samples blood and CSF for toxins, drugs (opioids, chemotherapy, digoxin) and uraemia. It is rich in dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT3 and neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptors.
  • Vagal afferents from the gut: chemotherapy and radiation damage enterochromaffin cells, which release serotonin that stimulates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal terminals.
  • The vestibular system (motion sickness, labyrinthitis) via histamine H1 and muscarinic M1 receptors.
  • Higher cortical centres (anticipatory nausea, smells, anxiety, raised intracranial pressure).

Antiemetic choice follows the input. 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, palonosetron) block gut and central serotonin receptors; adverse effects are headache, constipation and dose-related QT prolongation. D2 antagonists include metoclopramide (also a 5-HT4 agonist and prokinetic), prochlorperazine, promethazine (with prominent H1 and anticholinergic activity), haloperidol and droperidol. Blocking nigrostriatal D2 receptors causes acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and, with prolonged metoclopramide use, tardive dyskinesia; tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin. Several also prolong the QT interval. NK1 antagonists (aprepitant, fosaprepitant) block substance P and are added for highly emetogenic chemotherapy, especially the delayed phase; aprepitant interacts with CYP3A4 substrates. H1 antagonists (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) and the muscarinic antagonist scopolamine treat motion sickness; anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, confusion and urinary retention, which matter most in older adults. Dexamethasone and cannabinoids (dronabinol) are adjuncts. In pregnancy, doxylamine with pyridoxine is first line.

Acute dystonia after an antiemetic is a dopamine-blocking effect, not an allergy. It is treated with an anticholinergic (benztropine) or diphenhydramine, and the drug class is avoided in Parkinson disease.

Metabolic effects of vomiting

Gastric juice is rich in hydrogen and chloride ions. Persistent vomiting or nasogastric suction removes HCl, generating a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increases proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, so the kidney cannot excrete the extra bicarbonate (maintenance phase). Aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions in the collecting duct, causing hypokalaemia and, paradoxically, acidic urine. Urine chloride is low because the kidney avidly retains chloride, making this a saline-responsive alkalosis. Compensatory hypoventilation raises PaCO2.

Diarrhoea by mechanism

The stool osmotic gap = 290 minus 2 x (stool Na+ + stool K+). A gap above about 125 mOsm/kg means unabsorbed solutes hold water (osmotic); a gap below about 50 means electrolytes are being actively secreted (secretory).

MechanismExamplesClues
OsmoticLactase deficiency, magnesium or sorbitol, lactuloseHigh osmotic gap; stops with fasting
SecretoryCholera and enterotoxigenic E. coli toxins, VIPoma, carcinoid, bile acidsLow gap; large volume; persists with fasting and at night
InflammatoryIBD, invasive bacteria, C. difficileBlood, fever, faecal leukocytes or calprotectin
MotilityHyperthyroidism, IBS, diabetic autonomic neuropathyRapid transit; often small, frequent stools
MalabsorptiveCeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiencySteatorrhoea, weight loss, nutrient deficiencies

Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gs, locking adenylate cyclase on; cAMP opens the CFTR chloride channel, and sodium and water follow into the lumen. Glucose-coupled sodium absorption (SGLT1) is preserved, the basis of oral rehydration solution.

Constipation and laxatives

Constipation reflects slow transit, dyssynergic defecation (failure of the puborectalis and external sphincter to relax), or secondary causes: drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers such as verapamil, iron, calcium), hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes, Parkinson disease and obstructing lesions. Opioids act on enteric mu receptors to reduce propulsive motility and secretion; tolerance does not develop to this effect.

ClassExamplesMechanism
Bulk-formingPsyllium, methylcelluloseRetain water and increase stool mass
OsmoticPolyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium saltsDraw water into the lumen
StimulantSenna, bisacodylStimulate myenteric plexus and secretion
SecretagogueLubiprostone; linaclotide, plecanatideActivate ClC-2 chloride channels; guanylate cyclase-C agonists raise cGMP
SerotonergicPrucalopride5-HT4 agonist that increases propulsion
Peripheral opioid antagonistMethylnaltrexone, naloxegolBlock gut mu receptors without crossing into the brain

Lactulose is also used in hepatic encephalopathy: colonic bacteria ferment it to acids that trap ammonia as ammonium. Magnesium-based laxatives can accumulate in kidney disease.

Functional gut disorders are now called disorders of gut-brain interaction: visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility, altered central processing and the microbiome all contribute, which is why low-dose tricyclics and cognitive therapies can help.

s23d-s100401-s1.bodyHtml:
Structure of the mouth and salivary glands

The oral cavity is lined by stratified squamous epithelium. It is keratinized where chewing forces are high (gingiva, hard palate, dorsum of the tongue) and nonkeratinized on the buccal mucosa, floor of the mouth, ventral tongue and soft palate. The nonkeratinized sites are where most aphthous ulcers form, and the floor of the mouth and lateral tongue are the commonest sites of oral squamous cell carcinoma.

There are three paired major salivary glands. The parotid is almost purely serous and makes amylase-rich watery saliva; the submandibular gland is mixed; the sublingual gland is mostly mucous. Hundreds of minor salivary glands sit in the lip, palate and buccal mucosa, which is why a lip biopsy can sample salivary tissue. The parotid (Stensen) duct opens on the buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar; the submandibular (Wharton) duct opens beside the lingual frenulum.

The facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen and divides inside the parotid, between its superficial and deep lobes, but it does not supply the gland. Secretomotor parasympathetic fibers reach the parotid from the glossopharyngeal nerve through the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve, and reach the submandibular and sublingual glands from the facial nerve through the chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion. After parotid surgery, misdirected regrowth of these parasympathetic fibers into sweat glands causes gustatory sweating of the cheek (Frey syndrome).

Salivary physiology

Acinar cells secrete an isotonic, plasma-like fluid. As it flows down the ducts, ductal cells reabsorb sodium and chloride and secrete potassium and bicarbonate, and the ducts are relatively impermeable to water, so final saliva is hypotonic. At high flow rates there is less time for modification and saliva becomes closer to plasma in tonicity. Aldosterone acts on the ducts much as it does on the renal collecting duct.

Salivary secretion is controlled almost entirely by nerves, unlike most GI secretions. Parasympathetic stimulation through M3 muscarinic receptors (Gq, IP3, rising cytosolic calcium) drives large volumes of watery saliva; sympathetic beta-adrenergic input adds a small volume of protein-rich saliva. Saliva lubricates food, buffers acid with bicarbonate, starts starch digestion with alpha-amylase, and defends the mouth with lysozyme, lactoferrin and secretory IgA. Loss of saliva therefore produces caries, candidiasis and difficulty with swallowing dry food.

Drugs are the commonest cause of dry mouth, especially in older adults: antimuscarinics for bladder overactivity (oxybutynin), tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines, antipsychotics and many other agents with anticholinergic activity. Head and neck radiation and Sjogren syndrome are the other major causes. Muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline) act as sialogogues when some functioning gland remains.

White and red mucosal lesions

LesionAppearanceCause or settingMalignant potential
Pseudomembranous candidiasisCreamy white plaques that wipe off, leaving a red baseInhaled or systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, dentures, diabetes, HIV, dry mouthNone
Oral hairy leukoplakiaFixed, white, vertically corrugated plaques on the lateral tongueEpstein-Barr virus replication in immunosuppressed hosts, classically HIVNone; a marker of immunosuppression
LeukoplakiaFixed white plaque not explained by another diagnosisTobacco (smoked or smokeless), alcoholPremalignant; may show dysplasia
ErythroplakiaVelvety red patchTobacco, alcoholHighest; most show dysplasia or carcinoma

Both oral hairy leukoplakia and leukoplakia resist scraping. Hairy leukoplakia is caused by EBV, sits on the lateral tongue, has a ridged surface and is not premalignant; leukoplakia is a clinical label for a fixed white patch that carries a risk of dysplasia. Do not call hairy leukoplakia a precancer, and do not call it candidiasis because it is white.

Oral ulcers

Recurrent aphthous ulcers are shallow, painful, round ulcers with a gray-yellow base and a red halo on nonkeratinized mucosa. They heal without scarring in 1 to 2 weeks. Look for an underlying cause when they are frequent or severe: celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, deficiency of iron, folate or vitamin B12, HIV and Behcet disease. Deficiency states also produce glossitis (smooth red tongue) and angular cheilitis.

Behcet disease is a variable-vessel vasculitis with neutrophil hyperactivity. Recurrent oral ulcers are almost universal and are joined by genital ulcers that may scar, uveitis, skin lesions (erythema nodosum-like nodules, pustules) and pathergy, a pustule at a needle-stick site. It is strongly associated with HLA-B51 and is commonest along the old Silk Road from the Mediterranean to East Asia. Venous and arterial thrombosis, aneurysms and neurologic disease cause most of the serious harm.

Herpes simplex virus type 1 causes primary gingivostomatitis in children and recurrent herpes labialis after latency in the trigeminal ganglion. A painless indurated ulcer may be a syphilitic chancre or a carcinoma.

Oral and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma makes up the great majority of oral cancers. Tobacco in any form and alcohol act synergistically; betel quid is a major cause in South Asia. Because the whole mucosa has been exposed to the same carcinogens, patients often develop second primary tumors elsewhere in the upper aerodigestive tract (field cancerization). Lesions arise on the lateral tongue and floor of the mouth and spread first to cervical lymph nodes.

Carcinoma of the oropharynx (palatine tonsils, base of tongue) is increasingly caused by high-risk human papillomavirus, mainly HPV-16. Patients tend to be younger and are often nonsmokers; a cystic upper neck node is a common first sign. HPV E6 targets p53 for degradation and HPV E7 binds and inactivates the retinoblastoma protein. Rb normally represses p16 expression through a feedback loop, so loss of Rb function causes strong p16 overexpression, which pathologists use as a surrogate marker of HPV-driven tumors. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a better prognosis than tobacco-related disease. HPV vaccination is expected to prevent it.

Salivary gland tumors

Most salivary tumors arise in the parotid, and most parotid tumors are benign. The smaller the gland, the more likely a tumor is malignant, so a mass in the sublingual or a minor salivary gland deserves more suspicion.

TumorKey featuresHistology
Pleomorphic adenomaMost common salivary tumor; painless, slow, mobile parotid mass; recurs if enucleated; rare malignant changeEpithelial and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid stroma; incomplete capsule with finger-like projections
Warthin tumorParotid only; older smokers; may be bilateral or multifocal; benignCystic spaces lined by two layers of oncocytic epithelium over dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centers
Mucoepidermoid carcinomaMost common malignant salivary tumor; may cause pain or facial nerve weaknessMixture of mucin-secreting and squamoid (epidermoid) cells
Adenoid cystic carcinomaOften in minor salivary glands; slow but relentless; late recurrenceCribriform pattern; marked perineural invasion

A salivary mass that is painful, fixed, rapidly growing or accompanied by facial nerve weakness suggests malignancy. The facial nerve runs through the parotid, so any parotid surgery puts it at risk.

Inflammation of the salivary glands

Mumps is caused by an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA paramyxovirus whose surface hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins mediate entry. It causes painful parotitis, often bilateral, with raised serum amylase; orchitis after puberty, aseptic meningitis and pancreatitis are complications. The MMR vaccine prevents it.

Acute bacterial sialadenitis follows salivary stasis, usually in dehydrated, older or postoperative patients, and most often involves the parotid; Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism. Sialolithiasis mostly affects the submandibular gland because its saliva is more mucous and alkaline and its duct runs a long upward course; obstruction causes swelling and pain during meals.

Sjogren syndrome is autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands with dry eyes and dry mouth. Biopsy of minor salivary glands shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, and anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are typical. Chronic B-cell stimulation raises the risk of extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, which often presents as persistent unilateral parotid enlargement.

Teeth and periodontium

Dental caries results from bacteria, chiefly Streptococcus mutans, fermenting dietary sugars (especially sucrose) to acid that dissolves enamel hydroxyapatite. S. mutans also synthesizes sticky glucans (dextran) that help it adhere to tooth surfaces, and the same property helps viridans streptococci adhere to damaged heart valves. Fluoride is incorporated into enamel as fluorapatite, which resists acid dissolution, and it promotes remineralization of early lesions; too much fluoride during tooth development causes fluorosis (mottled enamel). Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues driven by anaerobes such as Porphyromonas gingivalis; it is worse in diabetes and in smokers.

Deep neck space infection

Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually from an infected lower molar. The roots of the second and third mandibular molars lie below the mylohyoid line, so infection drains into the submandibular space. Flora are mixed oral streptococci and anaerobes. Swelling pushes the tongue up and back and can obstruct the airway.

Biopsy of minor salivary glands shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, and anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are typical. Chronic B-cell stimulation raises the risk of extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, which often presents as persistent unilateral parotid enlargement.

Dental caries results from bacteria, chiefly Streptococcus mutans, fermenting dietary sugars (especially sucrose) to acid that dissolves enamel hydroxyapatite. S. mutans also synthesizes sticky glucans (dextran) that help it adhere to tooth surfaces, and the same property helps viridans streptococci adhere to damaged heart valves. Fluoride is incorporated into enamel as fluorapatite, which resists acid dissolution, and it promotes remineralization of early lesions; too much fluoride during tooth development causes fluorosis (mottled enamel). Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues driven by anaerobes such as Porphyromonas gingivalis; it is worse in diabetes and in smokers.

is a rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, usually from an infected lower molar. The roots of the second and third mandibular molars lie below the mylohyoid line, so infection drains into the submandibular space. Flora are mixed oral streptococci and anaerobes. Swelling pushes the tongue up and back and can obstruct the airway.

s23d-s100402-s1.bodyHtml:
Structure

The esophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long running from the pharynx at the level of C6 to the stomach. It is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and, unlike most of the gut, has no serosa over most of its length, which lets tumors and perforations spread easily into the mediastinum. Its muscle changes along its length: skeletal muscle in the upper third, a mixture in the middle third and smooth muscle in the lower third. That pattern explains why skeletal muscle diseases (myasthenia gravis, polymyositis) disturb the start of swallowing, while smooth muscle diseases (scleroderma) affect the distal esophagus.

Three normal narrowings are where pills and foreign bodies lodge: the upper esophageal sphincter, the point where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross, and the diaphragmatic hiatus. Venous drainage of the lower esophagus is partly to the left gastric vein (portal) and partly to the azygos system (systemic), forming a portosystemic anastomosis.

Sphincters and peristalsis

The upper esophageal sphincter is formed mainly by the cricopharyngeus muscle and stays tonically closed to keep air out of the esophagus. It relaxes for a moment as the bolus arrives. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a zone of tonically contracted smooth muscle, helped by the crural diaphragm, that prevents reflux. Swallowing triggers vagal inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, which release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide to relax the LES just before the peristaltic wave arrives. Excitatory cholinergic neurons produce the contraction behind the bolus. Primary peristalsis follows a swallow; secondary peristalsis is triggered by distension from residual food or refluxed acid.

LES tone is lowered by fatty meals, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, progesterone (pregnancy), and drugs such as nitrates, calcium channel blockers and anticholinergics. The main cause of reflux in most patients is transient LES relaxation unrelated to swallowing, made worse by a hiatal hernia that removes the crural support.

Motility disorders

Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory (NO and VIP) neurons in the myenteric plexus. The LES fails to relax completely with swallowing and resting LES pressure is often high, while peristalsis in the body is lost. Food and fluid pool above the sphincter, so dysphagia affects solids and liquids from the start, with regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss. Barium study shows a dilated esophagus tapering smoothly at the gastroesophageal junction (bird-beak). Most cases are idiopathic, probably autoimmune damage after a viral trigger. Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the feces of triatomine bugs in Latin America) destroys enteric ganglia and produces an identical picture, often with dilated cardiomyopathy and megacolon. Malignancy at the gastroesophageal junction can mimic achalasia (pseudoachalasia). Long-standing achalasia raises the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

Distal esophageal spasm causes intermittent chest pain and dysphagia; manometry shows premature contractions with normal LES relaxation, and barium may show a corkscrew esophagus. Hypercontractile (jackhammer) esophagus has very vigorous contractions with normal timing. Systemic sclerosis causes smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis in the lower two-thirds: LES pressure is low and distal peristalsis is weak or absent, so severe reflux, strictures and Barrett esophagus follow.

DisorderLESEsophageal bodyClassic clue
AchalasiaIncomplete relaxation, often high resting pressureAbsent peristalsisBird-beak on barium; solids and liquids
Distal esophageal spasmNormal relaxationPremature contractionsChest pain; corkscrew pattern
Systemic sclerosisLow resting pressureWeak or absent distal peristalsisSevere reflux with Raynaud phenomenon
NormalRelaxes fully with swallowCoordinated peristalsisNone

Achalasia and scleroderma both abolish distal peristalsis, but the LES behaves in opposite ways. Achalasia has a sphincter that will not open (obstruction, little reflux); scleroderma has a sphincter that will not close (severe reflux).

Reflux, Barrett esophagus and cancer

Gastroesophageal reflux disease causes heartburn and regurgitation; acid and pepsin injure the squamous mucosa. Histology of reflux esophagitis shows basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae and scattered eosinophils and neutrophils. Chronic injury can heal with a peptic stricture or with Barrett esophagus: replacement of squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), seen endoscopically as salmon-colored tongues extending above the gastroesophageal junction. Barrett esophagus can progress through low- and high-grade dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

FeatureSquamous cell carcinomaAdenocarcinoma
LocationUpper and middle esophagusDistal esophagus and junction
Risk factorsTobacco, alcohol, very hot drinks, achalasia, lye stricture, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, nitrosaminesChronic reflux, Barrett esophagus, obesity, tobacco
EpidemiologyMost common type worldwideMost common type in the United States

Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergen-driven, Th2 inflammation causing solid-food dysphagia and food impaction in atopic young people; biopsies show many intraepithelial eosinophils (it is covered with the immunologic disorders).

Infection and drug injury

Infectious esophagitis mainly affects immunosuppressed patients (advanced HIV, transplantation, chemotherapy, corticosteroids) and causes odynophagia. Candida forms white plaques with yeast and pseudohyphae. Herpes simplex virus produces small, punched-out ulcers; biopsy from the ulcer edge shows multinucleated squamous cells with ground-glass nuclei and intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions. Cytomegalovirus produces large, shallow, linear ulcers; enlarged endothelial and stromal cells at the ulcer base contain intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions.

Pill esophagitis occurs when a tablet lodges, usually at the level of the aortic arch, and releases a caustic drug onto the mucosa. Common culprits are doxycycline and other tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, iron, NSAIDs and quinidine. Taking pills with little water just before lying down is the classic setting.

Structural lesions

Zenker diverticulum is a false (pulsion) diverticulum of mucosa and submucosa that herniates posteriorly through Killian triangle, the weak area between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor, above a poorly relaxing cricopharyngeus. It causes halitosis, gurgling, regurgitation of old food and aspiration in older adults. A traction diverticulum of the mid-esophagus is a true diverticulum from scarring of nearby nodes; an epiphrenic diverticulum sits just above the LES and often accompanies a motility disorder.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome combines iron deficiency anemia, upper esophageal (postcricoid) webs and dysphagia, often with glossitis, angular cheilitis and koilonychia, mainly in middle-aged women; it carries a risk of squamous cell carcinoma. A Schatzki ring is a thin mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction that causes intermittent dysphagia to solid food, typically with meat.

Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful retching, causing hematemesis. Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural rupture, usually of the left posterolateral distal esophagus, causing mediastinitis.

Esophageal varices

Portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, reverses flow in the left gastric vein so that blood travels through submucosal esophageal veins to the azygos system. The dilated, thin-walled veins can bleed massively. Nonselective beta blockers lower portal pressure by reducing cardiac output (beta1) and allowing unopposed alpha-mediated splanchnic vasoconstriction (beta2 blockade); carvedilol adds alpha1 blockade that lowers intrahepatic resistance. Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal inflow.

s23d-s100501-s1.bodyHtml:
Gastric mucosa and its cells

The stomach has a cardia, fundus, body, antrum and pylorus. The fundus and body contain oxyntic glands; the antrum contains pyloric glands. Surface foveolar (mucous) cells cover the entire mucosa and secrete mucus and bicarbonate. Their layer of alkaline gel, together with rich mucosal blood flow, rapid cell renewal and prostaglandins, protects the epithelium from acid.

CellLocationProductMain regulators
Parietal (oxyntic)Body and fundusHCl, intrinsic factorStimulated by histamine, gastrin, ACh; inhibited by somatostatin, prostaglandins
ChiefBody and fundusPepsinogen, gastric lipaseStimulated by ACh and acid
G cellAntrumGastrinStimulated by peptides and amino acids, gastric distension, vagal gastrin-releasing peptide; inhibited by luminal acid via somatostatin
D cellAntrum and bodySomatostatinStimulated by acid; inhibits gastrin, histamine and acid
Enterochromaffin-like (ECL)BodyHistamineStimulated by gastrin and ACh

How the parietal cell makes acid

Acid leaves the parietal cell through the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in its canalicular membrane, which exchanges luminal potassium for cytosolic hydrogen ions. Carbonic anhydrase supplies the protons; bicarbonate exits on the basolateral side in exchange for chloride, so venous blood leaving the stomach after a meal is alkaline (the alkaline tide). Three stimuli converge on the pump. Histamine from ECL cells acts on H2 receptors (Gs, rising cAMP). Acetylcholine from vagal postganglionic neurons acts on M3 receptors (Gq, rising calcium). Gastrin acts on CCK-B receptors (Gq) on parietal cells and, more importantly, on ECL cells to release histamine. The stimuli potentiate one another, which is why blocking H2 receptors alone reduces acid driven by all three. Somatostatin and prostaglandin E2 act through Gi to lower cAMP.

Secretion has a cephalic phase (sight, smell and taste act through the vagus), a gastric phase (distension and peptides in the stomach) and an intestinal phase. A low antral pH stimulates D cells, and somatostatin then suppresses gastrin: a negative feedback loop. Loss of acid (atrophic gastritis, PPIs) removes this brake and gastrin rises.

Parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor, which binds vitamin B12 after pancreatic proteases release it from haptocorrin, allowing absorption in the terminal ileum. Loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis, gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency; reduced acid also impairs absorption of nonheme iron and calcium carbonate.

Gastritis

Acute erosive gastritis results from NSAIDs, heavy alcohol use, severe physiologic stress, uremia and chemotherapy. NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, cutting mucosal prostaglandin synthesis and so reducing mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow. Stress ulcers arise in critically ill patients: Curling ulcers follow severe burns, when hypovolemia causes mucosal ischemia; Cushing ulcers follow brain injury, when raised intracranial pressure increases vagal stimulation and acid secretion.

FeatureH. pylori gastritisAutoimmune gastritis
SiteAntrum first, may spread to bodyBody and fundus; antrum spared
MechanismUrease, cytotoxins and host inflammationT cells and antibodies against H+/K+ ATPase and intrinsic factor
AcidOften high with antral disease (duodenal ulcer)Very low (achlorhydria)
GastrinNormal or mildly raisedMarkedly raised (G cells unchecked)
ComplicationsPeptic ulcer, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphomaPernicious anemia, iron deficiency, adenocarcinoma, ECL-cell carcinoid tumors

In autoimmune gastritis the persistently high gastrin drives ECL-cell hyperplasia, which can progress to type 1 gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors. Iron deficiency often appears before B12 deficiency. The condition clusters with Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and vitiligo.

Peptic ulcer disease

Ulcers form when injury outweighs defense. The two dominant causes are H. pylori and NSAIDs (including low-dose aspirin); smoking impairs healing. Duodenal ulcers are more common, usually in the bulb, and are linked to antral-predominant H. pylori infection that reduces somatostatin and raises acid; pain classically improves briefly with food and returns 2 to 3 hours later or at night. Gastric ulcers usually lie along the lesser curvature, are linked to reduced mucosal defense, cause pain worsened by eating, and may be malignant, so they are biopsied. Ulcers in unusual sites (distal duodenum, jejunum), multiple or refractory ulcers, or ulcers with diarrhea suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Complications follow from anatomy. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed massively, or penetrate the pancreas. A lesser curvature ulcer can erode the left gastric artery. An anterior duodenal ulcer perforates into the peritoneum, releasing free air. Scarring near the pylorus causes gastric outlet obstruction.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

A gastrinoma, usually in the duodenum or pancreas (the gastrinoma triangle), secretes gastrin autonomously, causing parietal cell hyperplasia, thick gastric folds, acid hypersecretion and ulcers. Acid entering the duodenum inactivates pancreatic lipase and damages the mucosa, causing diarrhea and steatorrhea. About a quarter of cases are part of MEN1 (with hyperparathyroidism and pituitary adenomas). Secretin normally inhibits gastrin release, but it paradoxically stimulates gastrin release from gastrinoma cells, which is the basis of the secretin stimulation test.

Menetrier disease

Menetrier disease is a hypertrophic gastropathy caused by excess TGF-alpha signaling through the EGF receptor. Giant rugal folds in the body and fundus show massive foveolar hyperplasia with atrophy of the oxyntic glands, so acid output is low. Excess mucus production leaks protein, producing hypoalbuminemia and edema. Cancer risk is increased.

Giant gastric folds have opposite causes. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome the folds come from parietal cell hyperplasia with high acid; in Menetrier disease they come from foveolar hyperplasia with low acid and protein loss.

Motility: gastroparesis

Gastric emptying depends on fundic relaxation, antral peristalsis driven by interstitial cells of Cajal, and pyloric coordination, all under vagal and enteric control. In long-standing diabetes, autonomic neuropathy and loss of interstitial cells of Cajal delay emptying. Other causes are vagotomy, viral infection and drugs that slow emptying (opioids, anticholinergics, GLP-1 receptor agonists).

Pharmacology by mechanism

Drug classMechanismNotable adverse effects
Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, pantoprazole)Prodrugs activated in the acidic canaliculus; covalently and irreversibly inhibit H+/K+ ATPaseLong-term: hypomagnesemia, C. difficile infection, B12 and iron malabsorption, fractures, fundic gland polyps
H2 receptor antagonists (famotidine, cimetidine)Reversible competitive H2 blockadeCimetidine: CYP450 inhibition, antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia); confusion in older adults; dose-reduce in renal impairment
Potassium-competitive acid blockers (vonoprazan)Reversible blockade of the potassium site on the pump; acid-stableSimilar to PPIs
MisoprostolProstaglandin E1 analog: more mucus and bicarbonate, less acidDiarrhea, cramps; uterine contraction, so contraindicated in pregnancy when used for ulcer prevention
SucralfatePolymerizes in acid and binds the ulcer base, forming a protective barrierConstipation; binds other drugs; aluminum accumulation in kidney failure
BismuthCoats ulcers; antibacterial against H. pyloriBlack tongue and stool
MetoclopramideD2 antagonist (with 5-HT4 agonism): prokinetic and antiemeticTardive dyskinesia (boxed warning), parkinsonism, hyperprolactinemia
ErythromycinMotilin receptor agonistTachyphylaxis, QT prolongation, CYP3A4 interactions

PPIs work best taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, when pumps are being activated. Hypomagnesemia from long-term PPI use can cause secondary hypocalcemia and hypokalemia, because low magnesium impairs PTH secretion and action and promotes renal potassium loss.
