s23d-s100502-s1.bodyHtml:
Overview

The small intestine digests and absorbs nearly all nutrients; the colon recovers water and electrolytes and stores stool. Each segment has specialised transporters, so the site of disease predicts the deficiency: the duodenum handles iron and calcium, the jejunum folate, most carbohydrate, protein and fat, and the terminal ileum cobalamin (vitamin B12) and bile acids.

NutrientMain siteKey step or transporterDeficiency clue
Iron (nonheme)Duodenum, proximal jejunumDuodenal cytochrome b reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+; DMT1 uptake; ferroportin export, inhibited by hepcidinMicrocytic anemia after duodenal bypass
FolateJejunumBrush-border deconjugation, then carrier uptakeMacrocytosis with normal methylmalonic acid
Glucose, galactoseJejunumSGLT1 (Na+-coupled); GLUT2 basolateral exitOsmotic diarrhea with transporter defects
FructoseJejunumGLUT5 facilitated diffusionBloating with fructose loads
FatJejunumLipase/colipase, bile acid micelles, chylomicrons to lactealsSteatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
CobalaminTerminal ileumIntrinsic factor complex binds cubilinMegaloblastic anemia, neuropathy
Bile acidsTerminal ileumApical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter; FGF19 feedback to liverWatery diarrhea or steatorrhea after ileal loss

Carbohydrate absorption and lactose intolerance

Dietary starch is cleaved by salivary and pancreatic amylase to oligosaccharides; brush-border enzymes (lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, maltase-glucoamylase) finish the job. Only monosaccharides cross the epithelium. Lactase activity falls after weaning in most of the world's population (primary lactase nonpersistence); secondary lactase deficiency follows any mucosal injury, such as viral gastroenteritis. Unabsorbed lactose holds water in the lumen (osmotic diarrhea), and colonic bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids, hydrogen and methane, causing bloating and flatulence. Osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting and has a high stool osmotic gap; secretory diarrhea persists with fasting and has a low gap. The lactose hydrogen breath test is the usual confirmatory test.

Fat absorption

Pancreatic lipase, anchored by colipase, hydrolyses triglyceride to monoglyceride and free fatty acids. Conjugated bile acids form mixed micelles that ferry these products to the enterocyte. Inside, triglyceride is re-formed and packaged with apolipoprotein B-48 into chylomicrons, which enter lacteals and bypass the portal circulation. Fat malabsorption can therefore come from pancreatic insufficiency (no lipase), bile acid deficiency (no micelles), mucosal disease (no uptake) or lymphatic obstruction (no export). Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipase, producing oily stools and reduced fat-soluble vitamin absorption.

Cobalamin and iron

Cobalamin released from food by acid and pepsin binds haptocorrin (R-binder) in the stomach. Pancreatic proteases in the duodenum free it so that it can bind intrinsic factor from parietal cells; the complex is taken up by cubilin in the terminal ileum. Deficiency follows autoimmune gastritis, gastrectomy, pancreatic insufficiency, ileal resection or disease, bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm, and long-term metformin or acid suppression. Body stores last years, so deficiency appears late.

Heme iron is absorbed by a separate heme carrier. Nonheme iron must be reduced to the ferrous form before DMT1 takes it up; acid and vitamin C help, while acid suppression, calcium and tea tannins impair it. Ferroportin exports iron basolaterally, and hepcidin from the liver binds ferroportin and causes its internalisation and degradation. Inflammation raises hepcidin (anemia of chronic disease); HFE hemochromatosis lowers it.

Bile acids and the enterohepatic circulation

About 95% of bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver. Loss of a short ileal segment lets excess bile acids reach the colon, where they stimulate chloride and water secretion (bile acid diarrhea); the liver can still keep up synthesis, so fat absorption is preserved and bile acid sequestrants help. Loss of a long ileal segment exhausts the pool, micelles fail and steatorrhea results; sequestrants then worsen fat malabsorption. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in the colon, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed, which predisposes to calcium oxalate stones.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and short bowel

Gastric acid, the migrating motor complex, the ileocecal valve and secretory IgA keep small-bowel bacterial counts low. Overgrowth follows stasis (systemic sclerosis, diabetic neuropathy, strictures, blind loops after surgery, jejunal diverticula) or loss of the ileocecal valve. Bacteria deconjugate bile acids (fat malabsorption), consume cobalamin (low B12) and synthesise folate (normal or high folate), and ferment carbohydrate (bloating). In short bowel syndrome, the remaining length, the presence of colon and of the ileocecal valve determine outcome; patients with a colon can develop D-lactic acidosis with confusion after carbohydrate loads, because colonic bacteria ferment the excess sugar.

Low cobalamin with a high folate points to bacterial overgrowth, not to dietary deficiency: the bacteria eat B12 and make folate.

Intestinal ischemia: anatomy and mechanisms

The celiac trunk supplies the foregut, the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) the midgut to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, and the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) the hindgut to the upper rectum. The middle and inferior rectal arteries (internal iliac system) also feed the rectum, which is why the rectum is rarely ischemic. The splenic flexure (SMA-IMA boundary) and the rectosigmoid junction (IMA-internal iliac boundary) are watershed segments.

  • Arterial embolism: usually a cardiac thrombus from atrial fibrillation or recent myocardial infarction; it lodges in the SMA a few centimetres beyond its origin, often sparing the proximal jejunum.
  • Arterial thrombosis: atherosclerotic plaque at the SMA origin; often preceded by chronic postprandial pain (intestinal angina) and weight loss from food fear.
  • Nonocclusive ischemia: splanchnic vasoconstriction in low-output states (shock, cardiac surgery, dialysis, vasopressors, digoxin, cocaine).
  • Mesenteric venous thrombosis: hypercoagulable states, portal hypertension, intra-abdominal inflammation.
  • Ischemic colitis: the most common form, usually transient low flow in older adults; it causes crampy pain and bloody diarrhea at watershed segments.

The mucosa is injured first (pain, bleeding); transmural infarction leads to peritonitis, perforation and sepsis. Lactate rises late, so a normal value does not exclude early ischemia.

Diverticular disease, angiodysplasia and volvulus

Colonic diverticula are false (pulsion) diverticula: mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis propria where vasa recta penetrate. High intraluminal pressure, low-fibre diets and connective tissue changes with age contribute. In Western populations they cluster in the sigmoid; right-sided diverticula are commoner in East Asian populations. Stretching of the vasa recta over the dome causes painless arterial bleeding; obstruction of the neck with microperforation causes diverticulitis.

Angiodysplasias are thin-walled ectatic mucosal vessels, mostly in the cecum and ascending colon of older adults, thought to arise from chronic intermittent obstruction of submucosal veins by muscle contraction. Aortic stenosis is associated with bleeding angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome): shear stress unfolds von Willebrand factor so ADAMTS13 cleaves the large multimers, causing acquired von Willebrand disease type 2A.

Volvulus is twisting of a mobile segment on its mesentery. Sigmoid volvulus occurs in older, often institutionalised or neurologically impaired people with chronic constipation and a long redundant sigmoid; cecal volvulus occurs in younger adults with a mobile cecum. Closed-loop obstruction raises wall tension until venous and then arterial flow stops.

Obstruction, ileus and pseudo-obstruction

Mechanical small bowel obstruction is most often caused by adhesions after prior surgery, then hernias and tumours. Proximal dilation, fluid sequestration and vomiting lead to hypovolemia and metabolic alkalosis. Strangulation adds ischemia. Paralytic ileus is loss of propulsion without a blockage (after surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, sepsis). Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) is massive colonic dilation without obstruction, thought to reflect excess sympathetic or reduced parasympathetic tone, typically after surgery or severe illness.

Appendicitis

Luminal obstruction (fecalith in adults, lymphoid hyperplasia in children) raises pressure, impairs venous drainage and permits bacterial invasion. Early distension stimulates visceral afferents entering at about T10, felt as vague periumbilical pain; once the inflamed serosa irritates the parietal peritoneum the pain localises to the right lower quadrant. Anorexia and nausea usually follow the pain rather than precede it.

Visceral pain is poorly localised and midline because the gut is innervated bilaterally; parietal peritoneal pain is sharp and localised because it travels with somatic nerves.

s23d-s100503-s1.bodyHtml:
Anatomy of the anorectum

The rectum runs from the rectosigmoid junction to the anorectal junction, where the puborectalis sling creates the anorectal angle. The anal canal, about 3 to 4 cm long, ends at the anal verge. Within it lies the pectinate (dentate) line, formed by the anal valves at the bases of the anal columns. Anal glands open into the crypts at this level, which is why cryptoglandular abscesses and fistulas start here. The pectinate line marks the junction of hindgut endoderm (above) and ectoderm of the anal pit, the proctodeum (below), so almost every structure differs across it.

FeatureAbove the pectinate lineBelow the pectinate line
EmbryologyHindgut endodermEctoderm (proctodeum)
EpitheliumSimple columnar (glandular), transition zone near the lineStratified squamous, nonkeratinised then keratinised at the verge
Arterial supplySuperior rectal artery (from IMA)Inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal)
Venous drainageSuperior rectal vein to IMV and portal systemInferior rectal vein to internal iliac and IVC
Lymphatic drainageInternal iliac (and inferior mesenteric) nodesSuperficial inguinal nodes
InnervationVisceral (autonomic) afferents: stretch only, lesions painlessSomatic inferior rectal nerve (pudendal): lesions painful
Typical tumourAdenocarcinomaSquamous cell carcinoma
Vascular cushionsInternal hemorrhoidsExternal hemorrhoids

The middle rectal artery and vein (internal iliac system) supply the lower rectum and anastomose with the superior rectal vessels. In portal hypertension, the superior rectal (portal) and middle and inferior rectal (systemic) veins form a portosystemic anastomosis that can dilate into anorectal varices; these are distinct from hemorrhoids.

Sphincters and continence

  • Internal anal sphincter: thickened inner circular smooth muscle; provides most resting tone; involuntary. Sympathetic input increases tone; nitric oxide from inhibitory enteric neurons relaxes it. Rectal distension triggers reflex relaxation (rectoanal inhibitory reflex), which is absent in Hirschsprung disease because ganglion cells are missing.
  • External anal sphincter and puborectalis: striated, voluntary; generate squeeze pressure; innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) and direct sacral branches.

Continence depends on stool consistency, rectal capacity and compliance, intact sensation, the anorectal angle and both sphincters. Obstetric injury is the most common cause of incontinence in women, from sphincter tears or stretch injury to the pudendal nerve during prolonged second stage or instrumental delivery. Pudendal neuropathy lowers squeeze pressure with relatively preserved resting pressure.

Hemorrhoids

Hemorrhoids are normal vascular cushions that contribute to continence; they become symptomatic when straining, constipation, pregnancy or prolonged sitting cause engorgement and loss of supporting connective tissue. Internal hemorrhoids, above the line, bleed bright red blood without pain and may prolapse. External hemorrhoids, below the line and covered with anoderm, are painful when they thrombose. Internal hemorrhoids are graded by prolapse:

  1. Grade I: bleed, no prolapse.
  2. Grade II: prolapse with straining, reduce spontaneously.
  3. Grade III: prolapse, need manual reduction.
  4. Grade IV: prolapsed and irreducible.

Painless bleeding means an internal source above the pectinate line; severe pain means a lesion in the somatically innervated anoderm (fissure, thrombosed external hemorrhoid, abscess). Never attribute rectal bleeding in an older adult to hemorrhoids without considering colonoscopy.

Anal fissure

A fissure is a linear tear in the anoderm distal to the pectinate line, usually after passage of hard stool. Pain is severe, tearing and can last hours after defecation, with a little bright red blood. About nine in ten lie in the posterior midline, where perfusion of the anoderm is poorest. High resting tone of the internal sphincter compresses the small vessels, causing ischemia that prevents healing; spasm then raises pressure further. Chronic fissures develop a sentinel skin tag, a hypertrophied anal papilla and exposed sphincter fibres. Treatments lower sphincter pressure by mechanism:

TreatmentMechanismMain adverse effect
Topical nitroglycerinNO donor; activates soluble guanylate cyclase, raises cGMP, relaxes smooth muscleHeadache
Topical diltiazem or nifedipineBlocks L-type calcium channels in smooth muscleFewer headaches; local irritation
Botulinum toxin injectionCleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine releaseTemporary incontinence to flatus
Lateral internal sphincterotomyDivides part of the internal sphincterSmall risk of permanent minor incontinence

A fissure off the midline, multiple fissures, painless or nonhealing fissures suggest a secondary cause: Crohn disease, HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis or carcinoma.

Anorectal sepsis and pilonidal disease

Most anorectal abscesses begin as infection of an anal gland at the crypt. Pus tracks to the perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric or supralevator space. About a third or more of drained abscesses leave a fistula-in-ano, an epithelialised tract between the internal opening at the dentate line and an external opening on the skin. Fistulas are classified by their relation to the sphincters (intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric). Pilonidal disease arises in the natal cleft when hairs penetrate the skin through midline pits, causing a foreign body reaction, sinus formation and abscess, typically in hirsute young men.

Proctitis and anal neoplasia

Sexually transmitted proctitis follows receptive anal intercourse. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus; Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K cause mild proctitis, while serovars L1 to L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), which invades submucosa and lymphatics and can mimic inflammatory bowel disease. Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria that alternate between the infectious elementary body and the replicating reticulate body. Herpes simplex virus causes severe pain, vesicles and ulcers and can cause sacral radiculopathy with urinary retention. Radiation proctitis follows pelvic radiotherapy; late disease reflects obliterative endarteritis with telangiectasias.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma is driven mainly by high-risk HPV, especially type 16. Viral E6 binds p53 and targets it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation; E7 binds retinoblastoma protein (Rb), releasing E2F to drive the cell cycle. Precursor lesions are anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Risk is highest in people living with HIV, men who have sex with men, women with prior HPV-related genital neoplasia and organ transplant recipients. Tumours below the pectinate line spread first to superficial inguinal nodes. Rectal adenocarcinoma arises from the glandular mucosa through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, as elsewhere in the colon.

Rectal prolapse is full-thickness protrusion of the rectal wall with concentric folds; prolapsed internal hemorrhoids show radial folds separated by grooves. Hirschsprung disease is the congenital cause of a narrowed distal segment and absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex.

s23d-s100601-s1.bodyHtml:
Reading liver tests

"Liver function tests" mostly measure injury, not function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from damaged hepatocytes; ALT is more liver-specific, while AST is also found in muscle, heart and red cells. Alkaline phosphatase and GGT rise with cholestasis; a raised GGT confirms that a high alkaline phosphatase is hepatobiliary rather than bone. True synthetic function is reflected by albumin and the PT/INR (factors II, V, VII, IX and X are made in the liver; factor VII has the shortest half-life, so INR rises early in acute failure).

PatternMain abnormalityTypical causes
HepatocellularAST and ALT high out of proportion to alkaline phosphataseViral hepatitis, ischemia, drugs (including acetaminophen), autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease
CholestaticAlkaline phosphatase and GGT high out of proportion to aminotransferasesBiliary obstruction, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, infiltration, drugs
Alcohol-associatedAST:ALT ratio above 2, AST rarely above about 300 U/L, high GGTAlcohol-associated hepatitis and cirrhosis
Isolated hyperbilirubinemiaBilirubin raised, other tests normalHemolysis, Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor

The AST:ALT ratio exceeds 2 in alcohol-associated disease because alcohol damages mitochondria (which contain an AST isoenzyme) and because deficiency of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, the cofactor for both enzymes, depresses ALT activity more than AST.

Bilirubin metabolism

Macrophages degrade heme from senescent red cells: heme oxygenase opens the ring to biliverdin, releasing iron and carbon monoxide, and biliverdin reductase forms unconjugated bilirubin. This water-insoluble pigment travels bound to albumin and cannot be filtered by the kidney. Hepatocytes take it up through sinusoidal transporters (OATP1B1 and OATP1B3), and UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) conjugates it with glucuronic acid. Conjugated bilirubin is secreted into bile by the canalicular pump MRP2, the rate-limiting step. In the colon, bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; some is reabsorbed and excreted in urine as urobilin, and the rest is oxidised to stercobilin, which colours stool brown.

DisorderDefectBilirubin typeKey features
Gilbert syndromeReduced UGT1A1 expression (promoter variant)UnconjugatedMild jaundice with fasting, illness or stress; benign
Crigler-Najjar type IAbsent UGT1A1 activityUnconjugated, very highNeonatal kernicterus risk; no response to phenobarbital; phototherapy, liver transplant
Crigler-Najjar type IISeverely reduced UGT1A1UnconjugatedBilirubin falls with phenobarbital (enzyme induction)
Dubin-Johnson syndromeDefective MRP2 (ABCC2)ConjugatedBlack liver from pigment; worsened by estrogens and pregnancy; benign
Rotor syndromeDeficient OATP1B1 and OATP1B3ConjugatedNo pigment; benign

Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia makes urine dark because conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered; unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and never appears in urine, so hemolysis and Gilbert produce jaundice without bilirubinuria.

Alcohol-associated liver disease

Ethanol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase and, with chronic use, by the inducible CYP2E1 system; both generate NADH. A high NADH:NAD+ ratio blocks fatty acid oxidation and favours triglyceride synthesis, producing steatosis, and also diverts pyruvate to lactate and inhibits gluconeogenesis. Acetaldehyde forms protein adducts, and CYP2E1 activity generates reactive oxygen species. The spectrum runs from steatosis (reversible with abstinence) to alcohol-associated hepatitis and cirrhosis. Biopsy in hepatitis shows ballooned hepatocytes, neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies (aggregates of damaged keratin 8 and 18 intermediate filaments bound to ubiquitin) and perivenular, pericellular fibrosis. Hepatic stellate cells, activated by injury and cytokines such as TGF-beta, deposit the collagen of fibrosis.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease

MASLD replaces the term NAFLD: steatotic liver disease in a person with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight or central obesity, dysglycemia, hypertension, high triglycerides or low HDL) without another cause. MASH (formerly NASH) adds inflammation and ballooning. People who also drink moderate amounts fall into a combined category (MetALD). Insulin resistance increases lipolysis in adipose tissue, delivering free fatty acids to the liver, and hyperinsulinemia promotes hepatic de novo lipogenesis; lipotoxicity then drives hepatocyte injury. Fibrosis stage is the strongest predictor of outcome, and the leading cause of death is cardiovascular disease.

Inherited metabolic liver disease

  • HFE hemochromatosis: autosomal recessive, usually C282Y homozygosity. Low hepcidin lets ferroportin export iron freely from enterocytes and macrophages, so iron accumulates in liver, pancreas, heart, joints, skin and pituitary. Free iron generates hydroxyl radicals (Fenton reaction). Biopsy shows hemosiderin that stains with Prussian blue, initially in periportal hepatocytes. Women present later because menstruation and pregnancy remove iron.
  • Wilson disease: autosomal recessive mutation of ATP7B on chromosome 13, a copper-transporting ATPase that loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and exports it into bile. Copper accumulates in liver, then spills into blood, brain (basal ganglia: tremor, dysarthria, parkinsonism, psychiatric change), cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings in Descemet membrane) and red cells (Coombs-negative hemolysis). Ceruloplasmin is low because apoceruloplasmin without copper is rapidly degraded; urinary copper is high.
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: codominant SERPINA1 mutation; the PiZ protein misfolds, polymerises and is trapped in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, seen as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules, mainly periportal. The liver disease is a toxic gain of function (retained protein); the lung disease, panacinar emphysema, is a loss of function (unopposed neutrophil elastase).

Copper chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine increases urinary copper excretion; zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which binds dietary copper so it is lost when cells slough. Penicillamine can worsen neurologic symptoms early and causes rash, proteinuria and cytopenias; it antagonises pyridoxine.

Cirrhosis and its consequences

Cirrhosis is diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules that distort architecture. Increased intrahepatic resistance plus splanchnic vasodilation (mediated largely by nitric oxide) produce portal hypertension. Arterial underfilling activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, the sympathetic system and vasopressin, causing sodium and water retention (ascites, hyponatremia) and renal vasoconstriction (hepatorenal syndrome). Reduced hepatic clearance of estrogen causes spider angiomas, palmar erythema and gynecomastia.

Hepatic encephalopathy results largely from ammonia produced by gut bacteria and enterocyte glutaminase that escapes hepatic clearance through portosystemic shunts. Astrocytes detoxify ammonia by forming glutamine, which swells them; increased GABAergic tone contributes. Lactulose, a nonabsorbable disaccharide, is fermented by colonic bacteria to short-chain acids; the acidic lumen converts NH3 to NH4+, which is trapped and excreted, and the osmotic laxative effect speeds removal. Rifaximin, a minimally absorbed rifamycin, inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase and lowers ammonia production.

Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (hepatic veins or suprahepatic IVC), most often from thrombosis in a myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2 V617F), other thrombophilias, pregnancy or estrogen use. Congestion causes centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis, tender hepatomegaly and ascites; the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC, often enlarges. Acute liver failure is severe acute injury with coagulopathy and encephalopathy in a person without preexisting cirrhosis; the most common cause in the United States is acetaminophen toxicity (covered with drug-induced injury).

content.text: "Liver function tests" mostly measure injury, not function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from damaged hepatocytes; ALT is more liver-specific, while AST is also found in muscle, heart and red cells. True synthetic function is reflected by albumin and the PT/INR (factors II, V, VII, IX and X are made in the liver; factor VII has the shortest half-life, so INR rises early in acute failure).

Alkaline phosphatase and GGT high out of proportion to aminotransferases

s23d-s100602-s1.bodyHtml:
Bile: what it is and how it is made

Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi, which drain into interlobular bile ducts, the right and left hepatic ducts and the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct, which runs behind the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas to the ampulla of Vater, where it usually meets the main pancreatic duct. The sphincter of Oddi controls flow into the duodenum. Between meals the sphincter is relatively closed and bile is diverted into the gallbladder, which concentrates it by absorbing salt and water.

Bile is mostly water plus bile acids, phospholipid (chiefly phosphatidylcholine), cholesterol, conjugated bilirubin and electrolytes. Its main digestive job is to emulsify dietary fat and carry the products of lipolysis in mixed micelles to the enterocyte, which is essential for absorbing fat and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Bile is also the main excretory route for cholesterol and bilirubin.

  • Synthesis: cholesterol is converted to the primary bile acids cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid. The rate-limiting enzyme is cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase, which is feedback-inhibited by bile acids returning to the liver.
  • Conjugation: the liver conjugates bile acids with glycine or taurine. Conjugation lowers their pKa so they stay ionized in the gut lumen and are not passively absorbed in the proximal small bowel, where they are needed for micelles.
  • Secondary bile acids: colonic bacteria deconjugate and 7α-dehydroxylate primary bile acids to deoxycholic and lithocholic acid.
  • Bilirubin: unconjugated bilirubin from heme breakdown travels bound to albumin, is conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) and secreted into bile. Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; some is reabsorbed and excreted in urine, the rest becomes stercobilin, which colours stool.

Enterohepatic circulation and hormonal control

About 95% of the bile acid pool is reabsorbed, mainly by active sodium-dependent transport in the terminal ileum, and returned to the liver in portal blood. The small pool therefore cycles several times a day. Ileal resection or ileal Crohn disease interrupts the circuit. A short resection lets unabsorbed bile acids reach the colon, where they stimulate secretion (bile acid diarrhea, which responds to bile acid sequestrants). A long resection exceeds the liver's capacity to make new bile acids, so micelle formation fails and steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, gallstones and calcium oxalate kidney stones follow (unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon).

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids. It contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion. Secretin from S cells mainly drives ductal bicarbonate secretion and also increases bicarbonate-rich bile flow from cholangiocytes.

Gallstones

Cholesterol is insoluble in water and is held in bile only by bile acids and phospholipid. Stones form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, when nucleation is accelerated (mucin, sludge) and when the gallbladder empties poorly.

FeatureCholesterol stonesBlack pigment stonesBrown pigment stones
Main contentCholesterol monohydrateCalcium bilirubinate polymersCalcium bilirubinate with fatty acid soaps
Where they formGallbladderGallbladderBile ducts, including intrahepatic ducts
MechanismCholesterol supersaturation and gallbladder stasisExcess unconjugated bilirubin in sterile bileBacterial β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in infected, stagnant bile
Classic settingsFemale sex, pregnancy, estrogen therapy, obesity, rapid weight loss, fibrates, older ageChronic hemolysis (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis), cirrhosis, ileal diseaseBiliary strictures, liver flukes (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis), Ascaris; more common in East Asia
RadiographUsually radiolucentOften radiopaqueUsually radiolucent, soft and crumbly

Drug and nutrition angles: fibrates increase biliary cholesterol and inhibit 7α-hydroxylase; octreotide and prolonged fasting or parenteral nutrition reduce CCK-driven emptying and cause sludge; pregnancy combines estrogen-driven cholesterol secretion with progesterone-driven gallbladder hypomotility. Ursodeoxycholic acid is a hydrophilic bile acid that lowers biliary cholesterol secretion and can be used to prevent stones during rapid weight loss.

Ileal disease causes both cholesterol stones (bile acid loss) and black pigment stones (more bilirubin reaches the colon and is reabsorbed). Do not assume every gallstone in Crohn disease is a cholesterol stone; read the stem for hemolysis, radiopacity or stone colour.

Gallstone complications by site

  • Biliary colic: a stone transiently blocks the cystic duct while the gallbladder contracts. Pain is steady, not truly colicky, and settles within hours; there is no inflammation, so fever and leukocytosis are absent and liver tests are normal.
  • Acute cholecystitis: persistent cystic duct obstruction leads to distension, chemical injury of the mucosa (lysolecithin), ischemia and secondary infection, usually with enteric gram-negative rods. Histology shows edema, neutrophils and, if severe, gangrene.
  • Acalculous cholecystitis: gallbladder stasis and ischemia in critically ill patients (burns, major trauma, sepsis, prolonged parenteral nutrition, mechanical ventilation), without a stone.
  • Choledocholithiasis: a stone in the common bile duct causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT, dark urine, pale stools and pruritus. Infection of the obstructed duct causes acute cholangitis.
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: a stone at the ampulla obstructs pancreatic outflow.
  • Mirizzi syndrome: a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct and causes jaundice.
  • Gallstone ileus: a large stone erodes through an inflamed gallbladder wall into the adjacent duodenum (cholecystoenteric fistula), travels down the small bowel and lodges at the narrow terminal ileum, causing mechanical obstruction. Air in the biliary tree is a key clue.
  • Porcelain gallbladder: calcification of the gallbladder wall from chronic inflammation; it has been linked to gallbladder carcinoma. Gallbladder adenocarcinoma is strongly associated with long-standing gallstones.

A palpable, nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice points to slow malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct (often a pancreatic head cancer), not stones: a chronically inflamed, stone-filled gallbladder is fibrotic and does not distend.

Cholestatic and congenital duct disease

FeaturePrimary biliary cholangitis (PBC)Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
Typical patientMiddle-aged womanYoung or middle-aged man
Ducts affectedSmall intrahepatic (interlobular) ductsIntrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts of all sizes
HistologyLymphocytic, often granulomatous destruction of interlobular ducts (florid duct lesion)Concentric, onion-skin periductal fibrosis leading to fibro-obliterative scars
SerologyAntimitochondrial antibody against the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complexNo specific antibody; p-ANCA may be present
AssociationsSjogren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic sclerosisUlcerative colitis; cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal and gallbladder cancer
ImagingNormal large ductsMultifocal strictures with dilated segments (beading)

Both cause fatigue, pruritus and a cholestatic pattern with high alkaline phosphatase, and both can progress to biliary cirrhosis. Cholestasis also produces hypercholesterolemia with xanthelasma, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and osteoporosis. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis can mimic PSC but responds to glucocorticoids.

Choledochal (biliary) cysts are congenital dilations of the bile duct, most often a fusiform dilation of the extrahepatic duct. Many patients have an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction with a long common channel above the duodenal wall, which allows pancreatic juice to reflux into the bile duct and damage its wall. Presentation is abdominal pain, intermittent jaundice or a right upper quadrant mass, often in childhood and more often in girls. Cyst epithelium is at risk of cholangiocarcinoma, so the cyst is excised. Caroli disease is cystic dilation of the intrahepatic ducts from a ductal plate malformation and is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. Biliary atresia (progressive inflammatory obliteration of extrahepatic ducts in infants) is a separate entity that presents with persistent conjugated jaundice and acholic stools in the first weeks of life.

Exocrine pancreas: structure and secretion

Acinar cells make up most of the gland. They synthesize digestive enzymes, store them as inactive zymogens in apical granules and release them in response to cholecystokinin (CCK) and vagal acetylcholine. Ductal cells line the intercalated and interlobular ducts and secrete a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum and flushes enzymes out of the ducts. The main pancreatic duct usually joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater; the accessory duct drains through the minor papilla.

ProductSecreted asActivated byMain substrate or role
Trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidasesZymogens (trypsinogen and others)Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen; trypsin activates the restProteins and peptides
Pancreatic lipase with colipaseActive lipase; procolipase activated by trypsinNeeds colipase and bile saltsTriglycerides to monoglyceride and fatty acids
Phospholipase A2ZymogenTrypsinPhospholipids
AmylaseActiveNeeds chlorideStarch to oligosaccharides
BicarbonateDuctal fluidSecretin; CFTR chloride channel with chloride-bicarbonate exchangeNeutralizes acid; optimal pH for enzymes

Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border is the trigger: it converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other zymogens. Its congenital deficiency causes diarrhea, failure to thrive and hypoproteinemic edema in infancy. Inside the acinar cell, protection against early activation comes from zymogen packaging, the trypsin inhibitor SPINK1 and trypsin's ability to destroy itself (autolysis).

  • Secretin from duodenal S cells is released when luminal pH falls; it acts on ductal cells to secrete bicarbonate. Bicarbonate leaves through apical chloride-bicarbonate exchange and directly through CFTR.
  • CCK from I cells responds to fatty acids and amino acids; it stimulates acinar enzyme release (partly through vagal pathways) and contracts the gallbladder.
  • Somatostatin inhibits both, which is why octreotide reduces pancreatic output.
  • Pancreatic proteases also free vitamin B12 from haptocorrin (R-binder) in the duodenum so it can bind intrinsic factor; exocrine insufficiency can therefore cause B12 malabsorption.

Acute pancreatitis: mechanism and causes

Acute pancreatitis begins when trypsinogen is activated inside acinar cells, often by fusion of zymogen granules with lysosomes or by blocked secretion. Trypsin activates other enzymes, producing autodigestion. Phospholipase A2 and elastase injure membranes and vessel walls; lipase releases fatty acids from peripancreatic fat, which bind calcium (saponification) to form chalky fat necrosis and can lower serum calcium. Released cytokines produce a systemic inflammatory response that can progress to shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome and kidney injury.

CauseHow it injures the pancreasClue
GallstonesStone at the ampulla obstructs pancreatic outflow and may cause refluxRaised ALT early; stones on ultrasound
AlcoholDirect acinar toxicity, sensitizes cells to injury, protein plugs in ductsHeavy use, often repeated attacks
HypertriglyceridemiaLipase releases toxic free fatty acids; chylomicrons impair capillary flowLipemic serum; triglycerides usually above 1,000 mg/dL
HypercalcemiaCalcium triggers trypsinogen activationHyperparathyroidism, malignancy
Post-ERCPInstrumentation and contrast injure the ductPain within hours of the procedure
DrugsVarious, often idiosyncraticAzathioprine, valproate, didanosine, thiazides, sulfonamides
OthersIschemia, trauma, infection, scorpion venom, duct anomaliesMumps; blunt trauma in children

Familial chylomicronemia from lipoprotein lipase or apolipoprotein C-II deficiency causes extreme triglyceride elevation in childhood, with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis and recurrent pancreatitis.

Hereditary and genetic pancreatitis

  • PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen) gain-of-function mutations, autosomal dominant: trypsin resists autolysis or is activated too easily, so a single intracellular activation event is not shut off. Attacks begin in childhood, chronic pancreatitis follows and pancreatic cancer risk is much increased.
  • SPINK1 loss of function removes the first line of trypsin inhibition and acts mostly as a modifier that raises risk.
  • CFTR variants impair ductal chloride and bicarbonate secretion, so secretions are scant, acidic and protein-rich and plug the ducts.

Cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency

In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR leaves ductal secretions dehydrated and viscous. Inspissated material obstructs small ducts, retained enzymes destroy acini and the gland is replaced by fibrosis and fat, often starting before birth. Most patients are pancreatic insufficient from infancy, with bulky, greasy stools, poor weight gain and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K. Meconium ileus at birth and later diabetes related to cystic fibrosis reflect the same process. Islets are lost late, so diabetes appears after exocrine failure.

Chronic pancreatitis

Repeated injury leads to irreversible fibrosis, acinar loss, duct strictures and dilation, intraductal protein plugs that calcify, and eventually islet loss. Alcohol and smoking are the main risk factors; genetic variants, recurrent acute attacks and duct obstruction (strictures, tumours, pancreas divisum in some patients) contribute. The triad of late disease is calcifications on imaging, steatorrhea (once lipase output falls to a small fraction of normal) and diabetes (type 3c, with loss of both insulin and glucagon, so hypoglycemia is a risk with treatment). Pain is the dominant symptom. Enzymes are often normal in chronic disease because little acinar tissue remains. Fat malabsorption causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and osteoporosis.

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related disease. It typically affects older men and presents with painless obstructive jaundice and a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with a low-density rim, so it mimics cancer. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Serum IgG4 is often raised. Other organs may be involved: bile ducts, salivary and lacrimal glands, retroperitoneum and kidneys. It responds dramatically to glucocorticoids. Type 2 is a duct-centric disease of younger patients without raised IgG4 and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

A pancreatic pseudocyst is not a true cyst: its wall is fibrous and granulation tissue with no epithelial lining. A cystic pancreatic lesion lined by mucinous epithelium is a neoplasm (mucinous cystic neoplasm or intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm), which has malignant potential and is managed differently.

Low serum calcium in acute pancreatitis reflects calcium consumed by fat saponification and is a marker of severity; high serum calcium is a cause of pancreatitis. Read which comes first in the stem.

Phospholipase A2 and elastase injure membranes and vessel walls; lipase releases fatty acids from peripancreatic fat, which bind calcium (saponification) to form chalky fat necrosis and can lower serum calcium. Released cytokines produce a systemic inflammatory response that can progress to shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome and kidney injury.
Stone at the ampulla obstructs pancreatic outflow and may cause reflux

Lipase releases toxic free fatty acids; chylomicrons impair capillary flow

Instrumentation and contrast injure the duct

or apolipoprotein C-II deficiency causes extreme triglyceride elevation in childhood, with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis and recurrent pancreatitis.

(cationic trypsinogen) gain-of-function mutations, autosomal dominant: trypsin resists autolysis or is activated too easily, so a single intracellular activation event is not shut off. Attacks begin in childhood, chronic pancreatitis follows and pancreatic cancer risk is much increased.
loss of function removes the first line of trypsin inhibition and acts mostly as a modifier that raises risk.
variants impair ductal chloride and bicarbonate secretion, so secretions are scant, acidic and protein-rich and plug the ducts.

In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR leaves ductal secretions dehydrated and viscous. Inspissated material obstructs small ducts, retained enzymes destroy acini and the gland is replaced by fibrosis and fat, often starting before birth. Most patients are pancreatic insufficient from infancy, with bulky, greasy stools, poor weight gain and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K. Meconium ileus at birth and later diabetes related to cystic fibrosis reflect the same process. Islets are lost late, so diabetes appears after exocrine failure.

Repeated injury leads to irreversible fibrosis, acinar loss, duct strictures and dilation, intraductal protein plugs that calcify, and eventually islet loss. Alcohol and smoking are the main risk factors; genetic variants, recurrent acute attacks and duct obstruction (strictures, tumours, pancreas divisum in some patients) contribute. The triad of late disease is
(once lipase output falls to a small fraction of normal) and

(type 3c, with loss of both insulin and glucagon, so hypoglycemia is a risk with treatment). Pain is the dominant symptom. Enzymes are often normal in chronic disease because little acinar tissue remains. Fat malabsorption causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and osteoporosis.
Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is the pancreatic manifestation of

. It typically affects older men and presents with painless obstructive jaundice and a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with a low-density rim, so it mimics cancer. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Serum IgG4 is often raised. Other organs may be involved: bile ducts, salivary and lacrimal glands, retroperitoneum and kidneys. It responds dramatically to glucocorticoids. Type 2 is a duct-centric disease of younger patients without raised IgG4 and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

A pancreatic pseudocyst is not a true cyst: its wall is fibrous and granulation tissue with no epithelial lining. A cystic pancreatic lesion lined by mucinous epithelium is a neoplasm (mucinous cystic neoplasm or intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm), which has malignant potential and is managed differently.
Low serum calcium in acute pancreatitis reflects calcium consumed by fat saponification and is a marker of severity; high serum calcium is a cause of pancreatitis. Read which comes first in the stem.

s23d-s100801-s1.bodyHtml:
The peritoneal cavity and normal fluid balance

The peritoneum is a single layer of mesothelial cells on a thin connective tissue base. The parietal layer lines the abdominal wall and is innervated by somatic nerves, so parietal irritation gives sharp, well-localized pain and guarding; the visceral layer covers the organs and carries poorly localized autonomic pain. Normally only a small volume of lubricating fluid is present. Fluid moves across capillaries according to Starling forces, and peritoneal and hepatic lymphatics return the excess, mostly through the diaphragm into the thoracic duct.

Net filtration depends on capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure (pushing fluid out) against plasma oncotic pressure and interstitial hydrostatic pressure (holding it in), together with the permeability of the capillary wall. Ascites forms when filtration into the peritoneal space outpaces lymphatic return. Two broad mechanisms exist: raised hydrostatic pressure in the portal and hepatic sinusoidal bed (portal hypertension), and leaky or obstructed peritoneal surfaces and lymphatics (malignancy, infection, pancreatic juice, chyle).

Cirrhotic ascites: pathophysiology

  • Sinusoidal portal hypertension: fibrosis and regenerating nodules raise resistance to portal flow. Hepatic sinusoids are normally very permeable to albumin, so high sinusoidal pressure drives protein-containing lymph out of the liver surface; in cirrhosis, capillarization of sinusoids and the large hydrostatic gradient produce fluid with relatively little protein.
  • Splanchnic arterial vasodilation: portal hypertension and bacterial translocation increase production of vasodilators, chiefly nitric oxide. Splanchnic vessels dilate, the effective arterial blood volume falls and systemic blood pressure drifts down.
  • Neurohormonal activation: the kidney senses underfilling and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the sympathetic nervous system and antidiuretic hormone. The kidney avidly retains sodium (low urine sodium) and free water (dilutional hyponatremia). Retained fluid leaks into the abdomen as long as portal pressure stays high.
  • Low serum albumin from reduced hepatic synthesis lowers plasma oncotic pressure and adds to fluid shift, but it is a contributor, not the main driver.

Pushed further, renal vasoconstriction becomes intense and glomerular filtration falls despite structurally normal kidneys: this is hepatorenal syndrome. The tubules work normally, so urine sodium is very low, the sediment is bland and kidneys from such patients function when transplanted into other recipients.

Reading ascitic fluid: SAAG and protein

The serum-ascites albumin gradient (serum albumin minus ascitic albumin, measured the same day) reflects the hydrostatic pressure in the portal bed. A gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more indicates portal hypertension; less than 1.1 g/dL points to a peritoneal process. Ascitic total protein then separates causes within the high-gradient group: in cirrhosis the protein is low because capillarized sinusoids and liver scarring limit protein leak, whereas in heart failure or hepatic vein obstruction the sinusoids are normal and leak protein-rich lymph.

PatternSAAGAscitic proteinExamples
Sinusoidal portal hypertension1.1 g/dL or moreLow (below 2.5 g/dL)Cirrhosis, massive liver metastases
Postsinusoidal or cardiac1.1 g/dL or moreHigh (2.5 g/dL or more)Heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, Budd-Chiari syndrome
Peritoneal diseaseBelow 1.1 g/dLUsually highPeritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, pancreatic ascites
HypoalbuminemicBelow 1.1 g/dLLowNephrotic syndrome, severe malnutrition

Do not use the older transudate and exudate terms for ascites. Cardiac ascites is protein-rich yet caused by portal hypertension, and SAAG classifies it correctly when protein alone would mislabel it as an exudate.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

SBP is infection of ascitic fluid without a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. Enteric bacteria translocate across an edematous, leaky gut wall into mesenteric lymph and blood, then seed the ascites. Cirrhotic ascites has low protein and therefore low concentrations of complement and opsonins, so bacteria are cleared poorly; low ascitic protein is a recognized risk factor. Infection is usually monomicrobial: Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are most common, followed by streptococci (including Streptococcus pneumoniae) and enterococci. Anaerobes and multiple organisms are unusual and suggest a perforation instead. The defining finding is an ascitic neutrophil (PMN) count of 250/mm3 or more.

Secondary peritonitis arises from a perforated or inflamed viscus or abscess. The fluid has a very high neutrophil count and many organisms, including anaerobes, and the chemistry reflects intense local inflammation: high protein, low glucose (consumed by neutrophils and bacteria) and high LDH.

Other forms of ascites

  • Chylous ascites: milky fluid with a triglyceride level above 200 mg/dL, caused by disruption or obstruction of lymphatics. In adults, malignancy (especially lymphoma) is the leading cause; others are abdominal surgery or trauma, cirrhosis, tuberculosis and filariasis. Chylomicrons, absorbed by intestinal lacteals, give the milky appearance.
  • Pancreatic ascites: a disrupted pancreatic duct or leaking pseudocyst releases juice into the peritoneum, giving high ascitic amylase and a low SAAG. The same leak into the chest causes a pancreatic pleural effusion.
  • Tuberculous peritonitis: reactivation or hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis produces peritoneal nodules with caseating granulomas. Fluid is lymphocyte-predominant with high protein and low SAAG; smears and cultures are often negative, and adenosine deaminase in the fluid is raised. Risk factors are birth in an endemic area, HIV infection, cirrhosis and peritoneal dialysis.
  • Peritoneal carcinomatosis: tumour cells line the peritoneum (ovarian, gastric, colorectal, pancreatic primaries) and increase permeability; cytology is often positive.
  • Peritoneal mesothelioma: a rare malignancy of mesothelial cells strongly associated with asbestos exposure. Tumour cells are positive for mesothelial markers such as calretinin.

Pharmacology of diuretics in cirrhosis

DrugSite and mechanismKey adverse effects
SpironolactoneCompetitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist in principal cells of the collecting ductHyperkalemia; gynecomastia and impotence from androgen receptor antagonism
EplerenoneSelective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonistHyperkalemia, little gynecomastia
AmilorideBlocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in principal cellsHyperkalemia
FurosemideInhibits Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limbHypokalemia, volume depletion, azotemia, ototoxicity

Aldosterone antagonism is central because secondary hyperaldosteronism drives sodium retention in cirrhosis; loop diuretics alone work poorly. Combining the two keeps potassium balanced. NSAIDs blunt the renal prostaglandins that maintain glomerular filtration in cirrhosis and can precipitate kidney injury and diuretic resistance. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers lower an already low blood pressure and are generally avoided in patients with ascites.

Cirrhosis itself causes gynecomastia through raised estrogen relative to androgen, so a man with cirrhosis on spironolactone has two reasons for breast enlargement; switching to eplerenone or amiloride addresses the drug component.

s23d-s100901-s1.bodyHtml:
Abdominal wall hernias: anatomy first

A hernia is protrusion of a peritoneal sac, with or without contents, through a defect in the wall that normally contains it. Groin hernias are classified by where they leave the abdomen relative to two landmarks: the inferior epigastric vessels and the inguinal ligament.

The inguinal canal runs obliquely above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, from the deep (internal) ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, to the superficial (external) ring, a slit in the external oblique aponeurosis above the pubic tubercle. Its anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis (reinforced laterally by internal oblique), its posterior wall is transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), its floor is the inguinal ligament with the lacunar ligament medially, and its roof is formed by arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis. It carries the spermatic cord in males or the round ligament in females, plus the ilioinguinal nerve.

  • Indirect inguinal hernia: the sac enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follows the cord, sometimes into the scrotum. Cause is a patent processus vaginalis, the peritoneal outpouching that accompanies testicular descent and normally obliterates. It is the most common hernia in both sexes and at all ages, and is especially common in infants (more so in preterm infants and boys).
  • Direct inguinal hernia: the sac pushes straight forward through a weak posterior wall (transversalis fascia) medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, within Hesselbach triangle (medial: lateral border of rectus abdominis; lateral: inferior epigastric vessels; inferior: inguinal ligament). It is acquired, typical of older men, and usually exits only through the superficial ring, rarely reaching the scrotum.
  • Femoral hernia: passes below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath (lateral to medial: femoral nerve outside the sheath, then artery, vein, and canal containing lymphatics). The femoral ring is bounded by the inguinal ligament in front, pectineal ligament behind, lacunar ligament medially and femoral vein laterally. The tight, rigid ring gives femoral hernias the highest risk of incarceration and strangulation, so they are repaired even when asymptomatic. They are more common in women, but indirect inguinal hernias are still the most common groin hernia in women.
HerniaExit pointRelation to landmarksMechanismTypical patient
Indirect inguinalDeep inguinal ringLateral to inferior epigastric vessels, above inguinal ligamentPatent processus vaginalisInfants, young males; any age
Direct inguinalHesselbach triangleMedial to inferior epigastric vessels, above inguinal ligamentWeak transversalis fasciaOlder men, chronic straining
FemoralFemoral ring and canalBelow inguinal ligament, medial to femoral veinAcquired; narrow rigid ringOlder women; high strangulation risk
UmbilicalUmbilical ringMidline at umbilicusIncomplete ring closure (infant) or raised pressure (adult)Infants; adults with ascites, obesity, pregnancy
IncisionalPrior fascial incisionAlong the scarFailed fascial healingWound infection, obesity, smoking

Umbilical hernias in infants come from incomplete closure of the umbilical ring and usually close on their own in early childhood. In adults they reflect raised intra-abdominal pressure; in cirrhosis with tense ascites, skin breakdown over the hernia is dangerous. Incisional hernias follow failed healing of a fascial closure; wound infection is a major risk factor.

The landmark for direct versus indirect is the inferior epigastric vessels, not the inguinal ligament. Both inguinal hernias emerge above the ligament; only the femoral hernia lies below it. A bulge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral until proved otherwise.

Incarceration and strangulation

A hernia is reducible if contents return to the abdomen, incarcerated if they are trapped, and strangulated when trapped contents lose blood supply. The sequence is constriction at the neck, venous and lymphatic outflow obstruction, wall edema, rising tissue pressure, then arterial inflow failure, ischemeia, necrosis and perforation. Strangulated bowel causes a tense, tender, discolored hernia with fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis and rising lactate. A Richter hernia traps only part of the antimesenteric wall, so it can strangulate without complete obstruction.

Small bowel obstruction from adhesions

Fibrous bands form after peritoneal injury from surgery, infection or inflammation. In an adult who has had abdominal surgery, adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction; in someone with no prior surgery, look hard for a hernia. Obstruction produces proximal distension with swallowed gas, fluid sequestration in the bowel wall and lumen, vomiting with hypovolemia and metabolic alkalosis from gastric losses, and bacterial overgrowth. A closed-loop obstruction (both ends occluded, as with a band or volvulus) strangulates quickly.

Syndromes after gastric surgery

  • Early dumping (within about 30 minutes): loss of pyloric control delivers hyperosmolar chyme to the small bowel, drawing fluid into the lumen. Result: cramps, bloating, diarrhea and vasomotor symptoms (palpitations, flushing, light-headedness) from reduced effective plasma volume and released gut peptides.
  • Late dumping (about 1 to 3 hours): rapid glucose absorption drives an exaggerated, incretin-amplified insulin surge, then reactive hypoglycemia with sweating, tremor and confusion.
  • Afferent loop syndrome (Billroth II): kinking or stenosis of the duodenal limb traps bile and pancreatic juice; postprandial pain is relieved by forceful bilious vomiting that contains no food.
  • Blind loop syndrome: a stagnant limb allows small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Bacteria take up cobalamin (vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia) and deconjugate bile acids (fat malabsorption, steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency), while bacterial folate synthesis keeps serum folate normal or high.
Nutrient after Roux-en-Y bypassWhy it fallsClinical clue
IronDuodenum and proximal jejunum bypassed; less acid to reduce ferric ironMicrocytic anemia, low ferritin
Vitamin B12Little acid and intrinsic factor in the small pouchMacrocytosis, neuropathy
Calcium and vitamin DDuodenal bypass, fat malabsorptionSecondary hyperparathyroidism, bone loss
ThiamineLow stores plus persistent vomitingWernicke encephalopathy
Copper, folateProximal bypass, reduced intakeMyeloneuropathy (copper); macrocytosis (folate)

Esophageal rupture

Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural tear from a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed upper sphincter, typically during forceful vomiting. The weakest point is the left posterolateral wall of the distal esophagus, so air and gastric contents enter the mediastinum and often the left pleural space. The classic triad of vomiting, lower chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler triad) is present in only a minority. Mediastinitis and sepsis follow quickly. Contrast this with a Mallory-Weiss tear, a mucosal laceration near the gastresophageal junction that bleeds (hematemesis) but does not leak.

Trauma and perforation

The second to fourth parts of the duodenum are retroperitoneal and fixed across the vertebral column. A focused blow, such as a bicycle handlebar to the epigastrium in a child, crushes the duodenum against the spine, causing an intramural hematoma that narrows the lumen and presents a day or more later with bilious vomiting, or a tear that leaks into the retroperitoneum. The pancreas sits in the same plane and is injured by the same mechanism.

In blunt trauma the spleen and liver are the most commonly injured solid organs. Blood under the left hemidiaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) and produces referred left shoulder pain. Hollow viscus perforation (traumatic or from a peptic ulcer) releases gas that rises under the diaphragm; an anterior duodenal ulcer perforates into the peritoneal cavity, whereas a posterior ulcer tends to erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed.

Button batteries injure tissue by generating hydroxide at the negative pole where they touch moist mucosa, causing liquefactive necrosis within hours, so an esophageal battery is a time-critical emergency even when the child looks well.

s23d-s101001-s1.bodyHtml:
The primitive gut and its blood supply

During the fourth week, lateral and cephalocaudal folding of the embryo incorporates the dorsal part of the yolk sac into a tube lined by endoderm (epithelium and glands) and surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm (muscle, connective tissue, visceral peritoneum). The tube is divided by its arterial supply, and the same divisions predict autonomic innervation and referred pain: foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium, midgut pain around the umbilicus, hindgut pain in the hypogastrium.

DivisionArteryDerivativesParasympathetic supply
ForegutCeliac trunkEsophagus, stomach, duodenum to the major papilla, liver, gallbladder, pancreasVagus nerve
MidgutSuperior mesenteric arteryDuodenum beyond the papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal two-thirds of transverse colonVagus nerve
HindgutInferior mesenteric arteryDistal third of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate linePelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4)

The spleen is supplied by the celiac trunk but develops from mesoderm of the dorsal mesogastrium, not from gut endoderm. Below the pectinate line the anal canal is ectodermal, with somatic innervation (painful) and supply from the internal pudendal vessels.

Midgut herniation and rotation

Rapid growth of the midgut and liver outpaces the abdominal cavity, so in about the sixth week the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord (physiologic herniation). While herniated, and as it returns around the tenth week, it rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. This places the duodenojejunal junction to the left of the midline and the cecum in the right lower quadrant, with a broad mesenteric attachment that resists twisting.

  • Malrotation: incomplete rotation leaves the cecum high and near the midline, with fibrous peritoneal (Ladd) bands crossing and compressing the duodenum and a narrow mesenteric base that can twist around the SMA (midgut volvulus), compromising the whole midgut.
  • Omphalocele: herniated bowel fails to return; viscera sit in a midline sac of amnion and peritoneum into which the cord inserts. Often associated with chromosomal anomalies (trisomies 13 and 18), cardiac defects and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
  • Gastroschisis: a full-thickness body wall defect, usually to the right of a normally inserted cord, with bowel floating free in amniotic fluid and no covering sac. Usually isolated, associated with young maternal age; exposed bowel can be thickened, with intestinal atresia in some.

Both defects raise maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and are seen on prenatal ultrasound.

Foregut partitioning: esophageal atresia and tracheesophageal fistula

The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut and is separated from the esophagus by the tracheesophageal septum. Faulty partitioning yields esophageal atresia (EA) with or without tracheesophageal fistula (TEF). The most common form is a blind proximal esophageal pouch with the distal esophagus connected to the trachea. Fetuses cannot swallow amniotic fluid effectively, causing polyhydramnios. Newborns drool, cough and turn cyanotic with feeds, and a feeding tube coils in the upper pouch on radiograph. Air entering the stomach through a distal fistula produces a gas-filled abdomen; isolated EA without a fistula gives a gasless abdomen; an H-type fistula without atresia presents later with recurrent aspiration pneumonia and coughing with feeds. EA/TEF is part of the VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheesophageal, renal, limb anomalies).

Duodenum and pancreas

The duodenal lumen is temporarily occluded by epithelial proliferation and later recanalizes. Failure causes duodenal atresia or stenosis, strongly associated with trisomy 21. Most atresias are distal to the major papilla, so vomiting is bilious. Radiograph shows a double bubble (stomach and proximal duodenum) without distal gas. In contrast, jejunal and ileal atresias result from in utero vascular accidents, not failed recanalization.

The pancreas forms from a dorsal bud and a ventral bud. The ventral bud, which forms the uncinate process and part of the head, rotates behind the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud; the main pancreatic duct forms from the ventral duct joined to the distal dorsal duct. An annular pancreas forms when a bifid ventral bud migrates around both sides of the second part of the duodenum, creating a ring that can obstruct it. Pancreas divisum is failure of ductal fusion, so most pancreatic juice drains through the minor papilla.

Double bubble is not specific: duodenal atresia, annular pancreas and malrotation with Ladd bands or volvulus can all produce it. A double bubble with some distal gas in a newborn with bilious vomiting raises concern for malrotation.

Pyloric stenosis

Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric circular muscle develop after birth and obstruct the gastric outlet in the first weeks of life. Risk factors include male sex, first-born status, family history and macrolide exposure (erythromycin, azithromycin) in early infancy. Vomiting is nonbilious and projectile, and the infant is hungry afterward. A firm olive-shaped mass and visible gastric peristalsis may be felt and seen.

Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; the kidney preserves sodium and volume at the expense of pH, so aldosterone drives distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+, causing hypokalemia and, with severe depletion, paradoxical aciduria. Chloride depletion also impairs bicarbonate secretion by the collecting duct, sustaining the alkalosis.

Vitelline duct remnants and Meckel diverticulum

The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and normally involutes. Persistence of its intestinal end forms a Meckel diverticulum: a true diverticulum (all layers of the bowel wall) on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum, sometimes containing heterotopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. Acid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileal mucosa and causes painless rectal bleeding in young children. Other presentations include obstruction (intussusception lead point, volvulus around a band to the umbilicus) and diverticulitis mimicking appendicitis. A completely patent duct (vitelline fistula) drains intestinal contents from the umbilicus; a patent urachus, by contrast, drains urine.

Hirschsprung disease and biliary atresia

In Hirschsprung disease, neural crest cells fail to complete their craniocaudal migration, leaving a distal segment without ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses. The aganglionic segment always includes the rectum and extends continuously proximally; it stays tonically contracted, causing functional obstruction with a dilated proximal colon. It is associated with RET mutations and trisomy 21. Biopsy shows absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve fibers.

Biliary atresia is a progressive inflammatory, fibrosing obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts in early infancy, causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pale stools and dark urine, then biliary cirrhosis if untreated. Liver biopsy shows bile ductular proliferation, bile plugs and portal fibrosis.

Cleft lip and palate

DefectFailed fusionFeature
Cleft lipMaxillary prominence with the merged medial nasal prominences (intermaxillary segment)Cleft lateral to philtrum, may involve primary palate
Cleft palateLateral palatine shelves with each other, the nasal septum or the primary palateIsolated cleft palate is more often syndromic

The medial nasal prominences merge to form the intermaxillary segment (philtrum, premaxilla with incisors, primary palate); the secondary palate forms from the palatine shelves of the maxillary prominences. Cleft palate impairs suction, and dysfunction of the palatal muscles that open the eustachian tube predisposes to middle ear effusions.

Intussusception is acquired, not congenital, but a Meckel diverticulum is a classic pathologic lead point in a child outside the usual age range.

content.text: The primitive gut and its blood supply

During the fourth week, lateral and cephalocaudal folding of the embryo incorporates the dorsal part of the yolk sac into a tube lined by endoderm (epithelium and glands) and surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm (muscle, connective tissue, visceral peritoneum). The tube is divided by its arterial supply, and the same divisions predict autonomic innervation and referred pain: foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium, midgut pain around the umbilicus, hindgut pain in the hypogastrium.
Esophagus, stomach, duodenum to the major papilla, liver, gallbladder, pancreas
Duodenum beyond the papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal two-thirds of transverse colon
Distal third of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate line

The spleen is supplied by the celiac trunk but develops from mesoderm of the dorsal mesogastrium, not from gut endoderm. Below the pectinate line the anal canal is ectodermal, with somatic innervation (painful) and supply from the internal pudendal vessels.

Rapid growth of the midgut and liver outpaces the abdominal cavity, so in about the sixth week the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord (physiologic herniation). While herniated, and as it returns around the tenth week, it rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. This places the duodenojejunal junction to the left of the midline and the cecum in the right lower quadrant, with a broad mesenteric attachment that resists twisting.

NSAIDs and the gastroduodenal mucosa

Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2, the precursor of prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane. COX-1 is constitutive in gastric mucosa, platelets and kidney; COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation. Mucosal prostaglandins (mainly PGE2 and PGI2) stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintain mucosal blood flow, support epithelial renewal and reduce parietal cell acid secretion. NSAIDs injure the mucosa in two ways: systemic loss of COX-1 prostaglandins (the dominant mechanism, which is why parenteral and enteric-coated drugs still cause ulcers) and topical injury from weak acids trapped in epithelial cells. Platelet COX-1 inhibition (thromboxane A2) adds bleeding risk. COX-2-selective drugs (celecoxib) cause fewer ulcers but carry cardiovascular risk. NSAIDs also injure the small bowel and colon (erosions, strictures, diaphragm-like webs).

Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog that replaces lost prostaglandin: it reduces acid secretion and increases mucus and bicarbonate. Adverse effects are diarrhea and cramping; it stimulates uterine contraction and is contraindicated in pregnancy when used for ulcer prevention. Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly inhibit H+/K+-ATPase and are the usual prophylaxis.

Opioids, laxatives and the gut

Opioids act on mu receptors in the enteric nervous system to reduce propulsive peristalsis, increase segmental and sphincter tone and increase fluid absorption, producing hard stools and straining. Tolerance develops to sedation and respiratory depression but not to constipation or miosis, so opioid-induced constipation persists for the duration of therapy.

  • Peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists (PAMORAs): methylnaltrexone (a quaternary amine, subcutaneous or oral), naloxegol (PEGylated naloxone) and naldemedine do not meaningfully cross the blood-brain barrier, so they reverse gut effects without reversing analgesia. They are contraindicated in known or suspected mechanical obstruction.
  • Alvimopan is a PAMORA restricted to short-term inpatient use to speed recovery from postoperative ileus after bowel resection.
  • Lubiprostone activates type 2 chloride channels on enterocytes, increasing intestinal fluid secretion.

Stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl) increase motility and secretion. Chronic use of anthraquinones such as senna produces melanosis coli: brown-black colonic mucosa from lipofuscin-laden macrophages in the lamina propria, a harmless marker of use. Covert laxative misuse (eating disorders, factitious disorder) causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and volume depletion.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI)

Injury is either intrinsic (predictable, dose-dependent, e.g. acetaminophen) or idiosyncratic (unpredictable, immune or metabolic host factors, e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate, isoniazid). The pattern is classified by the R ratio: (ALT/upper limit of normal) divided by (alkaline phosphatase/upper limit of normal). R of 5 or more is hepatocellular, 2 or less is cholestatic, and in between is mixed.

Acetaminophen is mostly conjugated by glucuronidation and sulfation. A small fraction is oxidized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, a reactive electrophile normally neutralized by glutathione. In overdose the conjugation pathways saturate, more NAPQI forms, glutathione is depleted, and NAPQI binds cellular proteins, causing mitochondrial injury and necrosis. Damage is centrilobular (zone 3) because those hepatocytes have the most CYP2E1 and the least oxygen. Chronic alcohol use (CYP2E1 induction and low glutathione) and fasting increase risk. N-acetylcysteine provides cysteine to restore glutathione and also acts as a glutathione substitute.

DrugMain liver patternMechanism or feature
AcetaminophenHepatocellular, zone 3 necrosisNAPQI after glutathione depletion; dose-dependent
IsoniazidHepatocellular hepatitisToxic metabolites; risk rises with age and alcohol
Amoxicillin-clavulanateCholestatic or mixedIdiosyncratic, linked to clavulanate; often starts after the course ends
ValproateMicrovesicular steatosis, hepatic failureMitochondrial toxicity; highest risk in young children and mitochondrial disorders (POLG); also hyperammonemia
StatinsAsymptomatic aminotransferase riseSerious injury is rare
MethotrexateSteatosis and fibrosis with long-term useFolate antagonism; risk with alcohol, obesity, diabetes
AmiodaroneSteatohepatitis-like injury, possible cirrhosisPhospholipidosis; histology can resemble alcoholic hepatitis
Estrogens, anabolic steroidsBland cholestasisAlso hepatic adenoma

Amoxicillin-clavulanate injury often appears days to weeks after the antibiotic is finished, so the drug history must reach back beyond current medications. Amoxicillin alone rarely causes it.

Drug-induced pancreatitis

Drugs are an uncommon but important cause of acute pancreatitis, diagnosed after gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia and hypercalcemia are excluded. Mechanisms vary: immune or idiosyncratic reactions (azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, usually within the first weeks), direct toxic metabolites (valproate, didanosine, pentamidine), and indirect effects such as hypertriglyceridemia (estrogens, some retinoids) or hypercalcemia. Thiazides, L-asparaginase and corticosteroids are also implicated. GLP-1 receptor agonists have been associated with pancreatitis in reports, although causality is uncertain; they are stopped if pancreatitis is suspected.

Antibiotics and Clostridioides difficile

Antibiotics disrupt the colonic microbiota and the bile acid metabolism that normally restrains C. difficile spore germination. Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins and broad-spectrum penicillins carry the highest risk; age, hospitalization and acid suppression add risk. The organism is a spore-forming, gram-positive anaerobic rod. Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin) glucosylate Rho-family GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton and tight junctions, causing fluid secretion, inflammation and pseudomembranes of fibrin, mucus and neutrophils.

Pill esophagitis and other direct GI effects

Tablets that stay in contact with the esophageal mucosa, especially when taken lying down or with little water, cause local caustic injury, usually in the mid-esophagus where the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium narrows the lumen. Classic culprits are doxycycline and tetracycline, bisphosphonates (alendronate), potassium chloride, NSAIDs, iron and quinidine.

DrugGI effectMechanism
MetforminDiarrhea, nausea, bloating, metallic taste; B12 deficiency with long-term useDose-related intestinal effects; B12 malabsorption in the ileum
GLP-1 receptor agonistsNausea, vomiting, delayed gastric emptyingSlowed gastric emptying, central satiety effects
ErythromycinCramps, diarrheaMotilin receptor agonist
Colchicine, mycophenolateDiarrheaImpaired dividing epithelium
Verapamil, anticholinergics, ironConstipationReduced smooth muscle contraction or local effects
OrlistatOily stools, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencyPancreatic lipase inhibition

Immune checkpoint inhibitors

Monoclonal antibodies against CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) and PD-1/PD-L1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab) remove inhibitory signals that keep T cells tolerant. Antitumor immunity rises, but so does autoimmunity (immune-related adverse events). CTLA-4 blockade acts early in T-cell priming and causes colitis more often than PD-1 blockade, and combination therapy carries the highest risk. Colitis resembles inflammatory bowel disease histologically; hepatitis presents as asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation or a lobular hepatitis.

Tolerance never develops to opioid-induced constipation, so every patient started on a scheduled opioid needs a bowel regimen from day one.
