Approach to acute hepatitis

Marked aminotransferase elevation (often into the thousands) with jaundice points to viral, ischemic, toxic (acetaminophen) or autoimmune injury. The first viral panel is IgM anti-HAV, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and anti-HCV with reflex HCV RNA. Hepatitis E testing is added after travel to regions with poor sanitation or when other tests are negative. Always check the INR and mental status: a prolonged INR with encephalopathy defines acute liver failure and warrants transfer to a transplant centre.

HBsAgAnti-HBcAnti-HBsInterpretation
NegativeNegativePositiveImmune through vaccination
NegativePositive (IgG)PositiveResolved infection; can reactivate with strong immunosuppression
PositivePositive (IgM)NegativeAcute infection
PositivePositive (IgG)NegativeChronic infection (HBsAg present beyond 6 months)
NegativePositive (IgM)NegativeWindow period of acute infection

Hepatitis B: screening, treatment, prevention

CDC advises testing every adult at least once with HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs, and testing every pregnancy. Chronic HBV moves through phases: immune tolerant (HBeAg positive, very high DNA, normal ALT), immune active (high DNA with raised ALT or fibrosis), inactive carrier (HBeAg negative, low DNA, normal ALT) and HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (precore or core-promoter variants with raised DNA and ALT). Treatment targets immune-active disease, any patient with cirrhosis and detectable DNA, and acute liver failure. First-line drugs are entecavir and tenofovir (disoproxil fumarate or alafenamide), chosen for their high barrier to resistance; lamivudine is avoided because resistance develops quickly. Tenofovir disoproxil can cause proximal tubulopathy and bone loss; the alafenamide form has less renal and bone toxicity.

Anyone with HBsAg, or anti-HBc alone, who will receive rituximab or other potent B-cell depletion, chemotherapy or a stem cell transplant needs antiviral prophylaxis or close monitoring, because reactivation can be fatal. Patients with cirrhosis, and selected noncirrhotic carriers, need hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound (with or without AFP) every 6 months. Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers receive hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth; mothers with high viral loads are given tenofovir in the third trimester. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated.

Hepatitis C

Screen all adults at least once and every pregnant patient, and test repeatedly while risk continues. The screening test is anti-HCV; a positive result needs HCV RNA, because antibodies persist after cleared infection. Before treatment, estimate fibrosis (FIB-4 or elastography), test for HBV (DAAs can unmask HBV reactivation) and HIV, and review drug interactions. For most treatment-naive patients without decompensated cirrhosis, a pangenotypic regimen is used: glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks or sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks. Cure is a sustained virologic response (undetectable RNA 12 weeks after therapy). Key interactions: amiodarone with sofosbuvir (severe bradycardia) and acid suppression lowering absorption of some NS5A inhibitors. Cure does not remove HCC risk once cirrhosis is established, so surveillance continues.

A positive anti-HCV with undetectable HCV RNA means past, cleared infection (or a false-positive antibody). It needs no treatment, and reinfection is possible because antibodies are not protective.

Hepatitis A and E

Both are managed supportively. HAV post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks: hepatitis A vaccine for healthy people 1 year and older; immune globulin for infants under 12 months and for people who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease. HEV in pregnancy (especially in the third trimester) can cause acute liver failure, and chronic HEV in transplant recipients may respond to lowering immunosuppression.

Helicobacter pylori

Test patients with peptic ulcer disease (current or past), gastric MALT lymphoma, uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features in younger patients, unexplained iron deficiency, immune thrombocytopenia, and those starting long-term NSAIDs or aspirin when ulcer risk is relevant. Active-infection tests are the urea breath test, stool antigen and biopsy-based tests; serology cannot distinguish current from past infection. Hold PPIs for 2 weeks and antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks before a non-serologic test to avoid false negatives. When antibiotic susceptibility is unknown, bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days is the preferred first-line regimen; clarithromycin-based triple therapy is reserved for proven susceptibility. Every treated patient should have a test of cure at least 4 weeks after therapy.

Acute infectious diarrhea

Most episodes are viral and self-limited; oral rehydration solution (glucose-sodium cotransport is preserved even when secretion is high) is the cornerstone. Stool testing (usually a multiplex PCR panel) is reserved for fever, bloody stools, severe illness, symptoms beyond about a week, immunocompromise, hospitalisation, or outbreaks. Avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents when Shiga toxin-producing E. coli is suspected, because they may raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome; monitor the blood count and creatinine instead. Azithromycin is preferred for empiric treatment of dysentery in travelers because fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter is widespread. Giardia is treated with tinidazole, nitazoxanide or metronidazole; Cryptosporidium with nitazoxanide in immunocompetent hosts, while immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy is key in advanced HIV.

Clostridioides difficile infection

Test only patients with new, unexplained diarrhea (3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours) who are not taking laxatives; never test for cure. Testing uses a nucleic acid amplification test or a multistep algorithm (GDH antigen plus toxin, with NAAT arbitration). Stop the inciting antibiotic when possible, review PPI use, and place the patient on contact precautions.

Hepatitis E testing is added after travel to regions with poor sanitation or when other tests are negative. Always check the INR and mental status: a prolonged INR with encephalopathy defines acute liver failure and warrants transfer to a transplant centre.
Resolved infection; can reactivate with strong immunosuppression

Screen all adults at least once and every pregnant patient, and test repeatedly while risk continues. A positive anti-HCV with undetectable HCV RNA means past, cleared infection (or a false-positive antibody). It needs no treatment, and reinfection is possible because antibodies are not protective.

Both are managed supportively. HAV post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks: hepatitis A vaccine for healthy people 1 year and older; immune globulin for infants under 12 months and for people who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease. Test patients with peptic ulcer disease (current or past), gastric MALT lymphoma, uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features in younger patients, unexplained iron deficiency, immune thrombocytopenia, and those starting long-term NSAIDs or aspirin when ulcer risk is relevant. Most episodes are viral and self-limited; oral rehydration solution (glucose-sodium cotransport is preserved even when secretion is high) is the cornerstone. Test only patients with new, unexplained diarrhea (3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours) who are not taking laxatives; never test for cure. Testing uses a nucleic acid amplification test or a multistep algorithm (GDH antigen plus toxin, with NAAT arbitration). Stop the inciting antibiotic when possible, review PPI use, and place the patient on contact precautions.

Inflammatory bowel disease: diagnosis

Suspect IBD with chronic diarrhea (bloody in UC), abdominal pain, weight loss, perianal disease or extraintestinal features. Check blood count, CRP and albumin, stool tests to exclude infection (including C. difficile), and fecal calprotectin, which separates inflammatory from functional symptoms. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies is the key diagnostic test; small-bowel imaging (CT or MR enterography) defines Crohn disease extent and strictures, and pelvic MRI maps perianal fistulas.

Therapy ladder

SituationUlcerative colitisCrohn disease
Mild diseaseMesalamine: rectal for proctitis, oral plus rectal for left-sided or extensive diseaseBudesonide for ileocecal disease; 5-ASA is not effective for Crohn disease
Induction of moderate to severe diseaseOral corticosteroids as a bridge; start an advanced therapyOral corticosteroids as a bridge; start an advanced therapy
Advanced therapiesAnti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, IL-23 p19 antibodies, JAK inhibitors, S1P modulatorsAnti-TNF (often with a thiopurine or methotrexate), vedolizumab, ustekinumab, IL-23 p19 antibodies, upadacitinib
Fistulizing or perianal diseaseNot applicableDrain abscesses (seton) first, then anti-TNF therapy (infliximab best studied)
SurgeryProctocolectomy is curative for colonic diseaseResection of strictures or refractory segments; disease often recurs at the anastomosis

Corticosteroids induce remission but should never be used for maintenance. Thiopurines and methotrexate act slowly and are used mainly to maintain remission or to reduce antibodies against anti-TNF drugs; infliximab combined with azathioprine is more effective than either alone. Current guidance favours starting an advanced therapy early in moderate to severe disease rather than waiting for failure of 5-ASA or immunomodulators. JAK inhibitors are generally used after anti-TNF failure or intolerance. Smoking cessation is a core Crohn disease intervention.

Acute severe ulcerative colitis

Six or more bloody stools a day plus systemic toxicity (tachycardia, fever, anemia or high inflammatory markers) define acute severe UC. Admit; give IV corticosteroids; send stool for C. difficile; start pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis despite bleeding; obtain an abdominal radiograph for toxic megacolon; and avoid opioids, anticholinergics and NSAIDs. Flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy can exclude CMV in steroid-refractory disease. If there is no adequate response after about 3 days of IV steroids, give rescue infliximab or cyclosporine, and involve colorectal surgeons early; colectomy is needed for failure of rescue, perforation, uncontrolled hemorrhage or toxic megacolon that does not improve.

Do not start a slow-acting drug (azathioprine, vedolizumab) as rescue in acute severe UC. These take weeks to work; the rescue choices are infliximab, cyclosporine or colectomy.

Safety before and during immunosuppression

  • Before anti-TNF or other biologics and JAK inhibitors: screen for latent tuberculosis (IGRA or skin test) and hepatitis B; update inactivated vaccines; give live vaccines (such as MMR or varicella if non-immune) before immunosuppression begins, not during it.
  • Before thiopurines: TPMT (and where available NUDT15) testing; then monitor blood counts and liver tests. Thiopurines raise the risk of nonmelanoma skin cancer and lymphoma, including hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma in young men on combination therapy.
  • Anti-TNF drugs are avoided in moderate to severe heart failure and demyelinating disease.
  • Annual skin examination, cervical cancer screening per guidelines, bone health checks with prolonged steroid exposure.

Colorectal cancer surveillance in IBD

Begin surveillance colonoscopy about 8 years after symptom onset in UC extending beyond the rectum and in Crohn colitis involving at least a third of the colon, then repeat every 1 to 3 years according to risk. Patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis are an exception: start surveillance at the time PSC is diagnosed and repeat annually. High-definition colonoscopy with targeted or chromoendoscopy-guided biopsies is preferred. Visible dysplasia that can be completely removed endoscopically may be resected and followed; invisible multifocal or unresectable dysplasia usually leads to colectomy. Proctitis alone does not raise colorectal cancer risk meaningfully.

Celiac disease

Test with IgA anti-tTG plus total IgA while the patient is eating gluten. If total IgA is low, use IgG-based tests (deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or tTG IgG). A positive test in an adult is confirmed with upper endoscopy and multiple duodenal biopsies, including the bulb, still on a gluten-containing diet. A patient already on a gluten-free diet needs a supervised gluten challenge before testing, or HLA typing to rule the disease out. Treatment is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with a dietitian; check iron, folate, vitamin D and other deficiencies, assess bone density, and follow serology to monitor adherence. Persistent symptoms usually reflect gluten exposure; true refractory celiac disease is rare and needs evaluation for lymphoma. Dermatitis herpetiformis responds to dapsone (check G6PD first) plus the gluten-free diet.

Selective IgA deficiency is more common in people with celiac disease and makes IgA tTG falsely negative. Always order total IgA with the screening test.

Other disorders

  • Microscopic colitis: chronic watery diarrhea, often nocturnal, in an older adult with a normal-looking colonoscopy. Random biopsies from the right and left colon make the diagnosis. Stop possible culprit drugs (NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs) and treat with oral budesonide; test for celiac disease when symptoms persist.
  • Eosinophilic esophagitis: dysphagia or food impaction in an atopic adolescent or young adult. Diagnose with multiple esophageal biopsies at two or more levels showing 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field after excluding other causes. First-line options are PPI therapy, swallowed topical corticosteroids (budesonide or fluticasone) or dietary elimination; dupilumab is an option for refractory disease; dilate fibrotic strictures. Food impaction that does not pass requires urgent endoscopy.
  • Autoimmune hepatitis: often a young or middle-aged woman with fatigue or acute hepatitis, raised IgG and ANA or anti-smooth muscle antibody; biopsy confirms. Treat with prednisone plus azathioprine, or budesonide plus azathioprine in patients without cirrhosis. Exclude drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (minocycline, nitrofurantoin).
  • Autoimmune gastritis: macrocytic anemia or neuropathy with anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (specific) or anti-parietal cell antibodies (sensitive) and high gastrin. Replace B12 (intramuscular, or high-dose oral) and perform endoscopy to assess for neuroendocrine tumours and neoplasia.
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis: cholestatic liver tests in a patient with UC; MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilations. Lifelong surveillance covers cholangiocarcinoma (imaging with or without CA 19-9), gallbladder polyps (cholecystectomy) and colorectal neoplasia (annual colonoscopy). No drug has been shown to alter survival; liver transplantation treats end-stage disease.

s23d-s100201-s2.bodyHtml:
Colorectal polyps found at colonoscopy

Nearly all polyps found at colonoscopy are removed and sent for histology, because appearance alone does not reliably predict histology or dysplasia. Small polyps are usually removed with a cold snare. Large flat lesions are removed by endoscopic mucosal resection, sometimes in pieces, and the site is checked for residual tissue. A finding of more than 10 adenomas over a lifetime, or adenomas at a young age, should prompt genetic evaluation for a polyposis syndrome.

Surveillance after polypectomy (US Multi-Society Task Force, 2020)

Finding at a high-quality, complete colonoscopyNext colonoscopy
Normal examination10 years
1-2 tubular adenomas smaller than 10 mm7-10 years
3-4 tubular adenomas smaller than 10 mm3-5 years
5-10 tubular adenomas smaller than 10 mm3 years
Adenoma 10 mm or larger, or with villous histology or high-grade dysplasia3 years
More than 10 adenomas1 year (and consider genetic testing)
Adenoma or serrated lesion 20 mm or larger removed piecemeal6 months
Hyperplastic polyps smaller than 10 mm (up to 20)10 years
Hyperplastic polyp 10 mm or larger3-5 years
1-2 sessile serrated lesions smaller than 10 mm5-10 years
3-4 sessile serrated lesions smaller than 10 mm3-5 years
Sessile serrated lesion 10 mm or larger, with dysplasia, or traditional serrated adenoma3 years

These intervals assume a complete examination to the cecum with adequate bowel preparation and complete polyp removal. A poor preparation needs repeat colonoscopy within about a year. Surveillance should stop when the risks outweigh the benefits, which is weighed carefully in adults older than 75 and in those with limited life expectancy.

Small hyperplastic polyps do not shorten the interval: a patient whose only findings are small hyperplastic polyps returns in 10 years, as after a normal examination. Do not confuse them with sessile serrated lesions.

Hereditary polyposis: management

In familial adenomatous polyposis, at-risk relatives undergo genetic testing for the family APC variant; carriers start colonoscopy in childhood (around 10 to 12 years) and repeat it annually. Colectomy is planned once polyp burden can no longer be managed endoscopically, usually in late adolescence or early adulthood: total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis when the rectum is heavily involved, or colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis when rectal polyps are few (with lifelong rectal surveillance). After colectomy, upper endoscopy with a side-viewing scope monitors duodenal and ampullary adenomas, which are a leading cause of cancer death. Peutz-Jeghers and juvenile polyposis need surveillance of both upper and lower tract beginning in childhood, plus cancer screening for the extra-intestinal organs at risk.

Incidental liver lesions

An incidental liver lesion seen on ultrasound is characterised with multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI or CT. Most lesions can be diagnosed from imaging alone; biopsy is reserved for indeterminate lesions.

LesionImaging cluesManagement
HemangiomaPeripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in; very bright on T2No follow-up if typical and asymptomatic; avoid biopsy
Focal nodular hyperplasiaHomogeneous arterial enhancement, central scar that enhances late; retains hepatobiliary contrastNo treatment or follow-up when typical; oral contraceptives may continue
Hepatocellular adenomaArterial enhancement, may contain fat or hemorrhage; usually hypointense in the hepatobiliary phaseStop estrogen, lose weight; resect if 5 cm or larger after 6 months, in men at any size, or beta-catenin subtype; embolise if bleeding
Simple cystThin wall, no septations or nodules, water signalNo follow-up if asymptomatic; septations or nodules suggest a mucinous cystic neoplasm

A ruptured adenoma presents with sudden right upper quadrant pain and hemorrhagic shock; resuscitate and treat with transarterial embolisation, with later resection. Pregnancy should be discussed beforehand in women with adenomas because hormonal stimulation can enlarge them; small adenomas are usually monitored by ultrasound during pregnancy.

Pancreatic cysts

Cross-sectional imaging with pancreatic-protocol MRI and MRCP is preferred to characterise a cyst and its relation to the duct. Features of concern (often called worrisome features) include a cyst 3 cm or larger, a thickened or enhancing wall, a main duct of 5-9 mm, a non-enhancing mural nodule, an abrupt change in duct calibre, rising CA 19-9 and rapid growth; these lead to endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration. High-risk stigmata (obstructive jaundice from a cyst in the head, an enhancing solid component, or a main duct of 10 mm or more) lead to surgical evaluation. Cyst fluid that is viscous, mucin-rich and high in CEA favours a mucinous lesion; very high amylase favours a pseudocyst or a lesion that communicates with the duct. Main-duct IPMN and mucinous cystic neoplasms are usually resected in fit patients; branch-duct IPMN without concerning features is followed with imaging; asymptomatic serous cystadenoma needs no resection.

Before calling a cyst after pancreatitis a pseudocyst, ask whether the history fits. A cyst in a middle-aged woman with no pancreatitis history, or one with septations or a nodule, should be evaluated as a possible mucinous neoplasm.

Older adults, medications and lifestyle

In adults older than 75, the decision to continue surveillance weighs prior findings, comorbidity and the risks of bowel preparation (dehydration, electrolyte shifts) and sedation; a history of only small low-risk adenomas is a reasonable point to stop. Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs are managed around polypectomy because of delayed bleeding after removal of large polyps; cold snare removal of small polyps is generally safe on continued antiplatelet therapy. Physical activity, avoiding smoking, limiting red and processed meat and maintaining a healthy weight are associated with fewer adenomas. Hepatocellular adenoma is linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome as well as estrogen, so weight loss is part of management.

Benign mesenchymal tumours

Lipomas and leiomyomas found incidentally need no treatment unless they bleed, obstruct or cause intussusception. A submucosal lesion of uncertain nature is assessed by endoscopic ultrasound; a hypoechoic lesion from the muscularis propria may be biopsied to separate leiomyoma from GIST, which has malignant potential.

Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs are managed around polypectomy because of delayed bleeding after removal of large polyps; cold snare removal of small polyps is generally safe on continued antiplatelet therapy. Physical activity, avoiding smoking, limiting red and processed meat and maintaining a healthy weight are associated with fewer adenomas. Hepatocellular adenoma is linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome as well as estrogen, so weight loss is part of management.

Lipomas and leiomyomas found incidentally need no treatment unless they bleed, obstruct or cause intussusception. A submucosal lesion of uncertain nature is assessed by endoscopic ultrasound; a hypoechoic lesion from the muscularis propria may be biopsied to separate leiomyoma from GIST, which has malignant potential.

Step 2 CK questions on GI cancer ask who to screen and how, which test comes first, how to stage, and what the first treatment is. Most gastrointestinal cancers present late with weight loss, anaemia, dysphagia, jaundice or obstruction, so prevention and surveillance carry the most marks.

Colorectal cancer screening and diagnosis

For average-risk adults the USPSTF (2021) recommends screening from age 45 through 75, with individualised decisions from 76 to 85. Acceptable strategies include colonoscopy every 10 years, annual faecal immunochemical test (FIT), stool DNA-FIT every 1 to 3 years, CT colonography every 5 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years (or every 10 years combined with annual FIT). Any positive non-colonoscopy test must be followed by colonoscopy. A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer or an advanced adenoma diagnosed before age 60 (or two affected first-degree relatives) means colonoscopy every 5 years starting at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest relative's diagnosis, whichever is earlier; with one relative diagnosed at 60 or older, start at 40 with average-risk intervals.

GroupStartPreferred approach
Average riskAge 45Any USPSTF-endorsed test; colonoscopy every 10 years
First-degree relative with CRC40, or 10 years before relative's diagnosisColonoscopy, shorter interval
Lynch syndromeEarly adulthood (gene-specific)Colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years
Familial adenomatous polyposisChildhood or adolescenceAnnual endoscopy, then prophylactic colectomy
Ulcerative or Crohn colitisAbout 8 years after onset of extensive colitisSurveillance colonoscopy

Iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman, rectal bleeding after middle age, or a change in bowel habit needs diagnostic colonoscopy (often with upper endoscopy), not a stool test. Faecal occult blood testing is a screening tool for asymptomatic people only.

A negative stool test does nothing to exclude cancer in a symptomatic patient. Iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious source in an older adult means bidirectional endoscopy.

Colorectal cancer staging and treatment

Once colonoscopic biopsy confirms cancer, stage with contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and a baseline CEA. Rectal cancer adds pelvic MRI to define depth, nodal status and the circumferential margin. Tumour-node-metastasis staging guides therapy: stages I and II colon cancer usually need resection alone (with selective chemotherapy for high-risk stage II); stage III (node-positive) colon cancer needs resection plus adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX); locally advanced rectal cancer receives neoadjuvant chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy before resection. Every new colorectal cancer should be tested for mismatch repair deficiency (immunohistochemistry or MSI testing) to screen for Lynch syndrome and to identify tumours likely to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors. After curative resection, follow-up includes periodic history, CEA, CT imaging and colonoscopy at one year.

Esophageal and gastric cancer

Progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids with weight loss suggests esophageal cancer; the first test is upper endoscopy with biopsy. Staging uses CT, PET-CT and endoscopic ultrasound for depth and nodes. Barrett esophagus without dysplasia is managed with a proton pump inhibitor and surveillance endoscopy every 3 to 5 years depending on segment length. Confirmed dysplasia (low grade, and always high grade) or intramucosal cancer is treated with endoscopic eradication therapy: endoscopic resection of any visible lesion followed by ablation (radiofrequency ablation) of the remaining Barrett segment. Esophagectomy is reserved for deeper invasion.

Gastric cancer presents with dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia; diagnose by endoscopy with biopsies of any ulcer (gastric ulcers are biopsied, and re-scoped to confirm healing). Treat H. pylori when found, which lowers gastric cancer risk. Localised, H. pylori-positive gastric MALT lymphoma is treated first with eradication therapy, with endoscopic follow-up; radiation is used for persistent or H. pylori-negative disease. Carriers of germline CDH1 mutations are offered prophylactic total gastrectomy. GIST is resected when localised; imatinib is used for unresectable, metastatic or high-risk resected tumours.

Hepatocellular carcinoma

Adults with cirrhosis (and selected chronic hepatitis B carriers without cirrhosis) should have surveillance ultrasound with serum AFP every 6 months. A nodule under 1 cm is followed with repeat ultrasound in about 3 months; a nodule of 1 cm or more, or a rising AFP, needs multiphase contrast CT or MRI. In a high-risk liver, a lesion with nonrim arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout on portal venous or delayed phases (LI-RADS 5) is diagnostic of HCC, and biopsy is not required. Biopsy is for indeterminate lesions or a noncirrhotic liver.

Treatment follows tumour burden, liver function (Child-Pugh) and performance status. Options include resection for a solitary tumour in a well-compensated liver without portal hypertension, liver transplant within the Milan criteria (one lesion up to 5 cm, or up to three lesions each up to 3 cm, without vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread), thermal ablation for small tumours, transarterial chemoembolisation for intermediate disease, and systemic therapy (immunotherapy combinations or tyrosine kinase inhibitors) for advanced disease. Hepatitis B vaccination is the best primary prevention; antiviral therapy for HBV and cure of HCV reduce, but do not abolish, risk.

Pancreatic, biliary and anal cancer

Painless jaundice with weight loss in an older adult suggests a pancreatic head mass. The best initial test is a pancreas-protocol multiphase CT, which also assesses vascular involvement and resectability; endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration obtains tissue. CA 19-9 supports but never establishes the diagnosis (it is also raised by benign biliary obstruction and is absent in people who lack Lewis antigen). Resectable disease is treated with pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple) and adjuvant chemotherapy; many patients need biliary stenting and palliative chemotherapy. New unexplained venous thrombosis with weight loss should prompt a search for occult cancer guided by symptoms.

Cholangiocarcinoma is suspected in a patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis who develops a dominant stricture, worsening cholestasis or rising CA 19-9; MRCP and ERCP with brushings are the key tests. Gallbladder cancer found at cholecystectomy may need re-resection of the liver bed. Anal squamous cell carcinoma is diagnosed by biopsy and treated first with chemoradiation (5-fluorouracil and mitomycin), which preserves the sphincter; abdominoperineal resection is salvage for persistent or recurrent disease.

A tumour marker is never the screening test. AFP alone does not diagnose HCC, CA 19-9 alone does not diagnose pancreatic cancer, and CEA is a post-resection surveillance tool.

Neuroendocrine tumours

Flushing, watery diarrhoea and wheeze with hepatomegaly suggest carcinoid syndrome. Measure 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (avoid serotonin-rich foods beforehand) and image with CT or MRI and somatostatin receptor PET. Treat syndrome symptoms with a long-acting somatostatin analogue; before surgery, give octreotide to prevent a carcinoid crisis (hypotension, bronchospasm). Screen for carcinoid heart disease with echocardiography. An appendiceal carcinoid found at appendectomy is usually cured by the appendectomy when small.

Older adults: an asymptomatic person older than 85, or one with limited life expectancy, gains little from screening colonoscopy and carries higher procedural risk. Base decisions after age 75 on health, prior screening and preference.

Step 2 CK questions on metastatic GI disease test pattern recognition of signs of spread, the staging work-up, how follow-up after resection detects recurrence, which metastases can still be cured, and how to palliate obstruction and ascites while respecting the patient's goals.

Clinical signs of spread

On examination look for a hard left supraclavicular node, a periumbilical nodule, hepatomegaly with a hard or nodular edge, ascites, and a rectal shelf. In a woman, bilateral solid adnexal masses with weight loss and dyspepsia suggest Krukenberg tumours from a gastric primary. New jaundice in a patient with known cancer may be hepatic replacement or extrahepatic biliary compression by nodes at the porta hepatis; ultrasound or CT separates the two, and the second may be relieved by a stent. Bone pain, cough or neurologic change prompt targeted imaging.

Staging work-up

For a new colorectal cancer, stage with contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis plus a baseline CEA; add pelvic MRI for rectal cancer. MRI of the liver clarifies indeterminate lesions or maps metastases before resection. PET-CT is not routine at diagnosis but helps when CT is equivocal or before major metastasectomy to exclude occult disease. Gastric and esophageal cancer staging uses CT, endoscopic ultrasound and PET-CT; staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings is used in locally advanced gastric cancer because small peritoneal implants are invisible on CT. Pancreatic cancer is staged with pancreas-protocol CT.

QuestionBest test
Distant spread of colorectal cancerCT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast
Local extent of rectal cancerPelvic MRI
Characterising liver lesions before resectionContrast MRI of the liver
Occult peritoneal disease in gastric cancerStaging laparoscopy with washings
Cause of new ascites in a patient with cancerDiagnostic paracentesis with SAAG, protein and cytology

Tumour markers: follow-up, not screening

CEA, CA 19-9, CA-125 and AFP lack the sensitivity and specificity to screen healthy people: they are raised by smoking, cirrhosis, biliary obstruction, pancreatitis and inflammatory disease, and are normal in many early cancers. Their value is a baseline before treatment and serial measurement afterward. After curative resection of stage II or III colorectal cancer, follow-up for about 5 years includes periodic CEA, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and colonoscopy at 1 year. A rising CEA prompts CT imaging (and PET-CT if CT is negative) to look for resectable recurrence.

A healthy person who asks for a "cancer blood test" should be offered age-appropriate evidence-based screening (for example colonoscopy or FIT), not CEA or CA 19-9. A false-positive marker leads to cascades of imaging and anxiety.

Colorectal liver metastases: a curable stage IV

Unlike most metastatic cancers, isolated colorectal liver (and some lung) metastases can be cured by resection. The decision is made by a multidisciplinary team: can all disease be removed with clear margins while leaving an adequate, well-perfused future liver remnant, and is extrahepatic disease absent or also resectable? Number of lesions alone does not exclude surgery. Perioperative systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX or similar) is commonly combined with resection; unresectable disease may be converted to resectable after chemotherapy. Portal vein embolisation can enlarge a small remnant, and thermal ablation can treat small lesions. Patients with unresectable disease receive systemic therapy chosen by tumour biology: RAS and BRAF status, mismatch repair status (checkpoint inhibitors for MSI-high tumours), and sidedness. Neuroendocrine liver metastases are managed with somatostatin analogues, resection or liver-directed therapy.

Malignant ascites

New ascites in a patient with cancer needs diagnostic paracentesis: a SAAG below 1.1 g/dL with high protein and positive cytology indicates peritoneal carcinomatosis. Symptomatic tense ascites is relieved by therapeutic large-volume paracentesis; for rapidly reaccumulating fluid, a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter allows drainage at home. Diuretics help mainly when the SAAG is high (massive liver metastases with portal hypertension). TIPS is for portal hypertension and has no role in carcinomatosis. Selected patients with limited peritoneal disease from colorectal or appendiceal cancer may be candidates for cytoreductive surgery with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy at specialist centres.

Malignant bowel obstruction

Peritoneal carcinomatosis often causes partial or complete obstruction at several levels. CT confirms the level and number of transition points. Initial management is bowel rest, intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression for vomiting. Surgery (resection, bypass or stoma) suits a fit patient with a single site of obstruction and reasonable life expectancy; a self-expanding metal stent can relieve left-sided colonic or gastric outlet obstruction. For inoperable, multilevel obstruction, symptom control is pharmacologic: octreotide reduces gut secretions and vomiting, antiemetics such as haloperidol help nausea, opioids control colic and pain, and corticosteroids may reduce peritumoural oedema. Anticholinergics (hyoscine butylbromide) reduce colic and secretions. A venting gastrostomy avoids a long-term nasogastric tube. Prokinetics such as metoclopramide and stimulant laxatives are avoided in complete obstruction because they worsen colic.

SituationPreferred approach
Single obstruction, good performance statusSurgical resection, bypass or stoma
Left colon or gastric outlet obstruction, poor surgical candidateEndoscopic self-expanding metal stent
Multilevel carcinomatosis, inoperableOctreotide, antiemetic, opioid, steroids; venting gastrostomy

Parenteral nutrition is considered only for selected patients expected to live for months whose limiting problem is bowel failure rather than tumour progression; in most patients with far-advanced cancer it does not prolong life. Early palliative care involvement improves symptom control and helps align treatment with goals. Older adults are more prone to delirium from opioids and anticholinergics, so doses are started low.

Metastatic melanoma to the small bowel can present years after excision of the primary with iron-deficiency anaemia, melena or intussusception in an adult. Always ask about prior skin cancer when an adult has a small-bowel lead point.

Prognosis

Peritoneal carcinomatosis, malignant ascites and a Virchow node generally indicate incurable disease and limited survival, whereas resectable colorectal liver or lung metastases offer a real chance of long-term survival. Discussing prognosis honestly, eliciting goals and offering hospice when treatment no longer helps are core skills tested on Step 2 CK.

s23d-s100301-s2.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK questions on ill-defined GI symptoms ask you to separate the benign and functional from the dangerous: recognise alarm features, choose the one test that answers the question, correct fluid and electrolyte losses, and treat symptoms with drugs whose side effects you anticipate.

Acute abdominal pain: first steps

Assess haemodynamics and peritoneal signs first. Every person who could be pregnant needs a pregnancy test before imaging. Location narrows the differential (right upper quadrant: biliary disease, ultrasound first; epigastric: peptic ulcer or pancreatitis, lipase; right lower quadrant: appendicitis, CT in adults and ultrasound first in children and pregnancy; left lower quadrant in older adults: diverticulitis, CT). Pain out of proportion to examination in an older patient with atrial fibrillation suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia, and lactate may be normal early. Older adults and immunosuppressed patients may have catastrophic disease with few signs, so the threshold for imaging is low.

Chronic abdominal symptoms and alarm features

Alarm features shift the work-up from symptom treatment to investigation: unintentional weight loss, GI bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, persistent vomiting, a palpable mass, nocturnal diarrhoea waking the patient, new symptoms after middle age, and a family history of GI cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

DisorderKey featuresInitial evaluation
Irritable bowel syndrome (Rome IV)Recurrent pain at least 1 day per week for 3 months, related to defecation or a change in stool frequency or form; onset at least 6 months earlierCBC; celiac serology and faecal calprotectin or CRP if diarrhoea predominates
Functional dyspepsiaPostprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain or burning without structural causeUnder 60: test and treat H. pylori; 60 or older: endoscopy
Functional constipationHard, infrequent stools or straining without IBS-type pain dominanceClinical; colonoscopy only for alarm features or screening due

For IBS, a positive clinical diagnosis using Rome IV criteria is encouraged; routine colonoscopy is not needed in younger patients without alarm features. In diarrhoea-predominant symptoms, test for celiac disease (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA) and exclude inflammatory bowel disease with faecal calprotectin. Treatment includes reassurance, a low-FODMAP diet trial, soluble fibre (psyllium), antispasmodics, low-dose tricyclic antidepressants for pain, and gut-directed psychotherapy. For IBS with constipation, linaclotide or plecanatide; for IBS with diarrhoea, rifaximin, eluxadoline (avoid after cholecystectomy or with alcohol misuse, because of pancreatitis risk) or loperamide for stool frequency.

For dyspepsia, patients 60 or older need upper endoscopy. Younger patients are tested for H. pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen) and treated if positive; if negative or symptoms persist, a PPI trial and then a low-dose tricyclic or prokinetic follow.

Rome IV criteria do not protect against cancer. An older patient with new IBS-like symptoms, rectal bleeding or anaemia needs colonoscopy even if the pain pattern fits IBS perfectly.

Diarrhoea and dehydration

Acute watery diarrhoea is usually viral and self-limited. Stool testing is reserved for fever, bloody stools, severe illness, immunosuppression, recent antibiotics or hospitalisation (C. difficile), and outbreaks. Chronic diarrhoea (over 4 weeks) is approached by mechanism: stool electrolytes and osmotic gap, calprotectin, celiac serology, and colonoscopy with biopsies when indicated (microscopic colitis in older women taking NSAIDs or PPIs). In children with mild to moderate dehydration, oral rehydration solution in small, frequent volumes is first line; a single dose of ondansetron may help a vomiting child tolerate it. Intravenous fluid is for severe dehydration, shock or failure of oral rehydration. Sports drinks, juices and sodas have too little sodium and too much sugar.

Vomiting and metabolic alkalosis

Prolonged vomiting (gastric outlet obstruction, hyperemesis gravidarum, bulimia nervosa) produces hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with volume depletion. Treat with 0.9% saline plus potassium chloride; the kidney excretes the excess bicarbonate once volume and chloride are restored. Correct hypokalaemia before or alongside, and check magnesium. Persistent vomiting after a cause is excluded may be cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (chronic heavy cannabis use, relief with hot showers; definitive treatment is stopping cannabis).

Choosing an antiemetic

SettingPreferred drugCaution
Chemotherapy, postoperative nauseaOndansetron (plus NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone for highly emetogenic regimens)QT prolongation, constipation
GastroparesisMetoclopramide (short term)Tardive dyskinesia; limit duration
Motion sicknessScopolamine patch, meclizineUrinary retention, confusion in older adults
PregnancyDoxylamine-pyridoxineSedation
Parkinson diseaseOndansetron; avoid dopamine antagonistsMetoclopramide and phenothiazines worsen parkinsonism

Constipation

Ask about red flags (bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, family history of colorectal cancer, new onset in an older adult) and review drugs. Start with fibre and fluids, then osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol), then stimulants. For refractory chronic constipation, secretagogues (linaclotide, lubiprostone) or prucalopride; for suspected dyssynergic defecation, anorectal manometry and biofeedback. Opioid-induced constipation should be prevented with a stimulant or osmotic laxative when opioids start; if laxatives fail, a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine) restores bowel function without reversing analgesia. These are contraindicated in mechanical obstruction. In nursing home residents, faecal impaction may present as overflow diarrhoea.

Gastrointestinal bleeding: first steps

The ligament of Treitz divides upper from lower bleeding. Melena, haematemesis, coffee-ground emesis and a disproportionately raised BUN relative to creatinine (blood proteins digested and absorbed in the small bowel, plus volume depletion) point upstream. Brisk hematochezia with haemodynamic instability can also come from an upper source. Resuscitate first: two large-bore intravenous lines, crystalloid, and red-cell transfusion at a haemoglobin below 7 g/dL (a higher threshold in active coronary disease). Stop NSAIDs and antithrombotics where safe; reverse anticoagulation when bleeding is life-threatening. For suspected upper bleeding, give an intravenous PPI and perform upper endoscopy within 24 hours, after resuscitation. For lower bleeding, colonoscopy after rapid bowel preparation; CT angiography first if the patient is unstable with ongoing hematochezia. Risk scores such as Glasgow-Blatchford identify very-low-risk patients suitable for outpatient care.

Older adults on NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants present with more severe bleeding and fewer warning symptoms. Beta-blockers can mask tachycardia, so rely on orthostatic changes and urine output as well as heart rate.

content.text: Step 2 CK questions on ill-defined GI symptoms ask you to separate the benign and functional from the dangerous: recognise alarm features, choose the one test that answers the question, correct fluid and electrolyte losses, and treat symptoms with drugs whose side effects you anticipate.

Assess haemodynamics and peritoneal signs first. Every person who could be pregnant needs a pregnancy test before imaging. Location narrows the differential (right upper quadrant: biliary disease, ultrasound first; epigastric: peptic ulcer or pancreatitis, lipase; right lower quadrant: appendicitis, CT in adults and ultrasound first in children and pregnancy; left lower quadrant in older adults: diverticulitis, CT). Pain out of proportion to examination in an older patient with atrial fibrillation suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia, and lactate may be normal early. Older adults and immunosuppressed patients may have catastrophic disease with few signs, so the threshold for imaging is low.
Chronic abdominal symptoms and alarm features

Alarm features shift the work-up from symptom treatment to investigation: unintentional weight loss, GI bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, persistent vomiting, a palpable mass, nocturnal diarrhoea waking the patient, new symptoms after middle age, and a family history of GI cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

In diarrhoea-predominant symptoms, test for celiac disease (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA) and exclude inflammatory bowel disease with faecal calprotectin. Treatment includes reassurance, a low-FODMAP diet trial, soluble fibre (psyllium), antispasmodics, low-dose tricyclic antidepressants for pain, and gut-directed psychotherapy. For IBS with constipation, linaclotide or plecanatide; for IBS with diarrhoea, rifaximin, eluxadoline (avoid after cholecystectomy or with alcohol misuse, because of pancreatitis risk) or loperamide for stool frequency.

Acute watery diarrhoea is usually viral and self-limited. Stool testing is reserved for fever, bloody stools, severe illness, immunosuppression, recent antibiotics or hospitalisation (

), and outbreaks. Chronic diarrhoea (over 4 weeks) is approached by mechanism: stool electrolytes and osmotic gap, calprotectin, celiac serology, and colonoscopy with biopsies when indicated (microscopic colitis in older women taking NSAIDs or PPIs). In children with mild to moderate dehydration,

in small, frequent volumes is first line; a single dose of ondansetron may help a vomiting child tolerate it. Intravenous fluid is for severe dehydration, shock or failure of oral rehydration. Sports drinks, juices and sodas have too little sodium and too much sugar.
Prolonged vomiting (gastric outlet obstruction, hyperemesis gravidarum, bulimia nervosa) produces hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with volume depletion. Treat with

; the kidney excretes the excess bicarbonate once volume and chloride are restored. Correct hypokalaemia before or alongside, and check magnesium. Persistent vomiting after a cause is excluded may be cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (chronic heavy cannabis use, relief with hot showers; definitive treatment is stopping cannabis).
Ondansetron (plus NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone for highly emetogenic regimens)

Ask about red flags (bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, family history of colorectal cancer, new onset in an older adult) and review drugs. Start with fibre and fluids, then osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol), then stimulants. For refractory chronic constipation, secretagogues (linaclotide, lubiprostone) or prucalopride; for suspected dyssynergic defecation, anorectal manometry and biofeedback.

should be prevented with a stimulant or osmotic laxative when opioids start; if laxatives fail, a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine) restores bowel function without reversing analgesia. These are contraindicated in mechanical obstruction. In nursing home residents, faecal impaction may present as overflow diarrhoea.

The ligament of Treitz divides upper from lower bleeding. Melena, haematemesis, coffee-ground emesis and a disproportionately raised BUN relative to creatinine (blood proteins digested and absorbed in the small bowel, plus volume depletion) point upstream. Brisk hematochezia with haemodynamic instability can also come from an upper source. Resuscitate first: two large-bore intravenous lines, crystalloid, and red-cell transfusion at a haemoglobin below 7 g/dL (a higher threshold in active coronary disease). Stop NSAIDs and antithrombotics where safe; reverse anticoagulation when bleeding is life-threatening. For suspected upper bleeding, give an intravenous PPI and perform upper endoscopy within 24 hours, after resuscitation. For lower bleeding, colonoscopy after rapid bowel preparation; CT angiography first if the patient is unstable with ongoing hematochezia. Approach to an oral mucosal lesion

Ask about tobacco, alcohol, betel quid, inhaled corticosteroids, recent antibiotics, dentures and HIV risk. A white plaque that wipes off is candidiasis until proven otherwise. A fixed white or red lesion with no obvious cause should be observed only briefly after removing irritants; if it persists, biopsy it. Erythroplakia and mixed red-white lesions (speckled leukoplakia) carry the highest chance of dysplasia or carcinoma, so biopsy is the next step rather than repeated observation. Ulcers that do not heal within a few weeks, are painless and indurated, or bleed easily also need biopsy.

Oral candidiasis

Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed with a KOH preparation if needed (budding yeast and pseudohyphae). Mild oropharyngeal disease is treated topically with clotrimazole troches or nystatin suspension; moderate to severe disease, or disease in immunosuppressed patients, is treated with oral fluconazole. Remove the driver where possible. Patients using inhaled corticosteroids should rinse and spit after each dose and use a spacer with metered-dose inhalers. Denture wearers should remove and clean dentures overnight. Odynophagia with thrush in advanced HIV suggests esophageal candidiasis, which needs systemic therapy.

Recurrent oral ulcers

Treat simple aphthous ulcers with topical corticosteroids and topical analgesics; check a blood count, iron studies, folate, vitamin B12 and celiac serology when ulcers are frequent or severe. For Behcet disease, mucocutaneous disease is treated with topical corticosteroids, colchicine or apremilast, while eye, vascular or neurologic involvement needs systemic immunosuppression with specialist input.

Head and neck cancer

An adult with a persistent lateral neck mass should be presumed to have cancer until proven otherwise, particularly when there is no sign of infection. Repeated courses of antibiotics delay diagnosis. The work-up is a complete examination of the upper aerodigestive tract (including flexible laryngoscopy), contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the neck, and fine-needle aspiration of the mass. Open excisional biopsy is not the first step because it can spill tumor and complicate definitive surgery. FNA material from a cystic level II node is tested for HPV (p16), which points to an oropharyngeal primary.

Treatment of oral cavity cancer is mainly surgery with neck dissection, with radiation or chemoradiation for higher-risk features. Oropharyngeal cancer is often treated with chemoradiation. Smoking cessation improves outcomes and reduces second primaries. Long-term effects of radiation include xerostomia, radiation caries and osteoradionecrosis of the jaw, so patients need dental assessment before radiation and lifelong fluoride use afterward.

A young nonsmoker with a painless cystic neck mass is not reassuring. HPV-related oropharyngeal carcinoma often presents exactly this way, and a cystic metastasis can be mistaken for a branchial cleft cyst. Obtain FNA rather than prescribing another course of antibiotics.

Salivary gland swelling

A pleomorphic adenoma must be excised with a margin of normal tissue (for example superficial parotidectomy) rather than enucleated, because projections through its incomplete capsule cause recurrence. Complications of parotidectomy include facial nerve injury and Frey syndrome.

Dry mouth in older adults

Review the medication list first. Drugs with anticholinergic activity (oxybutynin, tricyclic antidepressants, diphenhydramine and other first-generation antihistamines) appear on the Beers list of drugs to avoid in older adults, and they cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and confusion. Deprescribe or switch where possible. Dry mouth raises the risk of root caries, candidiasis and poor nutrition from difficulty chewing and swallowing; advise frequent sips of water, sugar-free gum, avoidance of sugary drinks, and high-fluoride toothpaste.

Dental disease and prevention

Caries is the most common chronic disease of childhood. The USPSTF recommends that primary care clinicians apply fluoride varnish to the primary teeth of all infants and children starting when teeth erupt, and prescribe oral fluoride supplements from 6 months of age for children whose water supply is low in fluoride. Limit sugary drinks and avoid putting a child to bed with a bottle. Periodontitis is associated with poorer glycemic control in diabetes, and treating it is part of good diabetes care.

Ludwig angina

Suspect it in a patient with a recent lower molar infection who has bilateral firm submandibular swelling, a raised floor of mouth, drooling, a muffled voice, trismus or difficulty breathing. The airway comes first. Patients with any sign of airway threat need a controlled airway in an operating room or similar setting, usually awake fiberoptic intubation with a surgical airway ready, because sedation, paralysis and lying flat can precipitate complete obstruction. Do not send an unstable patient to the CT scanner. Once the airway is safe, give IV antibiotics covering oral streptococci and anaerobes (for example ampicillin-sulbactam; broader coverage in immunocompromised patients), obtain contrast CT to look for abscess, drain any collection and treat the dental source.

Ludwig angina is a cellulitis, often without a discrete abscess, so a lack of fluctuance does not make it less dangerous. Mediastinitis is the feared downward spread.

s23d-s100402-s2.bodyHtml:
Dysphagia: where is the problem?

The history localizes most dysphagia. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is difficulty starting a swallow, with coughing, choking, nasal regurgitation or a wet voice; causes include stroke, Parkinson disease, ALS, myasthenia gravis, head and neck cancer treatment and Zenker diverticulum. The first test is a videofluoroscopic swallow study, often with a speech-language pathologist. Esophageal dysphagia is a sensation that food sticks after it has been swallowed. Dysphagia to solids only suggests a mechanical lesion (progressive: peptic stricture or cancer; intermittent: ring, web or eosinophilic esophagitis). Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder (progressive: achalasia or scleroderma; intermittent: distal spasm).

For esophageal dysphagia, upper endoscopy is usually first because it can find and biopsy cancer, strictures, rings and eosinophilic esophagitis. A barium esophagram helps with subtle rings, diverticula and achalasia. High-resolution manometry is the test of choice for a suspected motility disorder once endoscopy has excluded an obstructing lesion.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Typical heartburn and regurgitation without alarm features are treated with an empiric 8-week trial of a once-daily proton pump inhibitor taken 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, plus weight loss if overweight, elevating the head of the bed, and avoiding late meals. If symptoms respond, taper to the lowest effective dose or stop. Inadequate response warrants checking adherence and timing, then twice-daily dosing.

Go straight to endoscopy for alarm features: dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia, unintentional weight loss or persistent vomiting. Also consider endoscopy for symptoms that fail PPI therapy and, once, for screening of patients with chronic reflux plus several risk factors for Barrett esophagus (male sex, age over 50, white race, tobacco use, central obesity, family history). Ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI confirms reflux when endoscopy is normal and the diagnosis is uncertain, and is required before antireflux surgery. Laparoscopic fundoplication or magnetic sphincter augmentation suits patients with proven reflux who want to stop medication or have refractory regurgitation. Complications of GERD include erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture (treated by dilation plus PPI), Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinoma; extraesophageal symptoms include chronic cough, hoarseness and asthma.

Do not order an empiric PPI trial for someone with reflux symptoms and dysphagia, weight loss or anemia. Alarm features mean endoscopy first, because PPIs can heal the surface and delay diagnosis of a cancer.

Barrett esophagus

HistologyManagement
No dysplasiaLong-term PPI; surveillance endoscopy every 3 to 5 years depending on segment length
Indefinite for dysplasiaOptimize PPI and repeat endoscopy with biopsies
Low-grade dysplasia (confirmed by an expert pathologist)Endoscopic eradication therapy or surveillance at about 12 months
High-grade dysplasia or intramucosal carcinomaEndoscopic eradication therapy: resection of any visible lesion, then ablation (for example radiofrequency ablation)

Dysplasia must be confirmed by a second, expert GI pathologist. Esophagectomy is reserved for deeply invasive or high-risk submucosal cancer or failure of endoscopic therapy.

Achalasia

Endoscopy comes first to exclude pseudoachalasia from a junctional cancer; suspect it in an older patient with a short history and rapid weight loss and add endoscopic ultrasonography or CT. Barium shows the bird-beak, and high-resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis (incomplete LES relaxation with absent peristalsis) and identifies the subtype. Definitive options are pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication, and peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM). They are broadly comparable for the common subtypes; POEM is favored for the spastic type III but causes more postoperative reflux. Botulinum toxin injection into the LES gives temporary relief and suits poor surgical candidates. Nitrates and calcium channel blockers help little. End-stage megaesophagus may need esophagectomy.

Odynophagia and infectious esophagitis

In a patient with advanced HIV, oral thrush and odynophagia, give empiric oral fluconazole and reserve endoscopy for failure to improve within a few days. Topical agents are inadequate for esophageal disease. Endoscopic biopsy guides therapy otherwise: acyclovir for HSV, ganciclovir (or valganciclovir) for CMV. Starting antiretroviral therapy prevents recurrence. Pill esophagitis is managed by stopping or changing the drug, a PPI or sucralfate for symptoms, and counselling: swallow pills upright with a full glass of water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes, as required for oral bisphosphonates.

Zenker diverticulum, webs and rings

Older adults with halitosis, gurgling, regurgitation of undigested food or recurrent aspiration should have a barium swallow first; blind passage of an endoscope or nasogastric tube can perforate the pouch. Symptomatic diverticula are treated by cricopharyngeal myotomy, endoscopically or by open surgery. Schatzki rings respond to dilation, and Plummer-Vinson webs to iron replacement and dilation.

Upper GI bleeding from the esophagus

A Mallory-Weiss tear typically follows repeated retching, often after alcohol, with a small amount of hematemesis in a stable patient; most stop spontaneously. Severe chest pain, fever, subcutaneous emphysema or a pleural effusion after vomiting suggests Boerhaave syndrome, an emergency confirmed with water-soluble contrast study or CT.

For variceal bleeding: resuscitate with a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse at hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure), start a vasoactive drug (octreotide) and antibiotic prophylaxis for every patient with cirrhosis (IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days) before endoscopy, and perform endoscopic variceal ligation within 12 hours. Early TIPS is used for high-risk patients and for bleeding that cannot be controlled.

s23d-s100501-s2.bodyHtml:
Dyspepsia

Dyspepsia is epigastric pain or burning, early satiety or postprandial fullness. In patients younger than 60 without alarm features, test for H. pylori noninvasively (urea breath test or stool antigen) and treat if positive; if negative, or if symptoms persist after eradication, give a PPI trial. Patients aged 60 or older should have upper endoscopy. Alarm features such as weight loss, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia lower the threshold for endoscopy at any age. Review NSAID and aspirin use in everyone.

H. pylori: testing and treatment

Choose a test of active infection: urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy-based testing during endoscopy. Serology does not distinguish current from past infection and is no longer recommended. PPIs, bismuth and antibiotics suppress the organism and cause false-negative breath, stool and biopsy tests, so stop PPIs for 2 weeks and antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks before testing when possible.

Under the 2024 ACG guideline, the preferred first-line regimen for treatment-naive patients when antibiotic susceptibility is unknown is optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days: a PPI, bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole. Rifabutin-based triple therapy and vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy are alternatives. Clarithromycin-based triple therapy is now reserved for infections known to be susceptible, because clarithromycin resistance is common. All treated patients should have a test of cure with a breath test, stool antigen or biopsy at least 4 weeks after therapy, off PPIs for 2 weeks. Failure prompts a different regimen, avoiding antibiotics already used where resistance is likely.

Peptic ulcer disease

Treat with a PPI (typically 4 to 8 weeks), eradicate H. pylori if present, and stop NSAIDs. If NSAIDs must continue, use the lowest dose with a PPI, or consider a COX-2 selective agent plus a PPI in high-risk patients. Gastric ulcers are biopsied to exclude cancer, and many are re-examined endoscopically to confirm healing. Refractory or atypically located ulcers prompt a check for NSAID use (including hidden over-the-counter sources), persistent H. pylori, gastrinoma and malignancy.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

Suspect it with multiple, refractory or distal duodenal ulcers, ulcers with diarrhea, ulcers without H. pylori or NSAIDs, or a family or personal history of MEN1. Measure fasting gastrin with simultaneous gastric pH (ideally after holding PPIs if this can be done safely): a markedly raised gastrin with acidic pH supports gastrinoma. A secretin stimulation test resolves equivocal results. Localize with somatostatin receptor PET imaging and endoscopic ultrasonography. Treat acid with high-dose PPI; resect localized sporadic tumors. Check calcium and PTH to screen for MEN1.

Acute upper GI bleeding

Presentation is hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis or melena; brisk upper bleeding can produce hematochezia with hemodynamic instability. A raised BUN out of proportion to creatinine suggests an upper source.

  1. Resuscitate: two large-bore IV lines, crystalloid, monitor, and protect the airway in massive hematemesis or altered mental status.
  2. Transfuse restrictively: red cells when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL in most patients; use a higher threshold (about 8 g/dL) with cardiovascular disease or active brisk bleeding.
  3. Risk-stratify: a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1 identifies patients who can be managed as outpatients.
  4. Medications before endoscopy: IV PPI is reasonable; IV erythromycin before endoscopy improves visualization. Suspected variceal bleeding adds octreotide and ceftriaxone.
  5. Endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation, after resuscitation.

Epinephrine injection should be combined with a second modality rather than used alone. Rebleeding is managed by repeat endoscopy; persistent bleeding goes to transcatheter arterial embolization or surgery. Afterward, test for H. pylori (biopsy at endoscopy; if a test done during the bleed is negative, repeat it later, because false negatives are common during acute bleeding). Restart aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention promptly once hemostasis is secure; stop aspirin taken only for primary prevention.

Do not transfuse a hemodynamically stable patient without heart disease to a hemoglobin of 10. Liberal transfusion increases rebleeding and, in variceal bleeding, raises portal pressure. Transfuse when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL.

Perforation and obstruction

Perforation causes sudden severe epigastric pain that spreads, a rigid abdomen and free air under the diaphragm on an upright chest radiograph or CT. Management is fluids, NPO, nasogastric decompression, IV PPI, broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency surgical repair, usually an omental (Graham) patch; nonoperative care suits only selected stable patients with a sealed perforation. Avoid barium when perforation is suspected. Gastric outlet obstruction causes early satiety and vomiting of undigested food with hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; treat with decompression, IV fluids with potassium, PPI, then endoscopic dilation or surgery, after excluding malignancy.

Stress ulcer prophylaxis

Prophylaxis with a PPI or H2 blocker is reasonable in critically ill patients with risk factors such as coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease or prolonged mechanical ventilation. It is not needed for ward patients without these risks, and unnecessary acid suppression adds risk of C. difficile and pneumonia.

Gastroparesis

Symptoms are nausea, vomiting of food eaten hours earlier, early satiety, bloating and postprandial fullness, often with poorly controlled diabetes. First exclude obstruction with upper endoscopy, then confirm delayed emptying with 4-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy, ideally with glucose controlled and with drugs that slow emptying stopped. Management: small, frequent, low-fat, low-fiber meals (liquids empty more easily), better glycemic control, and stopping opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists where possible. Metoclopramide is the only FDA-approved drug; use the lowest dose for the shortest time (generally no more than 12 weeks) because of tardive dyskinesia. Antiemetics help symptoms. Severe cases may need jejunal feeding or gastric electrical stimulation. Pause GLP-1 receptor agonists before elective endoscopy or anesthesia according to current guidance, because retained food raises aspiration risk.

Erythromycin speeds gastric emptying through motilin receptors, but its effect fades with continued use; it is most useful short term or before endoscopy for bleeding.

noninvasively (urea breath test or stool antigen) and treat if positive; if negative, or if symptoms persist after eradication, give a PPI trial. Patients aged 60 or older should have upper endoscopy. Alarm features such as weight loss, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia lower the threshold for endoscopy at any age. Review NSAID and aspirin use in everyone.

Under the 2024 ACG guideline, the preferred first-line regimen for treatment-naive patients when antibiotic susceptibility is unknown is

for 14 days: a PPI, bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole. Rifabutin-based triple therapy and vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy are alternatives. Clarithromycin-based triple therapy is now reserved for infections known to be susceptible, because clarithromycin resistance is common. All treated patients should have a
with a breath test, stool antigen or biopsy at least 4 weeks after therapy, off PPIs for 2 weeks. Failure prompts a different regimen, avoiding antibiotics already used where resistance is likely.

Measure fasting gastrin with simultaneous gastric pH (ideally after holding PPIs if this can be done safely): a markedly raised gastrin with acidic pH supports gastrinoma. A secretin stimulation test resolves equivocal results. Localize with somatostatin receptor PET imaging and endoscopic ultrasonography. Treat acid with high-dose PPI; resect localized sporadic tumors. Check calcium and PTH to screen for MEN1.

Approach to the acute abdomen of intestinal origin

Start with hemodynamics, peritoneal signs and a focused history (prior surgery, hernias, atrial fibrillation, anticoagulant use, constipation, recent operations). CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast answers most questions in adults; CT angiography is used when ischemia is suspected. Older adults, people taking glucocorticoids and immunocompromised patients often have muted findings, so keep the threshold for imaging low.

Small bowel obstruction versus ileus

FeatureMechanical SBOParalytic ileusColonic pseudo-obstruction
Typical settingPrior surgery (adhesions), herniaPostoperative, opioids, hypokalemia, sepsisAfter surgery or severe illness, older adults
PainCrampy, colickyMild, diffuseOften mild despite distension
Bowel soundsHigh-pitched early, absent lateReduced or absentVariable
ImagingDilated small bowel with a transition point, collapsed distal bowelDiffuse dilation of small bowel and colon, no transitionMarked colonic dilation, often cecum largest, no transition
ManagementFluids, NG decompression, water-soluble contrast challenge; surgery for strangulation or failureCorrect cause, stop opioids, electrolytesConservative, then neostigmine, then colonoscopic decompression

Partial adhesive obstruction without signs of strangulation is managed nonoperatively. Fever, tachycardia, continuous pain, peritonitis, rising lactate or CT signs of ischemia (reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric swirl, closed loop, pneumatosis) mandate urgent surgery. An incarcerated hernia is repaired promptly. A water-soluble contrast agent that reaches the colon within about a day predicts resolution without surgery.

A patient with SBO and no previous abdominal surgery needs a careful search for a hernia (including femoral and obturator) and for a neoplasm; adhesions are unlikely without prior surgery.

Mesenteric ischemia

Acute mesenteric ischemia presents with sudden severe periumbilical pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen, often with vomiting or a forceful bowel movement. Leukocytosis and lactic acidosis appear but may lag. The best initial test is CT angiography; do not wait for lactate to rise. Management: fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, immediate systemic heparin, and urgent revascularisation (surgical embolectomy or endovascular therapy) with laparotomy to resect nonviable bowel and a planned second look. Nonocclusive ischemia is treated by improving cardiac output, withdrawing vasoconstrictors and, in selected cases, intra-arterial vasodilator infusion. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation; surgery is reserved for infarction.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia causes postprandial pain, food fear and weight loss in a smoker with vascular disease; CT angiography shows stenosis, usually of more than one vessel, and endovascular stenting or surgical bypass relieves symptoms.

Ischemic colitis causes sudden crampy lower abdominal pain followed within a day by bloody diarrhea. CT shows segmental wall thickening; colonoscopy with biopsy confirms it. Most cases resolve with bowel rest, fluids and treatment of the cause; antibiotics are used for moderate or severe disease, and surgery for peritonitis, gangrene or perforation. Isolated right-sided ischemic colitis carries a worse prognosis and may signal SMA disease.

Diverticulitis

Classic diverticulitis is left lower quadrant pain, fever and leukocytosis. CT with IV contrast confirms the diagnosis and separates uncomplicated from complicated disease (abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction). Colonoscopy and contrast enema are avoided acutely.

  • Uncomplicated, immunocompetent, tolerating oral intake: outpatient care with diet as tolerated and analgesia. Current AGA and ACG guidance supports using antibiotics selectively rather than routinely; they are favoured with high fever, significant comorbidity, frailty, immunosuppression or persistent symptoms.
  • Abscess: IV antibiotics; larger collections (commonly 3 cm or more) are drained percutaneously under CT guidance; small ones often respond to antibiotics alone.
  • Free perforation with peritonitis: resuscitation, antibiotics and emergency surgery (sigmoid resection with end colostomy or, in suitable patients, primary anastomosis with or without diversion).
  • Fistula (colovesical is commonest: pneumaturia, fecaluria, recurrent UTI): elective resection.

After recovery, colonoscopy is advised if a high-quality colonoscopy has not been done recently, particularly after complicated disease, because a perforated cancer can mimic diverticulitis. Elective resection is individualised to frequency, severity and quality of life rather than a fixed number of attacks. A high-fibre diet is reasonable; avoiding nuts, seeds and popcorn is unnecessary.

Lower GI bleeding: diverticula and angiodysplasia

Diverticular bleeding is painless, often brisk hematochezia that stops on its own in most patients. After resuscitation, colonoscopy after a rapid bowel preparation is the usual first test; in an unstable patient, CT angiography localises bleeding before catheter embolisation. Brisk hematochezia with hemodynamic instability may be an upper GI source, so consider upper endoscopy. Angiodysplasia causes intermittent bleeding and iron deficiency in older adults and is treated with endoscopic argon plasma coagulation; aortic valve replacement often stops bleeding in Heyde syndrome.

Volvulus and pseudo-obstruction

FeatureSigmoid volvulusCecal volvulusOgilvie syndrome
PatientOlder, institutionalised, neurologic disease, constipationYounger adults, mobile cecum, prior surgeryPostoperative (orthopedic, cardiac), critical illness
RadiographInverted U loop from pelvis to right upper quadrantDilated loop in mid or left upper abdomenDiffuse colonic dilation, no transition
First treatmentEndoscopic detorsion, then elective sigmoid resection during the same admissionSurgery (right colectomy)Conservative care, then neostigmine
Emergency surgeryPeritonitis, gangrene, failed detorsionStandardPerforation or ischemia

For pseudo-obstruction, first exclude mechanical obstruction with CT. Conservative care means nothing by mouth, nasogastric and rectal tubes, correction of potassium and magnesium, mobilisation and stopping opioids and anticholinergics. A cecal diameter of about 12 cm or more raises the risk of perforation. If there is no improvement within 24 to 48 hours, give IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring and atropine available (bradycardia is the main risk; avoid in active bronchospasm or mechanical obstruction). Colonoscopic decompression follows if neostigmine fails or is contraindicated, and surgery is for perforation or ischemia.

Endoscopic detorsion of a sigmoid volvulus is not definitive: recurrence is common, so resection is planned during the same admission in fit patients.

Appendicitis

Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, low-grade fever and leukocytosis are typical. Imaging: CT with IV contrast in most adults; ultrasonography first in children and pregnant patients, followed by MRI without gadolinium in pregnancy if ultrasound is inconclusive. Appendectomy (usually laparoscopic) is standard. For selected adults with uncomplicated, CT-confirmed appendicitis without an appendicolith, an antibiotics-first strategy is an option after shared decision-making, accepting a meaningful chance of later appendectomy. A perforated appendix with a well-formed abscess is treated with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage, with appendectomy considered later. In pregnancy the appendix moves upward with the enlarging uterus, and delay increases fetal loss, so prompt diagnosis matters.

Malabsorption in practice

  • Lactose intolerance: diagnosis is often clinical (symptoms with lactose, relief on withdrawal); hydrogen breath test confirms. Reduce lactose, use lactase supplements, and ensure calcium and vitamin D intake from other sources.
  • Bile acid diarrhea: after limited ileal resection, cholecystectomy or idiopathic; trial of cholestyramine, colestipol or colesevelam. Separate sequestrants from other drugs because they bind them.
  • Bacterial overgrowth: glucose or lactulose breath test or jejunal aspirate culture; treat with rifaximin or other antibiotics, correct B12, and address the cause (prokinetics for dysmotility).
  • Short bowel syndrome: parenteral nutrition early, oral rehydration solutions, high-dose acid suppression for early gastric hypersecretion, antimotility drugs, and the GLP-2 analogue teduglutide to enhance adaptation; intestinal transplant is a last resort.

Older adults on opioids, anticholinergics or calcium channel blockers are prone to constipation, ileus and pseudo-obstruction; medication review is part of the work-up.
