Approach to anorectal complaints

Ask about pain (and its relation to defecation), bleeding, prolapse, discharge, itching, bowel habit, sexual history and red flags: age 45 or older, weight loss, change in bowel habit, iron deficiency, family history of colorectal cancer. Inspect the perianal skin with the buttocks parted, perform a digital examination if pain allows, and use anoscopy for the canal. Painful lesions in the anoderm may need examination under anesthesia. Any rectal bleeding in an adult who is due for colorectal screening, or who has red flags, warrants colonoscopy even when hemorrhoids are seen.

PresentationLikely causeFirst management
Painless bright red blood, prolapseInternal hemorrhoidsFibre, fluids; office banding for grade I to III
Acute severe pain, tender blue lump at vergeThrombosed external hemorrhoidExcision if within about 72 h; otherwise conservative
Tearing pain with defecation, posterior midline tearAnal fissureFibre, sitz baths, topical CCB or nitrate
Throbbing constant pain, fluctuant swelling, feverAnorectal abscessIncision and drainage
Persistent drainage from a perianal openingFistula-in-anoDefine anatomy; fistulotomy or seton
Tenesmus, purulent discharge after receptive anal sexSTI proctitisNAAT, empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline
Mass protruding with concentric foldsRectal prolapseSurgical repair

Hemorrhoids

All patients benefit from more fibre and water and less straining. Topical agents relieve symptoms briefly; prolonged topical steroid use thins the perianal skin. Grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail conservative care are treated in the office, most effectively with rubber band ligation; sclerotherapy and infrared coagulation are alternatives. Surgical hemorrhoidectomy is for grade III to IV disease, mixed internal and external disease, or failure of office procedures. Ligation is placed above the pectinate line so that it is relatively painless; severe pain, fever or urinary retention afterwards raises concern for pelvic sepsis.

A thrombosed external hemorrhoid causes sudden pain and a tense bluish lump at the verge. Within about 72 hours of onset, excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia gives faster relief and fewer recurrences than simple incision. After that, pain is already easing, and conservative care (stool softeners, sitz baths, analgesics, topical agents) is preferred.

Anal fissure

Acute fissures often heal with fibre, stool softeners, sitz baths and topical anesthetics. Chronic fissures (more than about 6 to 8 weeks, or with chronic features) are treated with topical calcium channel blockers or nitrates for several weeks; calcium channel blockers cause fewer headaches. Botulinum toxin is an option after topical failure, particularly for patients at higher risk of incontinence. Lateral internal sphincterotomy has the highest healing rate and lowest recurrence and is offered when medical therapy fails, accepting a small risk of minor incontinence; it is avoided or used cautiously in patients with weak sphincters, such as women after obstetric injury. An off-midline or atypical fissure calls for evaluation of the cause, which can include colonoscopy with ileal examination, HIV and syphilis testing, and biopsy.

Do not perform sphincterotomy for a lateral fissure in a patient with diarrhea and weight loss; look for Crohn disease, infection or cancer first.

Anorectal abscess and fistula

An abscess is treated with prompt incision and drainage, even before fluctuance is obvious when pain is severe; antibiotics alone fail. Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs, immunosuppression, diabetes or prosthetic valves. Deep (supralevator or intersphincteric) abscesses may need CT or MRI and drainage in the operating room. Fournier gangrene is a rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the perineum, more common in diabetes, that needs emergency debridement and broad antibiotics.

A fistula is suspected when an abscess recurs or a drainage opening persists. Pelvic MRI or examination under anesthesia defines its course. A simple low fistula that crosses little or no sphincter is treated with fistulotomy. Complex fistulas (high transsphincteric, anterior in women, recurrent, Crohn-related, or in patients with poor continence) are managed with a draining seton and sphincter-sparing techniques such as an advancement flap or ligation of the intersphincteric tract.

Pilonidal disease

An acute pilonidal abscess is drained, ideally through an incision just off the midline. Chronic or recurrent disease is treated with excision of the sinus tracts, often with an off-midline closure or flap. Hair removal and hygiene reduce recurrence.

Rectal prolapse and fecal incontinence

Full-thickness rectal prolapse is commonest in older women with chronic straining and pelvic floor weakness and in children with cystic fibrosis or malnutrition. It causes a protruding mass, mucus discharge, bleeding and incontinence. Diagnose by having the patient strain while squatting. Treatment is surgical: an abdominal rectopexy (often laparoscopic, sometimes with resection) for fit patients, or a perineal procedure for frail patients, which has a higher recurrence rate. Acute incarceration is reduced, sometimes after applying sugar to reduce edema.

Fecal incontinence is managed first by normalising stool consistency (fibre, loperamide for loose stool), pelvic floor biofeedback and treating the cause. Endoanal ultrasound identifies sphincter defects; overlapping sphincteroplasty can help recent defects, and sacral nerve stimulation is an option when conservative care fails.

Proctitis

Proctitis presents with anorectal pain, tenesmus, discharge and bleeding. Obtain rectal NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia, HSV testing if ulcers are present, syphilis serology and HIV testing. Under current CDC guidance, empiric therapy for acute proctitis after receptive anal intercourse is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Doxycycline is extended to 21 days for LGV, suspected with bloody discharge, perianal or mucosal ulcers, or tenesmus with a positive rectal chlamydia test. Ulcers suggest HSV (add antivirals) or syphilis. Offer HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, test and treat partners, and retest for reinfection. Radiation proctitis with bleeding responds to endoscopic argon plasma coagulation; sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are alternatives.

Anal and rectal cancer

Anal squamous cell carcinoma presents with bleeding, pain, a mass or inguinal nodes. Biopsy confirms it; staging uses pelvic MRI and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT, and examination of the inguinal nodes. Definitive chemoradiation with 5-fluorouracil (or capecitabine) and mitomycin, the Nigro approach, cures most patients while preserving the sphincter. Abdominoperineal resection is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation. Small, well-differentiated perianal margin tumours may be locally excised. People living with HIV and other high-risk groups may be offered screening with anal cytology or HPV testing followed by high-resolution anoscopy, and treatment of high-grade lesions reduces progression. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

Rectal adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by colonoscopy with biopsy and staged with high-resolution pelvic MRI (T stage, nodes, extramural venous invasion and the distance to the mesorectal fascia, which predicts the circumferential resection margin), CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and CEA. Early tumours go straight to surgery with total mesorectal excision. Locally advanced tumours are treated with neoadjuvant therapy, increasingly as total neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy plus chemoradiation or short-course radiation) before surgery; complete clinical responders may enter a watch-and-wait programme at experienced centres. Mismatch repair-deficient rectal tumours respond strikingly to PD-1 blockade.

Anal SCC is treated with chemoradiation, not surgery; rectal adenocarcinoma is treated with surgery, with neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced disease. The histology, not the location alone, sets the plan.

All patients benefit from more fibre and water and less straining. Topical agents relieve symptoms briefly; prolonged topical steroid use thins the perianal skin. Grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail conservative care are treated in the office, most effectively with rubber band ligation; sclerotherapy and infrared coagulation are alternatives. Surgical hemorrhoidectomy is for grade III to IV disease, mixed internal and external disease, or failure of office procedures. Ligation is placed above the pectinate line so that it is relatively painless; severe pain, fever or urinary retention afterwards raises concern for pelvic sepsis.

A thrombosed external hemorrhoid causes sudden pain and a tense bluish lump at the verge. Within about 72 hours of onset, excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia gives faster relief and fewer recurrences than simple incision. After that, pain is already easing, and conservative care (stool softeners, sitz baths, analgesics, topical agents) is preferred.

Acute fissures often heal with fibre, stool softeners, sitz baths and topical anesthetics. Chronic fissures (more than about 6 to 8 weeks, or with chronic features) are treated with topical calcium channel blockers or nitrates for several weeks; calcium channel blockers cause fewer headaches. Botulinum toxin is an option after topical failure, particularly for patients at higher risk of incontinence. Lateral internal sphincterotomy has the highest healing rate and lowest recurrence and is offered when medical therapy fails, accepting a small risk of minor incontinence; it is avoided or used cautiously in patients with weak sphincters, such as women after obstetric injury. An off-midline or atypical fissure calls for evaluation of the cause, which can include colonoscopy with ileal examination, HIV and syphilis testing, and biopsy.
Do not perform sphincterotomy for a lateral fissure in a patient with diarrhea and weight loss; look for Crohn disease, infection or cancer first.

An abscess is treated with prompt incision and drainage, even before fluctuance is obvious when pain is severe; antibiotics alone fail. Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs, immunosuppression, diabetes or prosthetic valves. Deep (supralevator or intersphincteric) abscesses may need CT or MRI and drainage in the operating room. Fournier gangrene is a rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the perineum, more common in diabetes, that needs emergency debridement and broad antibiotics.

A fistula is suspected when an abscess recurs or a drainage opening persists. Pelvic MRI or examination under anesthesia defines its course. A simple low fistula that crosses little or no sphincter is treated with fistulotomy. Complex fistulas (high transsphincteric, anterior in women, recurrent, Crohn-related, or in patients with poor continence) are managed with a draining seton and sphincter-sparing techniques such as an advancement flap or ligation of the intersphincteric tract.

An acute pilonidal abscess is drained, ideally through an incision just off the midline. Chronic or recurrent disease is treated with excision of the sinus tracts, often with an off-midline closure or flap. Hair removal and hygiene reduce recurrence.

Full-thickness rectal prolapse is commonest in older women with chronic straining and pelvic floor weakness and in children with cystic fibrosis or malnutrition. It causes a protruding mass, mucus discharge, bleeding and incontinence. Diagnose by having the patient strain while squatting. Treatment is surgical: an abdominal rectopexy (often laparoscopic, sometimes with resection) for fit patients, or a perineal procedure for frail patients, which has a higher recurrence rate. Acute incarceration is reduced, sometimes after applying sugar to reduce edema.

Fecal incontinence is managed first by normalising stool consistency (fibre, loperamide for loose stool), pelvic floor biofeedback and treating the cause. Endoanal ultrasound identifies sphincter defects; overlapping sphincteroplasty can help recent defects, and sacral nerve stimulation is an option when conservative care fails.

Proctitis presents with anorectal pain, tenesmus, discharge and bleeding. Obtain rectal NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia, HSV testing if ulcers are present, syphilis serology and HIV testing. Under current CDC guidance, empiric therapy for acute proctitis after receptive anal intercourse is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Doxycycline is extended to 21 days for LGV, suspected with bloody discharge, perianal or mucosal ulcers, or tenesmus with a positive rectal chlamydia test. Ulcers suggest HSV (add antivirals) or syphilis. Offer HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, test and treat partners, and retest for reinfection. Radiation proctitis with bleeding responds to endoscopic argon plasma coagulation; sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are alternatives.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma presents with bleeding, pain, a mass or inguinal nodes. Biopsy confirms it; staging uses pelvic MRI and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT, and examination of the inguinal nodes. Definitive chemoradiation with 5-fluorouracil (or capecitabine) and mitomycin, the Nigro approach, cures most patients while preserving the sphincter. Abdominoperineal resection is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation. Small, well-differentiated perianal margin tumours may be locally excised. People living with HIV and other high-risk groups may be offered screening with anal cytology or HPV testing followed by high-resolution anoscopy, and treatment of high-grade lesions reduces progression. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

Rectal adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by colonoscopy with biopsy and staged with high-resolution pelvic MRI (T stage, nodes, extramural venous invasion and the distance to the mesorectal fascia, which predicts the circumferential resection margin), CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and CEA. Early tumours go straight to surgery with total mesorectal excision. Locally advanced tumours are treated with neoadjuvant therapy, increasingly as total neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy plus chemoradiation or short-course radiation) before surgery; complete clinical responders may enter a watch-and-wait programme at experienced centres. Mismatch repair-deficient rectal tumours respond strikingly to PD-1 blockade.

Anal SCC is treated with chemoradiation, not surgery; rectal adenocarcinoma is treated with surgery, with neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced disease. The histology, not the location alone, sets the plan.

Evaluating abnormal liver tests

Repeat and confirm mild abnormalities, then classify the pattern. For hepatocellular injury, screen with alcohol history, medications and supplements, hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody, hepatitis C antibody, metabolic risk factors with ultrasonography for steatosis, iron studies (transferrin saturation and ferritin), autoimmune markers and immunoglobulins, and, in younger patients, ceruloplasmin; alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype complete the work-up. For cholestasis, ultrasound first separates obstruction (dilated ducts) from intrahepatic causes. Severity is judged by bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets and clinical signs of portal hypertension.

Alcohol-associated hepatitis

Typical features are rapid-onset jaundice within weeks of heavy drinking (often in the 2 months after stopping), fever, tender hepatomegaly, leukocytosis, AST above ALT and bilirubin often well above 3 mg/dL. Exclude infection (blood and urine cultures, chest radiograph, diagnostic paracentesis if ascites), GI bleeding and kidney injury. Severity scores guide treatment: the Maddrey discriminant function [4.6 × (patient PT − control PT in seconds) + bilirubin in mg/dL] of 32 or more, or a MELD score above 20, defines severe disease with high short-term mortality.

  • Severe disease without contraindications: prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days. Reassess with the Lille score on day 7; stop steroids in nonresponders.
  • Contraindications to steroids: active infection, uncontrolled GI bleeding, kidney failure, pancreatitis.
  • Pentoxifylline is no longer recommended because it does not improve survival.
  • All patients: abstinence support (counselling, and medications such as acamprosate or baclofen, which are preferred over naltrexone in significant liver disease), nutrition with protein and calorie targets, thiamine, and alcohol withdrawal management.
  • Early liver transplantation is considered at selected centres for carefully selected nonresponders.

MASLD and MASH

Steatotic liver disease is often found on imaging or with mildly raised ALT in patients with obesity or type 2 diabetes. Stage fibrosis noninvasively: calculate FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets). A value below 1.3 indicates low risk and repeat assessment every few years; higher values lead to vibration-controlled transient elastography or an enhanced liver fibrosis blood test, with hepatology referral when advanced fibrosis is likely. Biopsy is reserved for uncertain cases.

Management: weight loss through diet and exercise (a sustained loss of about 7 to 10% improves inflammation and can regress fibrosis), treatment of diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidemia (statins are safe and recommended when indicated), and limiting alcohol. GLP-1 receptor agonists help weight and steatosis; resmetirom (a thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist) and semaglutide are approved for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis. Bariatric surgery benefits eligible patients. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death, so risk-factor control is part of liver care.

Normal aminotransferases do not exclude advanced fibrosis in MASLD; risk-stratify with FIB-4 in every patient with steatosis and metabolic risk factors, rather than relying on ALT.

Cirrhosis: staging and complications

MELD (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, with sodium in MELD-Na, and sodium, albumin and sex in MELD 3.0) predicts 90-day mortality and orders the transplant waiting list; Child-Pugh class (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) estimates operative risk and reserve. Patients with decompensation or a MELD of about 15 or more should be evaluated for transplantation.

ComplicationKey testManagement
AscitesDiagnostic paracentesis: SAAG 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertensionSodium restriction, spironolactone with or without furosemide, large-volume paracentesis with albumin
VaricesEndoscopy or elastography and platelet-based screeningNonselective beta-blocker (carvedilol) or band ligation; acute bleed: octreotide, antibiotics, banding
Hepatic encephalopathyClinical diagnosis; ammonia level adds littleFind the precipitant; lactulose; add rifaximin for recurrence
Hepatocellular carcinomaUltrasound with AFP every 6 monthsStaging-based therapy

Hepatic encephalopathy ranges from subtle attention deficits to coma, often with asterixis. Precipitants include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration and diuretics, hypokalemia, and sedatives such as benzodiazepines and opioids. Treat the precipitant and give lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools daily; avoid sedatives. Protein restriction is not recommended; malnourished patients need adequate protein and a late-evening snack.

Hemochromatosis

Suspect it with fatigue, arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, diabetes, hypogonadism, cardiomyopathy or abnormal liver tests. Screen with fasting transferrin saturation and ferritin; if transferrin saturation is 45% or more, test for HFE mutations. First-degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote should have iron studies and HFE genotyping. MRI can quantify hepatic iron; biopsy is mainly for staging when ferritin is very high or liver enzymes are abnormal. Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy until ferritin falls to about 50 to 100 ng/mL, then maintenance. Patients with cirrhosis need HCC surveillance even after iron removal. Advise avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish (Vibrio vulnificus).

Wilson disease

Consider it, especially in children and young adults, with unexplained liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms or Coombs-negative hemolysis. Tests: serum ceruloplasmin (low), 24-hour urinary copper (high), slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings, ATP7B genetic testing, and hepatic copper on biopsy when needed. Treatment is lifelong chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine, then zinc for maintenance or for presymptomatic siblings; first-degree relatives should be screened. Patients presenting with acute liver failure (often with low alkaline phosphatase, Coombs-negative hemolysis and AST above ALT) rarely survive without transplantation.

Other disorders

  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: test serum level and phenotype or genotype in unexplained liver disease or early emphysema. No drug treats the liver disease; augmentation therapy helps the lung only. Avoid smoking; transplantation for liver failure.
  • Budd-Chiari syndrome: abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites with high SAAG and high ascitic protein. Doppler ultrasonography is the best initial test; CT or MRI confirms. Treat with anticoagulation and the underlying disorder, then angioplasty or stenting, TIPS or transplantation if needed.

Acute liver failure

Defined as an INR of 1.5 or more plus hepatic encephalopathy of any grade within 26 weeks of illness onset in a patient without preexisting cirrhosis (Wilson disease, vertically acquired hepatitis B and autoimmune hepatitis can qualify despite cirrhosis). Admit to intensive care and contact a transplant centre early. Give N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity and consider it in other causes; specific therapies exist for hepatitis B, herpes simplex, Budd-Chiari and acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Watch for cerebral edema, infection, hypoglycemia and kidney failure. Prognostic criteria such as the King's College criteria guide listing for urgent transplantation.

Prothrombotic and bleeding risks coexist in cirrhosis: a raised INR does not mean the patient is anticoagulated, and routine plasma before paracentesis is not recommended.

s23d-s100602-s2.bodyHtml:
Approach to right upper quadrant pain

Right upper quadrant pain after meals with or without fever is a common exam setting. Separate four questions: is the gallbladder inflamed, is the common bile duct blocked, is the duct infected, and is the patient stable? Liver tests and ultrasound answer most of them. Transabdominal ultrasound is the best initial test for almost every suspected gallbladder or duct problem: it shows stones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, a sonographic Murphy sign and duct dilation, without radiation, and it is the right first test in pregnancy.

ConditionFever and leukocytosisBilirubin and alkaline phosphataseKey testDefinitive treatment
Biliary colicNoNormalUltrasound shows stones onlyElective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Acute cholecystitisYesNormal or mildly raisedUltrasound; HIDA if equivocalEarly laparoscopic cholecystectomy
CholedocholithiasisNoRaised, cholestaticUltrasound, then MRCP or EUS if uncertainERCP stone removal, then cholecystectomy
Acute cholangitisYesRaisedClinical diagnosis plus imaging of the ductAntibiotics and biliary drainage (ERCP)
Acalculous cholecystitisYes, in ICU patientVariableBedside ultrasoundCholecystostomy if unstable; cholecystectomy if fit

Asymptomatic stones and biliary colic

Stones found incidentally on imaging in a patient without symptoms usually need no treatment, because most never cause symptoms. Once a patient has typical biliary colic, recurrence and complications are common enough that elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended. Ursodiol dissolution is slow, works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder, and stones often recur, so it is reserved for patients who cannot or will not have surgery.

Acute cholecystitis

Expect constant right upper quadrant pain lasting more than several hours, fever, a Murphy sign and leukocytosis. Ultrasound shows stones with a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid. When ultrasound is equivocal, cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan) is the most accurate test: failure of the tracer to fill the gallbladder while it reaches the duodenum confirms cystic duct obstruction. Treatment is fluids, analgesia, antibiotics covering enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes when severe, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission, ideally within about 72 hours of symptom onset. Delaying surgery for weeks increases readmission without lowering complications.

In pregnancy, laparoscopic cholecystectomy can be performed safely in any trimester and is preferred over conservative management for acute cholecystitis, because recurrent attacks raise the risk to the pregnancy. High-risk or unstable patients (septic shock, severe comorbidity) are treated with antibiotics and a percutaneous cholecystostomy tube, with interval cholecystectomy if they recover. Complications include gangrene, perforation, emphysematous cholecystitis (gas-forming organisms, more common in older diabetic men, needing urgent surgery) and cholecystoenteric fistula.

Ultrasound in a critically ill ICU patient may show sludge, a distended gallbladder and wall thickening without stones. That is acalculous cholecystitis, not a reassuring study. It carries high rates of gangrene and perforation, so treat with antibiotics and drain promptly; an unstable patient gets percutaneous cholecystostomy rather than an operation.

Choledocholithiasis and cholangitis

Common bile duct stones produce jaundice, pruritus, dark urine and a cholestatic pattern (alkaline phosphatase and GGT out of proportion to transaminases, although transaminases can spike briefly early on). Risk stratify by the likelihood of a duct stone. If ultrasound or CT shows a stone in the common duct, or the patient has cholangitis, proceed directly to ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction. If the probability is intermediate (dilated duct or abnormal liver tests without a visible stone), confirm first with MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or with intraoperative cholangiography at cholecystectomy. After clearance, cholecystectomy should follow during the same admission to prevent recurrence.

Acute cholangitis is bacterial infection of an obstructed duct. Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice form the classic triad; adding hypotension and confusion marks severe disease. Give blood cultures, fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, then arrange biliary drainage. ERCP is the preferred drainage route; the sicker the patient, the more urgent the drainage. Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the fallback when ERCP fails or the anatomy prevents it.

Other gallstone complications

  • Gallstone ileus: typically an older woman with intermittent then complete small-bowel obstruction. CT is the best test and shows obstruction, pneumobilia and an ectopic stone. Treatment is laparotomy or laparoscopy with enterolithotomy proximal to the stone; repair of the fistula and cholecystectomy can usually be deferred.
  • Mirizzi syndrome: jaundice from extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by an impacted stone; important to recognise before surgery because the anatomy is distorted.
  • Porcelain gallbladder: a calcified wall on imaging. The cancer risk appears lower than once believed, but cholecystectomy is commonly offered to fit patients; decisions are individualized.
  • Gallbladder polyps: larger polyps carry malignant potential and are removed; small ones are followed with ultrasound.

Primary biliary cholangitis

Suspect PBC in a middle-aged woman with fatigue, pruritus and an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase. The diagnosis rests on a cholestatic enzyme pattern plus a positive antimitochondrial antibody; liver biopsy is needed only when the antibody is negative or another disease is suspected. Ultrasound should exclude a mechanical obstruction. First-line therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid lifelong, which improves liver tests and slows progression; patients with an incomplete biochemical response should be referred for second-line therapy. Pruritus is treated first with a bile acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine, taken several hours apart from ursodiol and other drugs because it binds them. Screen for osteoporosis with bone density testing and for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and consider thyroid disease and sicca symptoms. Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for decompensated disease.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Most patients with PSC have inflammatory bowel disease, usually ulcerative colitis, so a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase in a patient with colitis should prompt MRCP, the best initial diagnostic test, which shows multifocal strictures and dilations (beading). ERCP is reserved for therapy, such as dilating a dominant stricture, and for brushings when cholangiocarcinoma is suspected. No drug has been shown to change the course of PSC, and high-dose ursodiol has been associated with harm. Management includes:

  • Colonoscopic surveillance at short intervals from the time of diagnosis in patients with colitis, because colorectal cancer risk is high.
  • Periodic imaging, often with a tumour marker, for cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder neoplasia; gallbladder polyps in PSC are treated with a low threshold for cholecystectomy.
  • Antibiotics and endoscopic drainage for bacterial cholangitis, and liver transplantation for end-stage disease or recurrent cholangitis.

Rapid worsening of jaundice, weight loss or a new dominant stricture in PSC should raise concern for cholangiocarcinoma rather than simple disease progression.

Choledochal cysts in practice

Ultrasound is the usual first test and MRCP defines the anatomy. Because of the cancer risk and recurrent cholangitis or pancreatitis, the standard treatment for the common extrahepatic types is complete cyst excision with a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy; simply draining the cyst into the bowel leaves the at-risk epithelium in place.

Diagnosing acute pancreatitis

Diagnose acute pancreatitis when at least two of three criteria are met: typical pain (acute, persistent, severe epigastric pain often radiating to the back), serum lipase (or amylase) at least three times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging findings. Lipase is preferred because it stays raised longer and is more specific. The height of the enzyme does not predict severity. If pain and enzymes are typical, CT is not needed at presentation; reserve contrast-enhanced CT for an unclear diagnosis or for a patient who fails to improve after 48 to 72 hours, when necrosis becomes visible.

Every patient needs a right upper quadrant ultrasound to look for gallstones, plus serum triglycerides and calcium. Raised ALT early in an attack favours a biliary cause. When no cause is found after one attack, review alcohol, drugs and family history; recurrent idiopathic attacks warrant endoscopic ultrasound, and older patients should be assessed for an underlying neoplasm.

Severity and early management

Severity follows organ failure: mild disease has no organ failure or local complications, moderately severe disease has transient organ failure (resolving within 48 hours) or local complications, and severe disease has persistent organ failure. Warning signs of a severe course include older age, obesity, SIRS, rising BUN or hematocrit despite fluids, and pleural effusions.

  • Fluids: give moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer solution, reassessed often against heart rate, blood pressure, urine output and BUN or hematocrit. Very aggressive fluid regimens increase fluid overload without improving outcomes.
  • Analgesia: adequate pain control, including opioids when needed.
  • Feeding: start an oral diet early, as soon as tolerated, in mild disease; it does not need to wait for normal enzymes. If oral intake fails, enteral feeding by nasogastric or nasojejunal tube is preferred over parenteral nutrition because it protects the gut barrier and lowers infection.
  • Antibiotics: no prophylactic antibiotics, even in severe or necrotizing disease. Give them for confirmed or strongly suspected infection (infected necrosis, cholangitis, pneumonia, line infection).
  • ERCP: urgent ERCP is for gallstone pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis, and is considered for persistent biliary obstruction; it does not help gallstone pancreatitis without these.
  • Cholecystectomy: after mild gallstone pancreatitis, remove the gallbladder during the same admission to prevent recurrence.

A rising lipase or a large necrotic area on CT is not an indication for antibiotics. Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infected necrosis and promote resistant organisms and fungal infection. Treat infection only when it is suspected clinically or shown by gas in a collection.

Cause-specific measures

  • Hypertriglyceridemia: acute treatment is supportive; intravenous insulin (with dextrose if glucose is normal) lowers triglycerides, and plasmapheresis is used selectively. Long-term prevention is a fibrate, strict dietary fat restriction, avoidance of alcohol and estrogen where possible, and good glucose control. Bile acid sequestrants raise triglycerides and should be avoided.
  • Hypercalcemia: look for primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy and treat the cause.
  • Drugs: stop the suspected drug; azathioprine, valproate and other agents are listed in the Step 1 section.
  • Post-ERCP pancreatitis: rectal indomethacin (or diclofenac) is given at the time of the procedure to all patients without a contraindication; high-risk patients also receive a temporary pancreatic duct stent when indicated, and periprocedural lactated Ringer hydration. Avoid unnecessary ERCP; use MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound for diagnosis.
  • Alcohol: brief intervention and referral for alcohol use disorder during the admission lowers recurrence.

Local complications

Collections are classified by whether the pancreatitis is necrotizing and by time since onset.

CollectionTimingContentUsual management
Acute peripancreatic fluid collectionFirst 4 weeksFluid, no wallObserve; most resolve
PseudocystAfter 4 weeksFluid in a fibrous wallObserve if asymptomatic; drain (usually endoscopically) if it causes pain, obstruction or infection
Acute necrotic collectionFirst 4 weeksFluid and necrotic tissueSupportive; antibiotics only if infected
Walled-off necrosisAfter 4 weeksEncapsulated necrotic debrisDrain or debride if infected or symptomatic, preferably endoscopically

Size alone is not an indication to drain a pseudocyst. Suspect infected necrosis when fever, leukocytosis or clinical decline appear in the second week or later, or when CT shows gas in a necrotic collection. Start antibiotics that penetrate necrosis, such as a carbapenem, and if the patient is stable, delay drainage until the collection is walled off (about 4 weeks). Then use a step-up approach: endoscopic transmural or percutaneous drainage first, and minimally invasive necrosectomy only if that fails. Early open necrosectomy has higher mortality. Other complications include splenic vein thrombosis (isolated gastric varices), pseudoaneurysm bleeding, abdominal compartment syndrome, pancreatic ascites or pleural effusion from a disrupted duct, and new diabetes.

Chronic pancreatitis

Expect recurrent or constant epigastric pain, weight loss, steatorrhea and diabetes, most often in someone with long-standing alcohol and tobacco use. CT is the best initial test and shows calcifications, atrophy and duct dilation; MRCP with secretin or endoscopic ultrasound helps in early disease. Low fecal elastase supports exocrine insufficiency.

  • Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals and snacks treats steatorrhea and improves nutrition; add acid suppression if response is poor. Replace vitamins A, D, E and K and screen bone density.
  • Pain: stop alcohol and smoking, use stepwise analgesia, and consider endoscopic or surgical drainage when a dilated obstructed duct is present.
  • Diabetes: usually needs insulin; take care with hypoglycemia because glucagon is also lost.
  • Cancer: chronic and hereditary pancreatitis raise the risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma; new weight loss or jaundice warrants imaging.
FeatureAlcohol-associated chronic pancreatitisAutoimmune (IgG4) pancreatitisHereditary pancreatitis
Typical patientMiddle-aged adult with heavy drinking and smokingOlder man with painless jaundiceChild or young adult with family history
ImagingCalcifications, dilated irregular ductDiffusely enlarged gland with a rimCalcifications at a young age
Key testCTSerum IgG4, biopsy to exclude cancerGenetic testing (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR)
TreatmentAbstinence, enzymes, pain controlGlucocorticoidsSupportive; cancer awareness

Cystic fibrosis

Newborn screening detects most cases. Pancreatic insufficient patients take enzyme replacement with every meal, a high-calorie diet and fat-soluble vitamins, and are screened annually for diabetes related to cystic fibrosis from about age 10. CFTR modulators improve lung function and nutrition in eligible genotypes. Very high enzyme doses have been associated with fibrosing colonopathy.

s23d-s100801-s2.bodyHtml:
Evaluating new ascites

Ascites causes abdominal distension, weight gain, shifting dullness and a fluid wave on examination; ultrasound confirms small volumes and examines the liver, portal flow and hepatic veins. Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated for every patient with new ascites, every patient with cirrhosis and ascites who is admitted to hospital (for any reason) and any patient with ascites who develops fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, kidney injury or other clinical deterioration. Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia from cirrhosis are not contraindications, and routine transfusion of plasma or platelets beforehand is not recommended; disseminated intravascular coagulation is the exception.

Initial fluid tests: cell count with differential, albumin (with same-day serum albumin to compute SAAG), total protein and culture inoculated into blood culture bottles at the bedside. Add glucose, LDH, amylase, triglycerides, cytology or mycobacterial studies according to the suspected cause.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

SBP may be subtle: fever, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, worsening encephalopathy or new kidney injury, or no symptoms at all. An ascitic PMN count of 250/mm3 or more confirms it, and treatment starts immediately without waiting for culture results.

  • Antibiotic: an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone for community-acquired infection; broader cover (for example a carbapenem) for nosocomial infection or recent antibiotic exposure, guided by local resistance.
  • Albumin: intravenous albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 lowers the risk of kidney injury and death, with the greatest benefit in patients who have raised creatinine, BUN or bilirubin.
  • Stop nephrotoxic drugs and hold diuretics and beta-blockers if blood pressure is low or kidney injury develops.
  • Secondary prophylaxis: after a first episode, give long-term daily oral antibiotic prophylaxis (for example ciprofloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and refer for liver transplant evaluation, because survival after SBP is poor.
  • Primary prophylaxis is offered to patients with cirrhosis and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (a short intravenous course, typically ceftriaxone) and is considered for patients with low ascitic protein and advanced liver or kidney dysfunction.

Secondary peritonitis

Suspect a surgical source when the fluid shows a very high PMN count, more than one organism on Gram stain or culture, or at least two of the following: total protein above 1 g/dL, glucose below 50 mg/dL, and LDH above the upper limit of normal for serum. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics that cover anaerobes and obtain urgent CT of the abdomen to look for perforation or abscess. Confirmed perforation needs surgical source control. Failure of the PMN count to fall after 48 hours of treatment for presumed SBP also raises concern for a secondary source.

FeatureSpontaneous bacterial peritonitisSecondary peritonitis
OrganismsOne, usually gram-negative entericSeveral, including anaerobes
Ascitic protein, glucose, LDHLow protein, normal glucose, LDH below serum levelHigh protein, low glucose, high LDH
ImagingNot needed routinelyCT for free air or abscess
TreatmentThird-generation cephalosporin plus albuminBroad antibiotics with anaerobic cover plus surgery or drainage

Managing cirrhotic ascites

  • Remove the cause where possible: alcohol abstinence or antiviral therapy can make ascites much easier to control.
  • Dietary sodium restriction to about 2 g (88 mmol) per day. More severe restriction worsens nutrition, so involve a dietitian and keep protein intake adequate; fluid restriction is needed only for severe hyponatremia.
  • Diuretics: start spironolactone with furosemide, usually in a ratio of 100 mg to 40 mg once daily, increasing both stepwise (to a maximum of 400 mg and 160 mg) while monitoring weight, electrolytes and creatinine. Spironolactone alone is an option for a small first episode.
  • Large-volume paracentesis is first-line for tense ascites. When more than 5 L is removed, give intravenous albumin, about 6 to 8 g per liter removed, to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
  • Refractory ascites (no response to maximal diuretics, or diuretics limited by complications): serial large-volume paracentesis with albumin, consideration of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in selected patients, and transplant referral. TIPS can worsen hepatic encephalopathy and is avoided in advanced liver failure or heart failure.
  • Avoid NSAIDs and, in general, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers.

A cirrhotic patient with a new right-sided pleural effusion and no heart or lung disease most likely has hepatic hydrothorax, fluid passing through small diaphragmatic defects. Do not place a chest tube: it causes massive protein and fluid loss, infection and kidney injury. Treat with sodium restriction and diuretics, thoracentesis for symptoms, and TIPS or transplant evaluation when refractory. Spontaneous bacterial empyema can complicate it.

Hepatorenal syndrome

Suspect hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites whose creatinine rises despite stopping diuretics and giving intravenous albumin for 2 days, in the absence of shock, current or recent nephrotoxic drugs, and signs of structural kidney disease (proteinuria, hematuria or abnormal kidney ultrasound). Urine sodium is usually very low. Common triggers are SBP and other infections, gastrointestinal bleeding and large-volume paracentesis without albumin.

Treat with a vasoconstrictor plus albumin. Terlipressin with albumin is the preferred regimen where available; it can cause ischemic complications and respiratory failure from fluid overload, so it is avoided in patients with hypoxemia or volume overload. Norepinephrine with albumin is an alternative in an intensive care unit, and midodrine with octreotide plus albumin is a weaker option when neither is possible. Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment. Dialysis can bridge patients to transplant but does not reverse the syndrome.

Prognosis and special situations

Ascites marks the transition to decompensated cirrhosis and signals substantially worse survival, so patients should be evaluated for liver transplantation. Elderly patients are especially prone to diuretic-induced hyponatremia, azotemia, falls and encephalopathy and need closer monitoring. Ascites with a low SAAG and a lymphocytic fluid in a patient from an endemic area should prompt testing for tuberculosis, including peritoneal biopsy when fluid studies are inconclusive; treatment is standard antituberculous therapy. Pancreatic ascites is treated by resting or stenting the disrupted duct. Chylous ascites is treated by addressing the cause and using a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides, which are absorbed directly into portal blood rather than lymph.

s23d-s100901-s2.bodyHtml:
Groin hernias in practice

Diagnosis is clinical: a bulge that enlarges with standing or coughing. Ultrasound helps when the examination is equivocal; CT is useful in obesity or when obstruction is suspected. Management:

  • Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in a man: watchful waiting is reasonable, with counseling about warning signs; many eventually need repair.
  • Symptomatic inguinal hernia: elective repair, open mesh (tension-free) or laparoscopic.
  • Femoral hernia: repair promptly even if asymptomatic because of the high strangulation risk.
  • Infant inguinal hernia: repair soon after diagnosis because incarceration risk is high; infant umbilical hernias are usually observed because most close spontaneously.
  • Incarcerated hernia without signs of strangulation: gentle manual reduction with analgesia can be attempted, then early elective repair.
  • Strangulation (fever, tachycardia, skin changes, peritonitis, leukocytosis, rising lactate): do not reduce; resuscitate, give antibiotics and operate emergently.

Never force a hernia back when strangulation is suspected: reducing dead bowel into the abdomen converts a localized problem into peritonitis.

Adhesive small bowel obstruction

Presents with colicky pain, distension, vomiting and obstipation. CT with IV contrast is the main test: it confirms obstruction, shows a transition point and looks for ischemeia or closed loop. Initial care is bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids with electrolyte correction and serial examinations. A water-soluble contrast challenge helps predict which patients will resolve without surgery. Operate for peritonitis, signs of strangulation, closed-loop obstruction or failure to resolve.

Problems after gastric and bariatric surgery

SyndromeTiming or clueKey testManagement
Early dumpingWithin 30 min of a meal; cramps, diarrhea, palpitationsClinicalSmall frequent meals, fewer simple sugars, more protein and fiber, fluids away from meals; octreotide if refractory
Late dumping1 to 3 h after carbohydrate; sweating, confusion, low glucoseGlucose during symptomsSame diet; acarbose; octreotide or surgery if refractory
Afferent loop obstructionBillroth II; pain relieved by bilious vomitingCTSurgical revision if obstruction persists
Bacterial overgrowthBloating, steatorrhea, low B12, normal or high folateBreath test or jejunal aspirate cultureAntibiotics (e.g. rifaximin), treat B12 deficiency
Marginal ulcerPain at gastrojejunal anastomosis; NSAIDs, smokingEndoscopyPPI, stop NSAIDs and smoking

After bariatric surgery, lifelong multivitamin, iron, calcium with vitamin D and B12 supplementation with periodic laboratory monitoring is standard. A patient with persistent vomiting needs thiamine before glucose-containing fluids to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Rapid weight loss also increases gallstone formation.

Esophageal perforation

Suspect it after forceful vomiting, endoscopy or dilation when chest, neck or epigastric pain is followed by fever, tachycardia and crepitus. Chest radiograph may show pneumomediastinum, left pleural effusion or hydropneumothorax. Confirm with CT with oral contrast or a water-soluble contrast esophagram; if water-soluble study is negative and suspicion remains, thin barium can follow because it is more sensitive but causes intense mediastinal inflammation if it leaks. Pleural fluid with food particles, low pH or high (salivary) amylase supports the diagnosis.

Treatment: nothing by mouth, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics with antifungal cover, acid suppression and urgent thoracic surgical consultation. Most spontaneous ruptures with mediastinal or pleural contamination need early operative repair with drainage; small contained iatrogenic leaks in stable patients may be managed nonoperatively or endoscopically. Delay sharply worsens mortality.

Do not order a barium swallow as the first study for suspected perforation, and do not mistake Boerhaave for myocardial infarction or pancreatitis: crepitus, pneumomediastinum and a left effusion after vomiting point to the esophagus.

Blunt abdominal trauma

Start with the primary survey (airway, breathing, circulation with hemorrhage control, disability, exposure). FAST examines the hepatorenal space, splenorenal space, pelvis and pericardium for free fluid. Current trauma care favors early blood products over large volumes of crystalloid in hemeorrhagic shock.

  • Hemodynamically unstable with positive FAST: exploratory laparotomy.
  • Unstable with negative FAST: search other sources (chest, pelvis, long bones, external bleeding); consider repeat FAST or diagnostic peritoneal aspiration.
  • Stable: CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to grade injuries.

Stable patients with splenic or liver injuries are managed nonoperatively with monitoring, serial examinations and hemoglobin checks, with angioembolization for active contrast extravasation. Failure (instability, peritonitis) means surgery. After splenectomy, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b). A child with a handlebar injury and delayed bilious vomiting needs CT; an isolated duodenal hematoma usually resolves with nasogastric decompression and parenteral nutrition, whereas a full-thickness tear needs repair. Consider abuse when the history does not fit the injury.

Penetrating abdominal trauma

Gunshot wounds that traverse the peritoneum usually require laparotomy. For stab wounds, go straight to laparotomy for hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, evisceration, an impaled object (remove it only in the operating room) or GI bleeding. Stable patients without these may be managed selectively with local wound exploration, CT and serial examinations. Update tetanus prophylaxis.

Perforated viscus

Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen suggests perforation. An upright chest radiograph shows free air under the diaphragm (left lateral decubitus film if the patient cannot sit); CT is more sensitive. Management is fluids, antibiotics, IV PPI for ulcer perforation and surgical repair (for a duodenal ulcer, an omental patch), with H. pylori testing and NSAID avoidance afterward.

Ingested foreign bodies

ObjectConcernAction
Button battery in esophagusMucosal burn within hours, fistula, perforation, vascular erosionEmergent endoscopic removal regardless of symptoms
Multiple magnets, or magnet plus metalBowel walls pinched together, fistulaUrgent gastroenterology or surgical removal
Coin in esophagus, asymptomaticMay pass spontaneouslyShort observation and repeat radiograph, or endoscopy
Food bolus impactionInability to handle secretionsUrgent endoscopy; biopsy for eosinophilic esophagitis
Sharp or long objectsPerforationEndoscopic retrieval if within reach

On a frontal radiograph a button battery shows a double-ring (halo) edge, and on lateral view a step-off, which distinguishes it from a coin. Do not induce vomiting. Honey (10 mL every 10 minutes, up to six doses) may be given to children older than 1 year within 12 hours of a suspected esophageal battery ingestion while on the way to endoscopy, and sucralfate may be given in hospital, but neither may delay removal.

Start with the primary survey (airway, breathing, circulation with hemorrhage control, disability, exposure).
examines the hepatorenal space, splenorenal space, pelvis and pericardium for free fluid. Current trauma care favors early blood products over large volumes of crystalloid in hemeorrhagic shock.
: search other sources (chest, pelvis, long bones, external bleeding); consider repeat FAST or diagnostic peritoneal aspiration.
: CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to grade injuries.

Stable patients with splenic or liver injuries are managed nonoperatively with monitoring, serial examinations and hemoglobin checks, with angioembolization for active contrast extravasation. Failure (instability, peritonitis) means surgery. After splenectomy, vaccinate against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b). A child with a handlebar injury and delayed bilious vomiting needs CT; an isolated duodenal hematoma usually resolves with nasogastric decompression and parenteral nutrition, whereas a full-thickness tear needs repair. Consider abuse when the history does not fit the injury.

Gunshot wounds that traverse the peritoneum usually require laparotomy. For stab wounds, go straight to laparotomy for hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, evisceration, an impaled object (remove it only in the operating room) or GI bleeding. Stable patients without these may be managed selectively with local wound exploration, CT and serial examinations. Update tetanus prophylaxis.

Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen suggests perforation. An upright chest radiograph shows free air under the diaphragm (left lateral decubitus film if the patient cannot sit); CT is more sensitive. Management is fluids, antibiotics, IV PPI for ulcer perforation and surgical repair (for a duodenal ulcer, an omental patch), with H. pylori testing and NSAID avoidance afterward.
Mucosal burn within hours, fistula, perforation, vascular erosion
Emergent endoscopic removal regardless of symptoms
Multiple magnets, or magnet plus metal
Short observation and repeat radiograph, or endoscopy
Urgent endoscopy; biopsy for eosinophilic esophagitis

On a frontal radiograph a button battery shows a double-ring (halo) edge, and on lateral view a step-off, which distinguishes it from a coin. Do not induce vomiting. Honey (10 mL every 10 minutes, up to six doses) may be given to children older than 1 year within 12 hours of a suspected esophageal battery ingestion while on the way to endoscopy, and sucralfate may be given in hospital, but neither may delay removal.

s23d-s101001-s2.bodyHtml:
Approach to the vomiting newborn or infant

Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until malrotation with midgut volvulus is excluded. Nonbilious projectile vomiting in a hungry infant of a few weeks suggests pyloric stenosis. Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours suggests Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis).

ConditionClueBest initial testTreatment
Esophageal atresia with distal TEFPolyhydramnios, drooling, choking with first feedRadiograph with tube coiled in pouch; gas in abdomenUpper pouch suction, upright positioning, echocardiogram, surgical repair
Duodenal atresiaTrisomy 21, bilious vomiting on day 1, no distensionRadiograph: double bubble, no distal gasGastric decompression, IV fluids, duodenoduodenostomy
Malrotation with volvulusSudden bilious vomiting in a previously well infantUpper GI series (duodenojejunal junction right of midline)Resuscitation and emergent Ladd procedure
Pyloric stenosisProjectile nonbilious vomiting, weeks old, olive massUltrasound: thick, elongated pylorusCorrect fluids and electrolytes, then pyloromyotomy
Hirschsprung diseaseDelayed meconium, distension, explosive stool after rectal examContrast enema (transition zone); rectal suction biopsy confirmsResection of aganglionic segment with pull-through
Meckel diverticulumPainless rectal bleeding in a toddlerTechnetium-99m pertechnetate scanSurgical resection

Esophageal atresia and tracheesophageal fistula

Prenatal polyhydramnios and a small or absent stomach bubble can suggest the diagnosis. After birth, inability to pass an orogastric tube confirms atresia. Keep the infant upright or prone, suction the upper pouch continuously and avoid feeds. Screen for VACTERL anomalies, particularly with echocardiography (which also identifies aortic arch side before thoracotomy) and renal and spinal ultrasound. Repair divides the fistula and joins the esophageal ends. Later complications include anastomotic stricture, gastresophageal reflux and tracheomalacia.

Duodenal atresia and annular pancreas

Management is nasogastric or orogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolyte correction, and evaluation for associated anomalies (echocardiography in trisomy 21), followed by duodenoduodenostomy. If distal gas is present, malrotation with volvulus must be excluded promptly.

Pyloric stenosis

Ultrasound is the test of choice. Before surgery, correct dehydration with isotonic fluid, then give maintenance fluid with dextrose and add potassium once the infant is voiding. Surgery waits until the alkalosis is corrected because persistent alkalosis is linked to postoperative apnea. Pyloromyotomy is curative. Prevention: avoid macrolides in young infants when an alternative exists.

Pyloromyotomy is never an emergency: rushing a dehydrated, alkalotic infant to anesthesia is the error. Fix volume, potassium and chloride first.

Malrotation with midgut volvulus

Presents with sudden bilious emesis, often in the first month, sometimes with distension, bloody stool and shock as ischemia progresses. A stable infant gets an urgent upper GI contrast study; an unstable infant or one with peritonitis goes directly to the operating room. The Ladd procedure detorses the bowel counterclockwise, divides Ladd bands, widens the mesentery and removes the appendix (because the cecum will lie in the left abdomen).

Abdominal wall defects

FeatureOmphaloceleGastroschisis
LocationMidline, at the umbilicusUsually right of the umbilical cord
SacCovered by amnion and peritoneumNo sac; bowel exposed
Associated anomaliesCommon: trisomies 13 and 18, cardiac defects, Beckwith-WiedemannUncommon; intestinal atresia in some
Immediate careProtect sac, look for associated anomaliesCover bowel in a sterile bowel bag, watch fluid and heat loss

For both, keep the infant warm, decompress the stomach, give IV fluids and arrange surgical repair (primary closure or staged reduction with a silo). Infants with gastroschisis lose large amounts of fluid and heat from exposed bowel. An omphalocele calls for echocardiography and genetic evaluation, and, if Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is suspected, glucose monitoring for neonatal hypoglycemia.

Meckel diverticulum

The classic patient is a child under about 2 years with painless, large-volume, maroon or bright red rectal bleeding. After resuscitation, a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa. Symptomatic diverticula are resected. A Meckel diverticulum found incidentally at surgery in an adult is often left alone.

Hirschsprung disease

Typical history: no meconium by 48 hours, distension and bilious vomiting, or chronic constipation from infancy. Digital rectal exam shows an empty, tight rectum and may release an explosive gush of stool. Contrast enema shows a transition zone; rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells confirms it. The main dangerous complication is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (fever, distension, foul diarrhea), which needs decompression and antibiotics.

Biliary atresia

Any infant still jaundiced at about 2 to 3 weeks needs total and direct bilirubin measured. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acholic stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly is biliary atresia until proved otherwise. Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder and a triangular cord sign; hepatobiliary scintigraphy shows no excretion into the bowel; intraoperative cholangiography confirms the diagnosis. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy restores bile flow best when done early, ideally before about 2 months of age. Many children still progress to cirrhosis, and biliary atresia is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children. Supplement fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and use formulas rich in medium-chain triglycerides.

Breast milk jaundice and physiologic jaundice are unconjugated. A breastfed infant who is jaundiced at 3 weeks with pale stools needs a direct bilirubin today, not reassurance.

Cleft lip and palate

Care is coordinated by a cleft team. Feeding is the first priority: infants with cleft palate cannot generate suction, so they use specialized squeeze bottles or valved nipples and are fed upright; many infants with cleft lip alone can breastfeed. Lip repair is typically done in the first months of life and palate repair within about the first year to 18 months, before speech develops. Watch for otitis media with effusion and hearing loss, speech problems and dental anomalies. An isolated cleft palate with a small mandible suggests Robin sequence, where airway obstruction is the main concern, and should prompt genetic evaluation (for example, 22q11.2 deletion).

s23d-s101101-s2.bodyHtml:
Preventing NSAID ulcers

Risk factors for NSAID-related ulcer complications include prior ulcer or ulcer bleeding (the strongest), older age, high-dose or multiple NSAIDs (including low-dose aspirin), and concurrent anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, glucocorticoids or SSRIs. H. pylori infection adds risk, so test and treat it in patients with an ulcer history before long-term NSAID use.

  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and consider acetaminophen or topical NSAIDs for osteoarthritis.
  • For patients at increased GI risk who need an NSAID, add a proton pump inhibitor. Misoprostol is effective but poorly tolerated (diarrhea) and must be avoided in pregnancy. Standard-dose H2 blockers and sucralfate are inadequate for preventing NSAID gastric ulcers.
  • For the highest GI risk, a COX-2-selective drug plus a PPI is preferred if cardiovascular risk allows, or NSAIDs are avoided.

Opioid-induced constipation

Start a stimulant laxative (senna or bisacodyl), with or without an osmotic agent (polyethylene glycol), whenever scheduled opioids begin. Docusate alone is not effective. If constipation persists despite an adequate laxative regimen, add a PAMORA (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine) after excluding obstruction and fecal impaction. Lubiprostone is an alternative.

Acetaminophen overdose

Symptoms evolve over days: nausea and vomiting or none at first; rising aminotransferases from about the second day with right upper quadrant pain; peak injury around days 3 to 4 with possible coagulopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and acute kidney injury; then recovery or liver failure. Patients may feel well while injury is beginning.

  • Measure a serum acetaminophen level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Levels on or above the treatment line require N-acetylcysteine.
  • The nomogram does not apply to repeated supratherapeutic ingestion or unknown ingestion time; treat these when acetaminophen is detectable or aminotransferases are elevated.
  • NAC is most effective when started within 8 hours of ingestion but still helps when started later, including in established liver failure. If the level will not be available within 8 hours, start NAC empirically.
  • Activated charcoal may be given if the patient presents soon after ingestion and can protect the airway.
  • Check for coingestants (salicylate level, ECG), and after medical stabilization, perform a suicide risk assessment.
  • Severe acidosis, coagulopathy, encephalopathy or renal failure despite therapy prompt referral to a transplant center.

A normal ALT at presentation does not exclude dangerous acetaminophen poisoning: injury lags by a day or more. Treat the level, not the transaminases.

Other drug-induced liver injury

Take a complete history of prescription drugs, over-the-counter products and herbal or dietary supplements, and exclude viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction (ultrasound) and autoimmune disease. Stopping the offending drug is the main treatment.

SituationAction
Isoniazid: symptoms of hepatitis with ALT above 3 times normal, or ALT above 5 times normal without symptomsStop isoniazid; resume or choose another regimen after recovery
Statin: mild asymptomatic aminotransferase riseUsually continue; routine monitoring is not needed after baseline
Methotrexate (long-term)Periodic liver tests, avoid alcohol, folic acid supplementation
Valproate in a young child with vomiting, lethargy or jaundiceStop drug, check liver tests and ammonia
Amiodarone with rising aminotransferasesReassess need, consider dose reduction or discontinuation

Drug-induced pancreatitis

Suspect it when pancreatitis starts after a new drug and gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides and calcium have been excluded. Treat as any acute pancreatitis (fluids, analgesia, early feeding) and stop the drug permanently; for thiopurines, switching to 6-mercaptopurine does not help because both share the same metabolism and risk.

Clostridioides difficile infection

Test only patients with new, unexplained diarrhea (about 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours) who are not taking laxatives, using nucleic acid amplification or a multistep algorithm with toxin testing. Stop the inciting antibiotic when possible and avoid antimotility drugs.

EpisodePreferred treatmentAlternative
Initial, nonsevere or severe (leukocytes at or above 15,000/mm3 or creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL)Oral fidaxomicinOral vancomycin
Fulminant (hypotension, shock, ileus, megacolon)High-dose oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole, rectal vancomycin if ileusEarly surgical consultation, colectomy if needed
First recurrenceFidaxomicinTapered and pulsed oral vancomycin
Multiple recurrencesFecal microbiota transplantation or an approved microbiome productProlonged vancomycin regimens

IV vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen. Infection control uses contact precautions and handwashing with soap and water, because alcohol does not kill spores.

Pill esophagitis

Presents with sudden odynophagia and retrosternal pain after starting a culprit drug. The diagnosis is often clinical; endoscopy (discrete ulcers with normal surrounding mucosa) is for severe or persistent symptoms. Stop or change the drug when possible and counsel patients to take pills upright with a full glass of water and to stay upright afterward. Alendronate must be taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, remaining upright for at least 30 minutes.

Metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists

Metformin GI intolerance is reduced by starting low, titrating slowly, taking it with meals and using the extended-release form. Check vitamin B12 periodically in long-term users, especially those with neuropathy or anemia. GLP-1 receptor agonists cause dose-related nausea, so they are titrated gradually; their slowed gastric emptying is relevant before procedures with sedation.

Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis and hepatitis

  • Exclude infection first (stool studies including C. difficile).
  • Mild diarrhea: continue therapy with close monitoring and hydration, with antidiarrheals after infection is excluded.
  • Moderate to severe colitis: hold the checkpoint inhibitor and start systemic glucocorticoids; give IV steroids for severe disease.
  • No response to steroids within a few days: add infliximab or vedolizumab.
  • Hepatitis: hold for significant aminotransferase rises and give glucocorticoids; mycophenolate is used for refractory cases, and infliximab is avoided because it is itself hepatotoxic.

Do not treat checkpoint-inhibitor colitis with antidiarrheals alone once it is moderate or severe; delaying steroids risks perforation.
